# Craft-cards provenance map

Out-of-runtime maintainer record. Neither consumer receives this file: a card carries the rule, its numbers and a compact `## Source` locator; this map carries the full citation with its fetch status, the topic and research note the card came from, the formulation source where a practitioner text supplied the wording, the reception, and the maintenance notes. Round-trip rule: a card plus its line here plus its topic's research note reconstruct everything known about the rule.

One line per card: `rule_id · evidence citation(s) with fetch status and the quoted statement · topic (research note) · formulation source · reception · notes` (evidence strength, ownership, caveats).

Fetch status per citation, as the design note's source policy defines it: `fetched` — opened from the authoring environment and quoted; **relayed** — the search index's statement of the claim, quoted, the paper itself unopened; **unfetched** — cited from memory, never a card's only anchor. A relayed or unfetched citation is openable by any reader and stands to be re-verified.

---
## CODE — code inside a function
- **CODE-01** · PMD, Java rule `LinguisticNaming`, category codestyle, since 6.7.0 (pmd/pmd, pmd-java/src/main/resources/category/java/codestyle.xml, rule description; defaults in pmd-java/src/main/java/net/sourceforge/pmd/lang/java/rule/codestyle/LinguisticNamingRule.java: booleanMethodPrefixes and booleanFieldPrefixes is, has, can, have, will, should; transformMethodNames to, as; checkTransformMethods false; checkFields and checkVariables true; ignoredAnnotations java.lang.Override; checkSetters skips a setter whose return type is the enclosing type; isBooleanType accepts an unboxed boolean, java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicBoolean and java.util.function.Predicate; the constructor registers only method, field and local-variable declarations, `super(ASTMethodDeclaration.class, ASTFieldDeclaration.class, ASTLocalVariableDeclaration.class)`, so formal parameters are never checked; commented out of rulesets/java/quickstart.xml), fetched: "This rule finds Linguistic Naming Antipatterns. It checks for fields, that are named, as if they should be boolean but have a different type. It also checks for methods, that according to their name, should return a boolean, but don't. Further, it checks, that getters return something and setters won't. Finally, it checks that methods, that start with "to" - so called transform methods - actually return something, since according to their name, they should convert or transform one object into another. There is additionally an option, to check for methods that contain "To" in their name - which are also transform methods. However, this is disabled by default, since this detection is prone to false positives." · SCANL Identifier Name Structure Catalogue (SCANL/identifier_name_structure_catalogue, README.md § Linguistic Antipatterns), fetched, reproducing the catalogue of Arnaoudova, Di Penta, Antoniol, 'Linguistic antipatterns: what they are and how developers perceive them', Empirical Software Engineering 21(1):104–158, 2016, DOI 10.1007/s10664-014-9350-8 (**relayed**): "Is returns more than a Boolean [...] the return type is not Boolean but rather a more complex type thus allowing a wider range of values without documenting them. [...] Set method returns [...] A set method having a return type different than void without proper documentation of the return type/values. [...] Expecting but not getting single instance [...] The name of a method indicates that a single object is returned but the return type is a collection. [...] Validation method does not confirm [...] the method neither provides a return value informing whether the validation was successful, nor documents how to proceed to understand. [...] Get method does not return [...] The name suggests that the method returns something (e.g., name starts with "get" or "return") but the return type is void. The documentation should explain where the resulting data is stored and how to obtain it. [...] Not answered question [...] The name of a method is in the form of predicate whereas the return type is not Boolean. [...] Transform method does not return [...] there is no return value and it is not clear from the documentation where the result is stored. [...] Expecting but not getting a collection [...] The name of a method suggests that a collection should be returned but a single object or nothing is returned. [...] Method name and return type are opposite [...] The intent of the method suggested by its name is in contradiction with what it returns. [...] Says one but contains many [...] It is unclear whether a change aspects one or multiple instances in the collection. [...] Name suggests boolean but type is not [...] The name of an attribute suggests that its value is true or false, but its declaring type is not Boolean. [...] Says many but contains one [...] The name of an attribute suggests multiple instances, but its type suggests a single one. [...] Attribute name and type are opposite [...] The use of antonyms can induce wrong assumptions." · Eclipse JFace `ControlEnableState.disable`, the catalogue's example of Method name and return type are opposite (eclipse-platform/eclipse.platform.ui, bundles/org.eclipse.jface/src/org/eclipse/jface/dialogs/ControlEnableState.java, master), fetched, documented in its source: "Saves the current enable/disable state of the given control and its descendents in the returned object; the controls are all disabled. [...] @return an object capturing the enable/disable state" · the same paper, abstract (Google Scholar snippet in a third-party crawl, AndresPonciano/finalprojectforsure data/elasticsearchScripts/data_finalfiles_ndjson/GIULIANOANTONIOL.json, **relayed**): "The aim of this work is to identify recurring poor practices related to inconsistencies among the naming, documentation, and implementation of an entity—called Linguistic Antipatterns (LAs)—that may impair program understanding. To this end, we first mine examples of such inconsistencies in real open-source projects and abstract them into a catalog of 17 recurring LAs related to methods and attributes." · the same paper, abstract, perception results (search-summary relay naming https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10664-014-9350-8, **relayed**): "Results showed that the majority of participants perceive LAs as poor practices and therefore must be avoided—69% and 51% of the external and internal developers, respectively." — the qualitative majority is also relayed by Peruma, Mkaouer, Decker, Newman, 'An empirical investigation of how and why developers rename identifiers', IWoR 2018, DOI 10.1145/3242163.3242169 (full-text copy in stefanik12/gensim_lda, **relayed**): "finding that the majority of programmers perceive anti-patterns as poor naming practices" · Fakhoury, Ma, Arnaoudova, Adesope, 'The Effect of Poor Source Code Lexicon and Readability on Developers' Cognitive Load', ICPC 2018, pp. 286–296, DOI 10.1145/3196321.3196347 (abstract from an IEEE Xplore metadata mirror, NicolasV15/CIRDC-Pro articleInfo/Conferences/1003168/8961319.json; DOI from BibSLEIGH, bibtex/bibtex.github.io ICPC-2018-FakhouryMAA.html; **relayed**): "we explore the effect of poor source code lexicon and readability on developers' cognitive load as measured by a cutting-edge and minimally invasive functional brain imaging technique called functional Near Infrared Spectroscopy (fNIRS). PoP1 §1.1 Names, 'Be accurate' (the inTable example); Clean Code ch. 2 'Avoid Disinformation' (accountList that is not a List); APOSD ch. 14 §14.3 'Names should be precise' (paraphrase, **unfetched**) · reception: not contested · notes: confidence moderate — the defect definitions are fetched and a static-analysis rule enforces the predicate, get, set and conversion cases, while the cost rests on two relayed abstracts (one developer survey, one fNIRS study); the perception search could not be re-run in the first drafting session (search budget exhausted), and the 69%/51% figures, from a search relay neither the drafter nor the skeptic could re-run verbatim, are not carried in the card; the card carries the qualitative majority from the Peruma et al. copy; in an earlier revision WebSearch answered twice with a summary restating the figures ("69% and 51% of the external and internal developers, respectively"; "69% of the external developers and 51% of the internal developers") without naming the result that carries the sentence, and a search restricted to link.springer.com did not state them, so the figures stay out; the catalogue's examples and the tool rule are Java; the card flags a subset of the catalogue: it accepts a documented mismatch in every case but the antonym rows, although Not answered question and the plurality rows carry no documentation clause; the antonym rows are excepted because the catalogue's own example, ControlEnableState.disable, is documented in its source (eclipse-platform/eclipse.platform.ui ControlEnableState.java, fetched; the comment is already present at tags R2_1 and R3_0); it reaches no parameter, since the catalogue covers methods and attributes and the static-analysis rule registers only method, field and local-variable declarations; it reads the plurality and antonym cases on fields, properties and routines only; number is read only in a noun phrase that names what a field or property holds or what a routine returns, alone or after get or return, since the catalogue's method rows condition on what the name says is returned; a noun phrase ending in a container word counts as plural, the reading the container-word pattern dispatches; a promise, future or task is read as the value it resolves to (TS1065 forces Promise<boolean> on an async predicate and Promise<T[]> on an async plural getter), and a set routine may return only a promise, error or result that carries nothing; dispatch gap: no pattern matches an antonym pair, a plural name on a single value or a collection type written without its element type (demonstrated by the skeptic with the corpus pre-pass on the catalogue's own examples), and a pattern for them would match no line of the Example, which is at its ten-line cap, so the Limits state the gap; the container-word pattern accepts PascalCase names so exported Go fields and C# properties dispatch; the behaviour-level and comment-level rows (Get more than accessor, Not implemented condition, Method signature and comment are opposite, Attribute signature and comment are opposite) are left to the routine-behaviour and comments topics; clippy wrong_self_convention was dropped because it checks how a conversion method takes its receiver, not its return type or plurality.

The Practice of Programming ch. 1 §1.1 Names, "Be accurate" (inTable returning true when the object is not in the table; paraphrase, **unfetched**) and "Use active names for functions"; Clean Code ch. 17 heuristic N7 "Names Should Describe Side-Effects" (getOos → createOrReturnOos, the source of the get-or-create wording); The Pragmatic Programmer 20th anniversary ed., Topic 44 "Naming Things", Tip 74 "Name Well; Rename When Needed" (the body changed under an unchanged name); johnousterhout/aposd-vs-clean-code README, "Method Length" (fetched: "If a reader trusts the name `isMultipleOfNthPrimeFactor` (which suggests a predicate with no side effects) and doesn't bother to read its code, they will not realize that it has side effects") · reception: not contested — in the same discussion the Clean Code author concedes the buried side effect ("Now that you've pointed it out I don't like it much"); no canon text defends a query-named routine that hides a write · notes: confidence moderate; the fetched evidence is normative official documentation from five languages (Swift and Python bind a name to its effect; Kotlin, Ruby and Julia name the mutating and copying forms of a pair apart, Ruby and Julia by marking the mutating form) plus one default-on lint whose reach is narrow (a getter returning a different field when a same-named field exists), and the research is relayed from abstracts and a catalogue, measuring cognitive load (fNIRS) and stating comprehension effort and wrong assumptions as the expected cost, not defect rates, so the severity rests on the lint's "most likely a bug" and the measured load; the predicate-truth clause rests on the relayed antipattern definition and the Boolean-assertion guideline, with no dedicated tool rule; the getter clause follows the lint's shape (another field returned where a same-named field exists), so a getter that returns a copy of, or a value computed from, its own field writes nothing and passes, and the catalogued getImageData example counts through its field write (this.imageData = new ImageData(...)); find, fetch and compute are left out of the query forms: no fetched or relayed text names them as words that promise no write; count is left to how it reads, as a noun accessor (which the lint reaches: clippy fires on fn count(&self) -> &u32 { &self.total } when a count field exists) or as a verb, and the cited guideline gives imperative verb phrases to routines with side effects; the documentation exemption reaches a get accessor only, following the fuller relayed row, while noun-phrase, predicate and conversion names are held to the name alone, since the Swift side-effect rule and the PEP 8 property note carry no documentation clause; the card does not carry the EMSE 2016 perception percentages (the relayed abstract is truncated before them), the "does more than it says / does the opposite" family names (not in any relayed text), the PoP inTable example (unfetched paraphrase), or Rust API guidelines C-CONV (fetched, but it states the cost and ownership of as_/to_/into_, not their side effects); the cache exemption follows PEP 8, while the log-line and interface-fixed-name bounds in Limits follow from the card's own definition of observable state, and so does the read bound, which passes a read that leaves its source unchanged and counts a consuming read from a held stream, queue or iterator as a write, as the fetched Julia style guide states for IO ('`read(io)` mutates `io`'); the self/this field-write and mutating-call triggers and the statement-level write trigger (a bare, @-prefixed or receiver-qualified name incremented or compound-assigned, or an @-prefixed or receiver-qualified field assigned) run on most object-oriented diffs by design, to reach a body changed under an unchanged name; a plain assignment to, or a mutating call on, an implicit-receiver field (count = 0; items.add(x);) is reached only when another added line of its hunk matches, since no pattern tells it from a local without matching every assignment; the query-word pattern also takes the bare word (get(, Get(, has(), and the accessor pattern takes property-accessor syntax (get {, get =>, get() =, Name =>, a computed var name: Type {)

Words over letters: the two letters-versus-words experiments above, the C# conventions, the Google Python guide, clang-tidy and clippy. Letters are fine: Beniamini et al. 2017, Go Code Review Comments ('Prefer c to lineCount'), the Google TypeScript guide (10-line tolerance), Linux kernel coding style, and the neverworkintheory review (2021-08-09), which calls the 19% difference "fairly small" and "not worth worrying about". The card resolves the dispute with two sourced conditions: whether the letter is conventional in its role, and whether a documented language or project convention allows short local names · notes: confidence moderate. Two experiments that compared letters with words found words better; the timed one found a modest 19% effect on finding semantic defects, none on finding syntax errors, in snippets in which every identifier used one style, and it counts speed, not defect rates. A third, Beniamini et al. 2017, gave single letters to local variables of limited scope or to substantial variables representing data structures (relayed: WebSearch summary of https://www.cs.huji.ac.il/w~feit/papers/SingleLetter17ICPC.pdf) and failed to show a significant difference in ability to modify the code; the card carries that result as the bound of the measured cost, not as support for conventional letters. Schankin et al. 2018 (DOI 10.1145/3196321.3196332) is not carried: its conditions were short single-word and long descriptive compound names (Table 1), so it compares words with phrases, which the Limits put outside the rule. Pylint's `good-names` default (i, j, k, ex, Run, _) was re-fetched but is not carried: Pylint's default snake_case regex `[^\W\dA-Z][^\WA-Z]*$` already accepts one-letter names, so the list is not an exemption in practice. The card lists no role for n: clang-tidy and clippy exempt n with no role, the Google TypeScript guide lists `n` as "Meaningless" among disallowed identifiers, and the Google C++ guide admits `int n = 0;` only with "limited scope and context", which the documented-tolerance condition covers. ESLint `id-length` (min 2, no default exceptions, flags a caught `e`) is not carried because it exempts no conventional letter by default. The EMSE 2019 extension of Hofmeister et al. (DOI 10.1007/s10664-018-9621-x, cited from memory) and Scanniello et al. 2017 (abbreviations, not letters) are not carried. Lambda and closure parameters are triggered by their arrow, bar, lambda-keyword and in-closure forms. The Lawrie and Beniamini abstracts are relayed by WebSearch summaries and match the GitHub-hosted IEEE metadata mirror; the Hofmeister full text is fetched from the authors' GitHub Pages repository.

The Rationale says look-alike identifiers "can render identically", not that they look alike in every font: the confusables skeleton also joins pairs a careful reader tells apart (m and rn, mathematical bold f and f). The card takes `triggers: []` and reads every hunk, because no added-line pattern marks two names one character apart. The Unicode clause reaches one file, the card's scope, though rustc compares a whole crate and clang-tidy a translation unit, and it covers pairs in which one identifier holds a non-ASCII character, as rustc's `confusable_idents` does. Checked by hand: clippy with `-W clippy::pedantic` and with `-W clippy::similar_names` flags the Example's `row_recs`/`row_reps` pair and raises no naming lint on the good half; clippy 1.94 with `-W clippy::similar_names` flags `splunk`/`splonk`, `checked_exp`/`checked_eap`, `orange`/`ornange`, `pos_x_max`/`pos_y_max`, `page1_total`/`page12_total`, `rows`/`rrows` and `lines`/`ilines`, and not `row`/`rows`, `page1`/`page2`, `pos_x`/`pos_y`, `x_pos`/`y_pos`, `lhs`/`rhs`, `iter`/`item`, `parsed`/`parser` or `args`/`arms`; rustc warns `confusable_idents` on a Latin/Cyrillic `total` pair; the good half compiles with rustc 1.94.1 --emit=metadata. Not carried: clang-tidy's comparison of all-ASCII pairs through the confusables skeleton (`comer`/`corner`, `row_ll`/`row_l1`), which rustc does not report; clippy's skip of `#[test]` functions, of names containing an uppercase letter and of names beginning with an underscore (Rust conventions, not the misreading mechanism); rustc's `mixed_script_confusables` and `uncommon_codepoints` single-identifier lints; the type-parameter case, which the letter-check sources do not name, so Limits bounds it out. SonarSource's RSPEC-1479 text for Java, Go, PHP, JavaScript and Kotlin calls a switch with a large set of cases usually an attempt to map two sets of data and asks for a map. Its C# and VB.NET rule reports a switch above the same thirty only when a case clause holds more than one statement. Its text holds that a switch whose case clauses are all single-line keeps its readability, and it fixes a multi-line clause by extracting it into a method, which leaves a switch whose cases each return a value or call one routine. No fetched source separates the two positions, so the card leaves every switch and match outside the rule and states both positions in its Limits. Ruff classes its own SIM116 as pedantic ("highly opinionated or prone to false positives"); the card names that classification in its Limits as a project tolerance. · notes: confidence moderate. The evidence is a standard's description with no threshold (SWEBOK §4.7) and one tool rule written for one language (Ruff SIM116), bounded below by PMD TooFewBranchesForSwitch; the two RSPEC-1479 texts are cited for the Limits only. No study measuring table-driven code against conditional chains was found: the topic's search of the neverworkintheory and papers-we-love bibliographies found none, Vessey and Weber (CACM 29(1), 1986) and Pooch, "Translation of decision tables" (ACM Computing Surveys 6(2), 1974) could not be opened, and Harel (1987) and Heninger (1980) concern statecharts and requirements tables, not this claim. WebSearch was unavailable in this run. The three-branch count is a tool default and comes from a Python rule. Not carried, for want of a separating condition: a switch, a match or an if/else-if chain of more than thirty non-empty cases over a non-enumerated key, and a table of routines for a selection whose cases each call one routine. They rested on the Java and Go text of RSPEC-1479 and on two Python sources, the Design and History FAQ, "Why isn't there a switch or case statement in Python?" ("For cases where you need to choose from a very large number of possibilities, you can create a dictionary mapping case values to functions to call."; fetched from `python/cpython` main, `Doc/faq/design.rst`) and PEP 275 "Switching on Multiple Values" (2001, Rejected), §Problem ("This works well for state machines which require complex and lengthy processing in the different case methods. It does not perform well for ones which only process one or two instructions per case"; fetched from `python/peps` main, `peps/pep-0275.rst`); the C# and VB.NET text of RSPEC-1479 contests both. Not carried either: Code Complete's direct, indexed and stair-step access (formulation only). Range lookup, table-miss handling and closing a handler table against reflective dispatch are other rules of the topic. The Java example's good half compiles with javac 21 under `import java.util.Map`. The triggers keep the research spine's two chain patterns, the first without its end anchor, and add string-equality chains; the spine's case and match-arm patterns go with the thirty-case clause.

The run-time failures the card carries are the two that depend on reach (the member reached is not a function; an inherited standard method is called with the wrong arguments); the failure on a name with no entry, which the qhelp also names, is not carried, because the forms the card accepts (a closed table, a fixed prefix) also fail on such a name and its handling is left out of the rule. The validator passes an own-entry check only on a table that holds only the handlers, as the CodeQL help ("At the very least, check that the method is an own property") allows for its `actions` table. It does not pass one on the global object, a module namespace or a general object: for the global object the CodeQL `js/unsafe-dynamic-method-access` help gives only an allowlist or a change of the object the methods are stored on, the Semgrep `dangerous-globals-use` rule has no exemption for a membership check, and `eval` and `Function` are own properties of the global object (checked in Node 21). The Semgrep `unsafe-dynamic-method` exemption, which accepts a `hasOwnProperty` guard on any object, is not followed there. Scope kept to the selection of a method or function: class instantiation by a computed name (`Class.forName`), the pattern of the Semgrep `unsafe-reflection` rule itself, is stated in the Limits as outside the rule and is not triggered or judged, although that rule's message covers method invocation too. The prefix allowance rests on the FAQ's statement about methods on one object and is not extended to a module or global namespace, where the sources give an allowlist, a map or code that stops indexing the namespace; the getattr, getMethod and MethodByName triggers skip only a name argument that is a whole string literal, and the getattr trigger accepts a subscripted first argument such as sys.modules[__name__], so a prefixed name and a lookup among the current module's functions still reach the finder. The finder works at scope hunk, so a key whose untrusted origin the hunk does not show is not flagged. The table's default entry and the handling of a missing key are left out of the rule. In a language with no lookup of a member by a runtime name only the table form exists. Fetched but not cited: the OWASP www-community page "Unsafe use of Reflection" (a community wiki page outside the admissible classes; its command-dispatcher example shows a `Class.forName(ctl + "Command")` refactoring that "allows an attacker to instantiate any object that implements the Worker interface"), the experimental CodeQL `java/unsafe-reflection` query help, and eslint-plugin-security `detect-object-injection` (flags every bracket access and does not state the reach claim). Formulation: the topic's canon locator, Code Complete 2nd ed. §18.1 (a table entry that stores a reference to the routine implementing the action; unfetched), is not named as the formulation because the openable FAQ carries the same formulation; R. Pike, "Notes on Programming in C" §"Function pointers" was not opened from this environment and is not named either

Nichols, The Rust Programming Language, ch. 18.3 "Implementing an Object-Oriented Design Pattern": requirements "A blog post starts as an empty draft." and "Only published blog posts return content to print so that unapproved posts can’t accidentally be published."; "Any other changes attempted on a post should have no effect. For example, if we try to approve a draft blog post before we’ve requested a review, the post should remain an unpublished draft."; "we call an internal `request_review` method on the current state of `Post`, and this second `request_review` method consumes the current state and returns a new state"; "when we request a review on a post already in the `PendingReview` state, it should stay in the `PendingReview` state"; "if we call the `approve` method on a `Draft`, it will have no effect because `approve` will return `self`"; "we might instead use `match` expressions in the methods on `Post` or even in the `main` code that checks the state of the post and changes behavior in those places"; § Encoding States and Behavior as Types: "Rather than encapsulating the states and transitions completely so that outside code has no knowledge of them, we’ll encode the states into different types. (fetched from `rust-lang/book` main, `src/ch18-03-oo-design-patterns.md`). The Embedded Rust Book, Static Guarantees: "Peripherals as State Machines": "this would allow us to modify certain registers that do not make sense. For some hardware, this may not matter. On other hardware, it could cause unexpected or undefined behavior!"; "Although this interface is convenient to write, it doesn't enforce the design contracts set out by our hardware implementation."; "Design Contracts": "If we instead checked the state before making use of the underlying hardware, enforcing our design contracts at runtime", with setters that `return Err(());` under the comments "Must be enabled to set direction", "Must be enabled to set input mode", "Direction must be input" and "Direction must be output" before `self.periph.modify(...)`, while `set_enable` carries no check; "Because we need to enforce the restrictions on the hardware, we end up doing a lot of runtime checking which wastes time and resources, and this code will be much less pleasant for the developer to use."; § Compile Time Functional Safety: "Because we are enforcing our design constraints entirely at compile time, this incurs no runtime cost."; "there is no runtime penalty due to checking the current state before executing a function"; "If they try to perform an illegal state transition, the code will not compile!" (fetched from `rust-embedded/book` master, `src/static-guarantees/state-machines.md` and `design-contracts.md`). Hands-on, not cited in the card: javac 21.0.10 with `-Xlint:all` compiles the Example's good half without warnings inside `class Order { enum Status { IN_PROGRESS, PAID, SHIPPED } private Status status = Status.IN_PROGRESS; ... }`; run, it refuses `ship()` in IN_PROGRESS ("cannot ship an order in state IN_PROGRESS", status unchanged) and in SHIPPED, and ships after `pay()`, while the bad half ships an unpaid order (local run under /tmp/craft-research; not openable until committed under the skill's `evals/fixture/`). · topic: table-driven-and-state-machines (research/software-craft/table-driven-and-state-machines.md) · formulation: N. Nilsson, "Thinking in States", 97 Things Every Programmer Should Know, thing 84, the paragraph after the order's three states ("These states are important and you need to check that you're in the expected state before doing operations, and that you only move to a legal state from where you are. In short, you have to protect your objects carefully, in the right places.") and final paragraph ("If your state is incorrect, there's a bug and you risk trashing data if you don't abort.") (opened from `97-things/97-things-every-programmer-should-know` master, `en/thing_84/README.md`); D. Thomas and A. Hunt, The Pragmatic Programmer 20th anniv. ed., Topic 29 (an event with no entry in the transition table moves the machine to an explicit error state; not opened); S. Wlaschin, "Designing with types: Making state explicit" (2013), state-by-event table with disallowed cells marked n/a (not opened) · reception: not contested · notes: confidence moderate. The evidence is documentation, not measurement: standard libraries of Java, Python and Go refuse an operation the current state does not allow, by an exception, a panic or a false result; the Rust book's workflow specifies documented no-ops for its illegal pairs and shows dispatch to the current state's handler and branching on the state as the two run-time forms of the check; the Embedded Rust Book shows unchecked setters reaching states the machine does not define, with "unexpected or undefined behavior" on some hardware only, the run-time check returning an error, and the type-encoded alternative. No study measuring defects from unchecked state changes was found (WebSearch budget exhausted; no GitHub-hosted paper located). The card's title says "refused" where the spine said "refused with an error", since the evidence also shows a refusal reported by a returned result (`Future.cancel` returning False, the GPIO setters returning `Err(())`). The concurrent.futures `Future` is a type shared between threads; it is cited only for its refusal semantics, and the card keeps thread-shared state machines out of scope. The rule every-state-event-pair-decided is folded into the Thesis's third sentence. Not carried as claims: the Pragmatic Programmer's error state for an unlisted event (unopened); what a transition-table lookup yields for a pair without an entry, owned by the table-miss card and present here only as a Validator check; an object found in an impossible state, owned by ERR-06 and named in the Limits only as excluded scope; the last Limits sentence is the topic's ownership scope, not an evidence claim. The type-encoded form is described in the Limits without naming a language and is conditioned on the transition consuming the old state's value, as the Rust book states, since a language that lets a caller keep the old state's value keeps the illegal call possible. Triggers: one pattern, an assignment to a name ending in state, status, phase or stage (receiver-qualified or bare), which matches the Example's bad half.

the card's Example good half compiles, runs, and type-checks clean under both · topic: table-driven-and-state-machines (research/software-craft/table-driven-and-state-machines.md) · formulation: Error Prone MissingCasesInEnumSwitch ("Switches on enum types should either handle all values, or have a default case") and typescript-eslint switch-exhaustiveness-check ("if the union type or the enum changes, it's easy to forget to modify the cases to account for any new types"), cited above, whose wording the Thesis and Rationale follow (openable) · reception: not contested. Tool defaults differ on whether a default branch stands in for a named member. typescript-eslint (considerDefaultExhaustiveForUnions false) and exhaustive (without -d) still report a missing member when a default is present. Error Prone MissingCasesInEnumSwitch, PMD NonExhaustiveSwitch and the Google Java Style Guide accept a default. The anchors are three Java checks or style rules, one TypeScript and one Go checker, and the language specifications and official documentation of Python, Go, TypeScript, Rust and Java for which constructs fall out silently and which are compiler-checked. They document the practice and its reason; no empirical study measures failures from a missing member. Error Prone is WARNING severity; typescript-eslint's rule needs type information and is in neither the recommended nor the strict preset. The Go FAQ entry on variant types was dropped because it says nothing about switch exhaustiveness. The Go claim that a named integer type can hold values outside its constants (hands-on label(State(42)) = "?") was also dropped: only the unopenable local check states it, and it bears on whether a fully covered switch keeps a default, which another rule of the topic owns. What a default does with a value believed impossible, and whether a default on an already-exhaustive switch is kept, are left to their own cards. A table or map lookup that misses a member (hands-on: a Go map and a Java EnumMap return the zero value or null) belongs to the topic's table-completeness rule.

One side wants a default in every switch: Checkstyle MissingSwitchDefault, the Google TypeScript Style Guide, and SonarSource S131 for Go, which has no enumeration exception. The other side wants no catch-all default on a checked exhaustive switch: Error Prone UnnecessaryDefaultInEnumSwitch, typescript-eslint switch-exhaustiveness-check with allowDefaultCaseForExhaustiveSwitch: false, and rust-clippy wildcard_enum_match_arm. The Google C++ Style Guide states neither position: it exempts a switch on an enumerated value from its default requirement because the compiler warns about unhandled values, and asks that a default that should never execute be treated as an error. Every tool rule on the no-default side is opt-in: UnnecessaryDefaultInEnumSwitch is among Error Prone's disabled checks, allowDefaultCaseForExhaustiveSwitch defaults to true, and clippy's two lints are restriction and pedantic. The separating condition is whether a value outside the compiled-against members can reach the switch at run time. It is sourced in Error Prone's 'When the default can be removed' and 'Library skew', typescript-eslint's allowDefaultCaseForExhaustiveSwitch Caveats, the Rust Reference's non_exhaustive attribute and the mypy documentation. Checkstyle MissingSwitchDefault and sonar-java S131 themselves exempt compiler-checked switch expressions and pattern switches, and enum switches that use every constant · notes: confidence moderate. Static-analysis rule pages, language documentation and style guides agree on the mechanism, and no source measures a defect rate. The binary-compatibility argument is Java's (the Error Prone page cites JLS §13.4.26, **unfetched**, docs.oracle.com denied), so the card states it conditionally ("where adding a member does not force dependent code to be recompiled") and asks, for the library case, that the dependency can be upgraded beneath the switch without its exhaustiveness being checked again. The fall-through precondition and the no-report case for a default whose removal breaks compilation are Error Prone's own; the Rationale's exception for a language that raises on an unmatched value rests on the MatchException Javadoc (JLS §14.11.3 and §15.28.2, which it cites, **unfetched**). Step is implement and refactor: the rule concerns code inside a switch, not the shape of the change. Hands-on checks, none a card anchor: tsc 6.0.2 --strict compiles the Example's good half inside `function weight(state: "open" | "closed"): number` and fails it with TS2366 once a third member is added, while the bad half compiles silently in both versions; the good half protects only where the function declares its return type. javac/java 21: with a Lib compiled against `Color { RED, GREEN }` and run with BLUE added, the statement switch fell out and returned -1 while the default-less switch expression threw java.lang.MatchException; an enum switch whose cases all return draws "missing return statement" and compiles with `throw new AssertionError(s);` after it; a case falling into the default gave 12 with the default and 2 once it was removed. go vet reports "missing return" for the same Go switch over iota constants. rustc 1.94.1 warns "unreachable pattern" on a `_` arm after every variant of a local enum; the skeptic's rustc 1.97.0 run (not repeated here) showed that a Rust library built against one version of a dependency does not link with a newer one (E0460) and that recompiling reports the uncovered variant (E0004). The TypeScript handbook's never default returns rather than raises, so the card's raising form rests on typing.assert_never, Error Prone MissingCasesInEnumSwitch and the Google C++ guide. non_exhaustive_omitted_patterns is allow-by-default and feature-gated, which is why the card does not flag a counted wildcard that the language forces where no check sees through it. The Go exhaustive analyzer is a third-party tool, cited for the Go mechanism only. The card does not carry a default that deliberately groups members a switch leaves unnamed, because tool defaults split on it: Error Prone MissingCasesInEnumSwitch and rustc accept it, typescript-eslint by default and the exhaustive analyzer report it, and clippy reports it only in restriction and pedantic. Nor does it carry the default, fallthrough and form of a switch over a non-enumerated value, which belong to control flow

The rule rests on style-guide, language-reference and tool-rule documentation that agrees across the Go, Java, TypeScript and C++ guidance. There is no empirical study and no measured defect rate, so the severity is minor. The constant clause follows the Go guide, whose constants are compile-time values. The card therefore limits it to a constant whose value is a literal or a constant expression, in a language with a constant declaration usable inside a routine. In a language whose constants are module-level names by convention, the constant stays at module level, and that is the condition separating the Go and Python positions. A value built at run time, such as a compiled regular expression, a constructed collection or a formatter, stays at class or module level. The Sonar rule states the compile cost for java.util.regex.Pattern only, and Python's re module caches recently compiled patterns, so the Limits say a routine-local declaration "can" rebuild the value, not that it always does. The private-field clause follows PMD SingularField, which checks only private fields and ignores threading; the card's concurrency limit covers the threading gap. A variable, field or module-level variable that carries a value from one loop iteration or routine call to the next stays outside that loop body or routine. SingularField converts a field only when every method assigns it before reading it. ES.6's remedy is the for-statement initializer, which runs once. A Rust let binding's scope ends at the end of its block, where it is dropped. The resource-retention cost is stated for languages where leaving a scope releases resources, as Rust's destructors do. Go runs deferred calls when the surrounding function returns, so narrowing a block there does not move a deferred release. The example is in Rust and uses the Go guide's own constant case. Triggers: three patterns. One matches all-caps constant declarations, one matches column-zero declarations, and one matches declaration lines at any indentation (const, let or var; a short variable declaration; a private or protected field declared without an initializer). Each matches the Rust bad-half line const RETRY_LIMIT: u32 = 3;. A typed local declaration without a keyword has no trigger. Not carried: declaring a variable close to its first use and initializing it at declaration, which are a separate rule of the topic; mutability of module-level state (mutable-state-and-immutability); shadowing; naming (naming-identifiers); and the trade-off in 'Comments on Minimizing Scope' between convenient access and intellectual manageability, which is unfetched.

The side that holds related or intentional shadowing legitimate is the Rust book ch. 3.1, clippy's shadow lints (restriction group, allow by default), the golang/tools shadow analyzer (outside the go vet suite, not enabled by default, "too many false positives"), the TypeScript Handbook and Google Go best practices ("Intentional shadowing can be a useful practice"). The card separates them by whether the outer entity is still needed after the declaration, using the shadow analyzer's span heuristic and Google Go decisions on import renaming. Built-in names are a second contested point: Uber Go, Ruff A001, ESLint no-shadow-restricted-names and Pylint W0622 flag them, while the shadow analyzer calls universe-scope shadowing "fine". The card flags a built-in only where the scope still needs it · notes: confidence moderate. All anchors are fetched style-guide, language-documentation and tool-rule texts, and no measured study backs the rule, so the card carries no rate. The after-the-block bug is evidenced in Go (Google Go best practices; the shadow analyzer's BadRead), the field case in Java (S1117, HiddenField) and the built-in case in Go, Python and JavaScript. The card generalizes these mechanisms, as the Source caveat states. The card narrows the spine's wording in five ways. (1) The spine title's "unless it deliberately rebinds a closely related value" is dropped from the title, because Google Go's buggy ctx example is a closely related rebinding that is still a defect: code after the block needs it. The related-rebinding exemption is carried in the Thesis's last sentence and in Limits, bounded by "no code after the declaration needing the original". (2) An unrelated rebinding whose outer entity nothing needs afterwards is not carried as a standalone defect. clippy shadow_unrelated (opt-in) says it "may indicate a mistake", and the shadow analyzer's span heuristic calls it "inconsequential". No sourced condition separates the two, so the card leaves it outside and lets a project context that adopts such a check hold code to it. (3) Reusing a built-in name where the scope never needs the built-in is likewise left outside, on the shadow analyzer's comment against Uber, Ruff and ESLint restricted names. (4) The shadow analyzer's same-type restriction is not carried; the card applies the still-needed condition whatever the types and says so in Limits. (5) The after-scope read is bounded to the same routine in the title, the Thesis and the validator question, the span the evidence shows (Google Go's ctx block, the shadow analyzer's BadRead loop); a routine-level local named like a module-level variable that later module code reads is not flagged. On the separate exemptions: the pytest-fixture case rests on Pylint's details.rst, which calls the warning "a common issue" and offers renaming the fixture or a plugin, not a blanket exemption. The constructor/setter-parameter case rests on S1117's implementation excluding parameters and on HiddenField's opt-in options (default false). Triggers: the spine's short-declaration pattern is widened from nested blocks to routine depth and to if, switch and for headers. Google Go's `url :=` package shadow sits at routine depth, and the Go specification (golang/go doc/go_spec.html, fetched) says "Each "if", "for", and "switch" statement is considered to be in its own implicit block." The Go built-in pattern also matches `var` declarations and parameters (Uber Go's `var error string` and `func handleErrorMessage(error string)`). The Python built-in pattern also matches a plain name binding indented at routine depth. A typed-local pattern (Java/C-family types, `var`) dispatches the Java example. A `let`/`const` binding pattern, at routine depth and in a for header, covers TypeScript, JavaScript and Rust. Share of code lines the six patterns match, over Go net/http, strings and encoding/json, 80 CPython 3.13 standard-library modules, six java.base classes (jdk-21-ga), eight rust-lang/rust and ripgrep files and five VS Code TypeScript files: Go 8.6%, Python 17.0%, Java 8.7%, Rust 9.7%, TypeScript 10.4%. The drafted five matched 2.2%, 0.2%, 8.3%, 0.0% and 0.0%. Both example halves were compiled with javac -Xlint:all (javac 21) under /tmp/craft-research/vsn-code03-drafter2/ex: the good half compiles, and the bad half also compiles with no warning, which illustrates the silent defect; after add({1,2,3}) and add({10}) the good half's total is 16 and the bad half's is 0. Not verified: S1117's membership in the Sonar way profile (the guessed path returned 404). You'll see 2147483648"; "p is the precision (24 for float, 53 for double)" · reception: not contested · notes: confidence high. Three language specifications or official library documentation state the silent rounding of an over-precise literal and its examples. They also state its bounds: 15 and 6 decimal digits, 53 and 24 binary digits, and 2^53 − 1 for whole numbers. They give the normal range in which the decimal bounds hold, from MIN_POSITIVE to MAX, and the infinity, zero and denormalized values outside it. Checks that are on by default state the claim too: ESLint's recommended set, Error Prone's default warnings and clippy's style group. No source measures how often such a literal causes a failure, so the severity is minor. Scope: the card covers only literals stored in binary floating-point types. Integer types reject an out-of-range literal instead of rounding it, and untyped exact constants keep every digit. The digit-count shortcut holds only inside the normal range; outside it, the ESLint tests flag one-digit literals such as `2e999` and `1e-350`. The tools differ at the edges, and the card follows the ESLint test: (1) ESLint counts zeros written after a decimal point as carried digits and reports `1230000000000000000000000.0`. (2) Error Prone compares values and ignores scale. (3) clippy's default-on `excessive_precision` skips whole-number floats; its whole-number case, the `16_777_217.0` example, belongs to the restriction lint, which is allowed by default. (4) clippy exempts constant items of 30 or more digits, and the card turns that exemption into a project-context tolerance. (5) Error Prone and clippy's `excessive_precision` compare against the shortest round-trip form, so they also report 17-digit literals such as `0.10000000000000001` that ESLint and the card accept. The statement's sentence on default enforcement names tools, so it moved to the Source footer. The formulation's 2147483647 example stays out of the card. Testing widened the triggers from the proposed three to six. The proposed fraction pattern missed digit separators, digits split across the decimal point and a literal that starts at its decimal point, such as ESLint's `.1230000000000000000000000`. The proposed 32-bit pattern missed suffixed fractions and type-annotated literals such as clippy's own `let v: f32 = 0.123_456_789_9;`. A hexadecimal pattern was added for ESLint's `0X20000000000001` case. An exponent pattern, 38 or more in magnitude, was added for ESLint's out-of-range cases `2e999`, `1e-350` and `1e-324`; the Example carries one. The whole-number and hexadecimal patterns take an optional long-integer suffix. That way they reach a long literal that a declaration gives a 64-bit float type, such as `9_007_199_254_740_993L`, and the Example carries one. The Validator compares a hexadecimal literal in its own base. The card does not cover floating-point equality, accumulated rounding, binary floating point for decimal quantities such as money, integer overflow, lossy narrowing of computed values or magic numbers; other rules of the topic own those. Candidate evidence not used: Goldberg 1991 and Di Franco et al. 2017. Neither had an openable copy in this run, and the fetched specifications state the claim directly.

The tools rank the defect differently: SpotBugs files it under STYLE, Error Prone as a WARNING, SonarSource as a Bug of Minor severity with LOW reliability impact. The card's `major` follows the corpus definition of a correctness defect. No study in reach measures how often the defect occurs: the WebSearch budget was exhausted, and the topic's candidate papers (Di Franco, Guo, Rubio-González, ASE 2017, on numerical bugs; Dietz, Li, Regehr, Adve, on C/C++ integer overflow) could not be opened as text, so neither is cited. Clippy's own "Why restrict this?" sentence, "When outside of some very specific algorithms, integer division is very often a mistake because it discards the remainder.", is fetched but not carried: it states a frequency that nothing measures, and the restriction group's README and staticcheck's deliberate truncations in Go's time package point the other way, so the card locates the defect in the fractional use of the quotient and not in the division. The decimal alternative in the Thesis rests on the decimal documentation showing that decimal division keeps the fraction (1/7 is 0.142857 at precision 6). It does not rest on a tool rule. A floor division keeps no fraction whatever its operands: the Numeric Types note (1) gives a float floor division a float type and a whole-integer value, and the decimal documentation says // returns the integer part of the true quotient, so the conversion remedy is stated for a division that is not a floor division; checked by hand, float(2) // 5 is 0.0 and Decimal(2) // Decimal(5) is Decimal('0'). The fix converts both operands where a binary operator requires one operand type: Go's §Operators and ECMAScript's SameType step make a one-operand conversion a compile error or a TypeError, as checked by hand (`go run` rejects `float64(part) / whole` with "mismatched types float64 and int", rustc rejects `part as f64 / whole` with E0277 "cannot divide `f64` by `i64`", node throws "Cannot mix BigInt and other types" for `Number(p) / w` with bigint operands), while converting both prints 0.4 in each. The drafter changed three facets from the topic plan. `step` went from `[implement, review]` to `[implement, refactor]`, because the taxonomy reserves `review` for the shape, size and description of the change, and the rule applies while arithmetic is written and while a refactoring extracts a quotient into a variable or changes an operand's or target's type. `applies_to` went from `[static-types]` to `[universal]`, because the rule holds wherever an operator keeps an integer quotient, including floor division in a dynamically typed language and the card's Python example. `scope` went from `hunk` to `file`, because deciding that both operands are integers and that the quotient's target is floating-point needs the operand declarations and the routine's return type, which are often outside the hunk. The triggers are wider than the plan: `//?` admits floor division in the declaration, return, conversion and percentage patterns; a `return` pattern reaches a quotient returned from a floating-point routine (S2184's `compute2`); `Number(` reaches a converted arbitrary-precision quotient; the declaration, return and conversion patterns accept a call, selector or index operand on either side of the slash (`list.size() / n`, `float64(len(done) / len(all))`, `float64(s.done / s.total)`); and the conversion pattern also reaches a quotient passed to ceil, floor or round (SpotBugs' `ICAST_INT_CAST_TO_DOUBLE_PASSED_TO_CEIL`, `(int) Math.ceil(total / pageSize)`). The return pattern also reaches an assignment or compound assignment to a variable or field declared elsewhere (`average = total / count;`, `sum += part / whole;`, `self.ratio = part // whole`), the case S2184 names as assigned to a floating-point variable, and the cast pattern also reaches the lossless conversion `f64::from(a / b)`, the form clippy's `cast_lossless` (rust-lang/rust-clippy clippy_lints/src/casts/mod.rs, fetched) recommends over `as`. Not carried: the multiplication-overflow half of NarrowCalculation and S2184 (integer overflow before widening, a separate numeric rule); staticcheck's exemption of named constants, which serves that tool's noise budget and is not part of the rule; the CWE-192, CERT NUM50-J and INT18-C references on the SpotBugs and SonarSource pages, which cannot be opened from the authoring environment. Checked by hand: the good half compiles with python3 compile() and both halves pass `mypy --strict`; `share(2, 5)` is 0.4 for the good half and 0.0 for the bad; the bad half's `return float(part // whole)` matches the `return` trigger and the conversion trigger; each of the shapes named above matches a trigger; all six triggers compile and none contains backslash-dot; the corpus validator reports 0 errors on the card.

The One Thing Rule behind the wording is argued in johnousterhout/aposd-vs-clean-code README.md 'Method Length' (fetched). Ousterhout calls it vague and without guardrails. He holds that "If two things are closely related, it might well make sense to implement them in a single method", and that acquiring a lock and then carrying out the function are "two "things", but they belong in the same method". Asked whether "a single method that initializes two completely independent objects with nothing in common" is acceptable, he answers "I suspect not". Martin extracts wherever a piece can be meaningfully named and does less than the original. He calls two field resets "strongly related so as to qualify for doing _one thing_: initialization". In 'Method Length Summary' both agree that modular design is good and that over-decomposition is possible; they disagree on how far to decompose. The card stays off that ground. Its test is shared data, not extractability, and decomposition depth is outside the rule. The Validator counts a lock, a resource bracket, a precondition check or a log line as part of the operation it serves, and counts writes to several fields of one object as one effect, and it counts the object a method runs on, and an object both traces reach through one parameter or variable and use only through its fields, as shared only through a field both traces touch. The measure paper defines functional cohesion on data slices and demonstrates it on abstract transformations, without defect data. The refactoring study measures readability with comprehension metrics over mined refactorings, not with human readers. The bug study is small (125 smell-caused bugs, 11 projects) and separates length from doing too much. No opened study ties the shared-data test itself to defects. Not carried from the spine statement: "a boolean selector is often the visible symptom", because no opened source ties a selector flag to bundled tasks and the flag rule owns it; and the phrasing "size is not the test", which the Limits carry as "length alone is not the finding" on the kernel guide and the bug study. Facets: step 'review' was dropped because the corpus reserves it for the shape and description of the change. The triggers were broadened to Go method receivers, typed or modified method declarations, class methods without modifiers and const-bound function expressions. Ownership: routine length bounds and decomposition depth stay with this topic's long-routine and split-only rules, and the extract-method move stays with refactoring.

The Rust example's good half compiled with rustc 1.94.1 `--emit=metadata` inside a `fn main` scope with `struct Report;`. Ownership: a single boolean that selects a code path stays with this topic's boolean-selector rule; the parameter-count bound and the many_parameters signal with the parameter-count rule; the caller-facing shape of public API operations with api-design-and-use. No measured study of defect cost backs the severity. The **relayed** Parnin, Bird and Murphy-Hill study of Java generics adoption (MSR 2011, https://dl.acm.org/doi/abs/10.1145/1985441.1985446; EMSE 18(6) 2013, https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10664-012-9236-6) reports from 40 Java projects only that "generics sometimes reduce the number of type casts". The card does not carry it: the result is hedged with "sometimes" and covers one language. Each style-guide source is written for one language; the cast-semantics sources carry the rule to Java, Python, TypeScript, Go and Rust alike. Rust's `dyn Any` admits only `'static` types, so the example uses the language's nearest equivalent of a top type. The card does not carry: the memory and speed effect of a type parameter on a data structure (implementation-specific, reserved to low-latency tuning); a generic type written without its type arguments (the first half of Google Python Style Guide §3.19.15, and raw types); type parameters that appear only in the return type (Google TypeScript Style Guide §Return type only generics); bound width; or variance. The Validator reads the hunk only, so a top-typed declaration whose casts sit in callers outside the hunk is judged from the declaration's own shape.

This is official documentation and is also cited in the card's Source, as with other official-documentation formulations in the corpus. The topic's SWEBOK locator SW4.3 frames the topic but says nothing about unused parameters · reception: not contested · notes: confidence moderate. The anchors are one compiler's error index and core-library documentation, three static-analysis rules across three ecosystems (Rust, Java, TypeScript) and one language handbook with its FAQ. No measured study of cost exists among them. SonarSource rates the rule Major on its own scale, but the card keeps minor because no source ties the defect to failures or to a measured cost. The tools disagree on what counts as a use: the TypeScript rule counts the signature only, clippy also counts types in the body, and Sonar counts any usage. The card counts body uses, so a parameter used only in the body is no finding here. The rule that a constraint bounding the parameter itself is not a use follows the TypeScript rule's comment and clippy's handling of a plain bound. Wording changes from the draft, each made to stay within what the sources state: (1) "callers must supply a type argument" became "depending on the language", because the FAQ shows inference falling back to `{}` rather than requiring an argument. (2) "scheduling the removal with the API's evolution" became a project-context tolerance, because the only sourced handling of exported code is clippy's default suppression for exported items. (3) "unless the language marks it as a deliberate type-level tag" became a deliberate parameter that is given a use, such as a zero-size marker field, following E0392 and PhantomData, with Go's `_ [0]*T` as a second case. (4) The method-implements-interface exemption carries the qualifier "where the language requires the same type parameters" (E0049), because some languages let an override drop them. The card adopts clippy's empty-body skip for routines that test types (`is_empty_body`; UI test module `issue10319` leaves `fn assert_send<T: Send>() {}` and `fn assert_send_where<T>() where T: Send {}` unlinted), which typescript-eslint's "When Not To Use It" also names ("functions that use type parameters solely to test types"; "disable this rule on files that test types"), and leaves out clippy's skip for parameters bounded by non-exported traits. It also leaves out language-specific consequences: the hard error on unused parameters of structs and enums in one language, the conversion between instances whose fields do not mention the parameter in another, and structural compatibility in a third. The relayed Parnin et al. study and Featherweight Go say nothing about unused parameters and are not cited.

Ten fetched sources agree on the rule and on how it works: the official documentation of both languages, two pages of the typing community's documentation, one style guide and five linter rules, all from the two ecosystems that have both an unchecked dynamic type and a checked top type. They agree that the unchecked type checks no operation and no assignment out of it, and that the checked top type requires narrowing. Google's guide and typescript-eslint tie the unchecked type to masked errors and bugs, which is what the major severity rests on, but no source measures a defect rate. No paper was found that states the claim. The topic's candidate papers say nothing about an unchecked dynamic type, so neither is cited: Featherweight Go (arXiv:2005.11710), and Parnin, Bird, Murphy-Hill on Java generics adoption (DOI 10.1145/1985441.1985446 and 10.1007/s10664-012-9236-6), whose relayed snippet concerns adoption and cast reduction. Scope: the rule holds where a type system has both kinds of top type. Among the five example languages those are the TypeScript and Python type systems. In Java, Go and Rust the top type (Object, interface{}/any, dyn Any) is checked, so the rule has nothing to flag there. The Validator sets aside a checked top type that shares the spelling and a trait or interface named Any used as a bound; the first trigger's alternative `(:|->|[\[,=|])\s*["\x27]?(\w+[.])?Any\b` also matches a Rust `T: Any` bound or a Kotlin `x: Any`. The clause that a comment states why each written unchecked type is legitimate rests on the Google TypeScript Style Guide, with typescript-eslint suggesting disable comments. On the Python side the stub-writing style guide of the typing documentation states the same clause for stub files and waives it where the reason is obvious, naming two such reasons that the card carries; the general best-practice page asks for no comment, so in code other than stubs the clause rests on that stub guide and the TypeScript style guide. Not carried, and why: casts through the unchecked type (`as any`, `cast(Any, x)`), which `no-explicit-any` also reports, because the rule addresses declarations and the triggers do not dispatch on casts; the bottom type (`never[]`) for the parameters of a constraint that admits any function, from `no-explicit-any`, left out as one language's idiom; Java raw types, which the topic covers under its own rule; return-type-only type parameters, which the Google guide warns against in a separate section and the topic covers under another rule; Ruff's false positive on aliases of `Any`, a tool limitation rather than a limit of the rule; Ruff's skip of methods decorated with typing.override, a tool choice that typescript-eslint no-explicit-any does not make.

Against return-only type parameters: Error Prone TypeParameterUnusedInFormals, the Google TypeScript Style Guide, typescript-eslint no-unnecessary-type-parameters (its page lists eslint-plugin-etc and wotan no-misused-generics and DefinitelyTyped-tools no-unnecessary-generics as related rules; those three were not opened) and the TypeScript handbook's "strongly reconsider". For them where a check produces the value: the Rust standard library (`str::parse` through the `FromStr` bound) and the Go standard library (`errors.AsType`, preferred "for most uses" over the any-typed `errors.As`). The card states the rule on the unchecked side, which the first side's type-safety mechanism reaches, and carries the separating condition in Limits: whether each value of the type parameter is produced by an operation checked against the type argument · notes: confidence moderate. The evidence is tool-rule pages, a style guide and the official documentation of five languages, all fetched, and no source measures a defect rate. The Error Prone check matches only a result that is the bare type parameter, and typescript-eslint skips a type parameter used as a type argument; the card applies their unchecked-cast mechanism to each value of that type the result carries, and it sets aside a new or empty container and the zero value, which convert nothing. Scope, as revised after review: a type parameter that appears in the bound of another type parameter a parameter uses is set aside, as Error Prone's finder visits type-variable bounds and Go's `slices.Max` fixes `E` from its argument through `S ~[]E`; a conversion the checker verifies for every type in the bound's type set counts as checked (Go spec, Conversions); a bodiless declaration counts as unchecked only when its result is the bare type parameter, matching the Error Prone check and typescript-eslint's unreported `createStateHistory<T>(): T[]`; the statement that a type assertion carries no run-time check is limited to languages that remove assertions at compile time, since a Go type assertion panics or reports false. Not carried: (1) the style guide's call-site half (name the type argument explicitly when calling an existing API), a second check, stated in Limits as outside the rule; (2) Go `reflect.TypeFor`, whose type parameter appears in neither its parameters nor its result; (3) the claim that the Go team calls `AsType` less error-prone, which `wrap.go` does not state; (4) a local tsc 6.0.2 --strict / node 22 run in which `parseJSON<number>('"not a number"')` compiles and yields a string, which is not openable until committed under `evals/fixture/`; (5) the Java generics adoption study (MSR 2011, DOI 10.1145/1985441.1985446; EMSE 18(6), DOI 10.1007/s10664-012-9236-6), which measures adoption, not this claim; (6) Featherweight Go (arXiv:2005.11710), a calculus, not this claim. Example checked locally with go 1.24.7: gofmt is clean on both halves; the good half passes go vet, and its run printed 513, "binary.Read: invalid type *string" and "unexpected EOF"; go vet reports nothing on the bad half.

(**relayed**); The Practice of Programming ch. 1 §1.3 'Use a consistent indentation and brace style' ("the specific style is much less important than its consistent application") (**relayed**); Software Engineering at Google ch. 8 'Building in consistency' (first quote) and 'Be consistent' › 'Advantages of consistency' (second quote) (abseil/abseil.github.io, resources/swe-book/html/ch08.html, fetched): "Things like naming conventions, indentation spacing, import ordering: there is usually no clear, measurable, technical benefit for one form over another"; "It’s the consistency of having one answer rather than the answer itself that is the valuable part here."; 97 Things Every Programmer Should Know, thing_04 'Automate Your Coding Standard' (97-things/97-things-every-programmer-should-know, en/thing_04/README.md, fetched): "it does not help if one developer uses three spaces to indent code, and another one four" · reception: not contested on one character and one unit per file; contested on which governs when a file's existing indentation and the project's declared style differ (PEP 8 ranks the module first; google/eng-practices makes the style guide the absolute authority), so the card accepts either there; the width is contested: the 1983 experiment found 2–4 spaces best for one program, the 2019 eye-tracking replication found no effect of indentation level, and the style documents set 2, 4 or a tab. The card therefore fixes no width and takes neither side · notes: confidence moderate. Tool rules, a language reference and the style documents of four languages agree on one character and one unit per file, with comments at the code's level, but no study measures what an inconsistently indented line costs, and the two experiments vary width, not consistency. The hands-on Python 3.11.15 run of mixed.py ("TabError: inconsistent use of tabs and spaces in indentation") is not cited: it is not committed under evals/fixture/, and the Python Language Reference states the same behaviour. The gofmt command documentation (golang/go, src/cmd/gofmt/doc.go, fetched: "It uses tabs for indentation and blanks for alignment.") is not cited in the card, because the topic keeps formatter names to Examples; Effective Go's Formatting section and ESLint's smart-tabs option carry the same two facts. The Example's indentation is literal tab characters after the six-space prefix, except the bad half's `count++`, which is indented with three spaces. Its good half compiles inside a function (go vet clean) and is gofmt-stable, and gofmt turns the bad half into the good half. The triggers catch a line that mixes tabs and spaces in its leading whitespace and an odd number of leading spaces. A line off the unit by an even count, or indented wholly in the other character, reaches the finder only when another added line of the same file matches. Ownership: indentation that shows a statement inside or outside a body other than as parsed belongs to the topic's layout-versus-parse card; line length and line breaking are separate layout rules; running a formatter in CI belongs to build-warnings-static-analysis-ci; re-indenting untouched lines belongs to small-steps-and-minimal-diffs.

The style documents and the default-on linter checks state the claim directly, so it is high as documentation, but no comprehension or defect measurement of continuation-line layout was found. The candidate indentation studies (Miara et al. 1983; Bauer et al. 2019) concern how wide indentation is and whether it is present, not continuation lines, and WebSearch was unavailable this run. I changed the original statement's "never land at the body's indentation". The Rust Style Guide keeps continuation lines at block indentation and separates them from the block with a brace line or a closing-parenthesis line at the header's indentation, so the card admits a separating line as well as deeper indentation. A separating line is one at the header's indentation that begins with the header's closing bracket and carries only the rest of the header (the Rust `) -> i32 {`, a `):` or a `) {`), or holds only the opening brace, or is blank. The card does not require continuation lines to sit deeper than the block, only that none sits at the block's column, because the Rust guide's wrapped match patterns sit shallower. PEP 8 accepts a parenthesis-aligned condition at the body's column (option "No extra indentation"), while pycodestyle E129 reports it by default. The card treats that form as a project-configured tolerance in Limits, and a hanging continuation at the body's column remains a finding under PEP 8's Wrong example. The comment-line separator rests only on PEP 8's options for a condition aligned with its opening parenthesis, so the card admits it only there; a hanging continuation at the block's column followed by a comment line stays a finding, and pycodestyle E125 reports it. The Rationale says the linter checks test the collision on the header's last continuation line, since they do not see a blank or comment line between header and block. The Java and JavaScript continuation indent is measured from the header's first line, as "from the original line" states. The first three triggers are merged into one alternation; it matches every line the three matched except a modifier written with no space after it (`export{`, `async(`), and also `} else if`, `case` and `except` headers and lines ending in `[`, `|` or a backslash. The closing-line trigger also admits a `throws` clause before the block opener. I dropped Checkstyle Indentation (`lineWrappingIndentation`) from the evidence. Its defaults are basicOffset 4 and lineWrappingIndentation 4, so a +4 continuation lands at the block's level. With forceStrictCondition true, its own Example3 reports "violation 'level 16, expected level should be 12'" on `&& y) {` above a body at level 12, which means it demands the collision rather than forbidding it. The TypeScript example follows the Google JavaScript guide's +4 continuation over a +2 block, and the good half compiles under tsc --noEmit --strict --target es2020 (TypeScript 6.0.2). The card leaves out the column limit that forces the wrap, nesting depth, and running formatters in CI, which neighbouring topics own, and it names no formatter.

Scope: spaces between tokens on consecutive lines, plus re-padding of unchanged neighbours. The exemption follows the separating condition, who maintains the alignment: columns emitted by the formatter the project runs on the file are exempt as well as those of the language's standard formatter, because a language without a standard formatter may run one that aligns (clang-format 18.1.3 with --style=Google, run locally, turns 'const w = 1; // px' / 'const height = 200; // px' in a TypeScript file into 'const w = 1;         // px' / 'const height = 200;  // px'); no fetched source states this extension, which rests on the condition rather than on a quoted fragment. Under a project tolerance for hand alignment (Google Java §4.6.3 'permitted, but is never required'), padding on added or changed lines is not flagged; only a re-padded unchanged neighbour is. The first two triggers fire on padding before an operator or colon and before a trailing comment; the third fires on any interior run of two or more spaces, so padding after a key's colon and between a declaration's type and its name also dispatches the card (gofmt go1.24.7 aligns a multi-line key-value literal but rewrites the single-line `a  := Pt{x:  1}` to `a := Pt{x: 1}` and the ungrouped `var w    int = 10` to `var w int = 10`); it also fires on formatter-aligned Go struct fields and on two-space inline comments, which the Validator's formatter and column checks filter. The trailing-comment trigger also matches ordinary two-space inline comments in Python; the Validator's column check filters them. Continuation-line visual indentation is excluded and left to each language's guide, because PEP 8 and Google Python list alignment with the opening delimiter as correct while the Rust guide prefers block indent. The design input's claim that formatter-maintained alignment "carries no such cost" is not carried: no source states it, and a gofmt probe (go1.24.7) shows the formatter itself re-pads unchanged struct-field lines when a longer field is added; the card says only that formatter-emitted columns are its output and need no hand time. The trailing-comment clause rests on Google Python §3.6 and the Rust comment recommendation (marked skippable by a formatter); PEP 8 sets only a two-space minimum before an inline comment and does not itself forbid aligning comments. No TypeScript-specific source states the rule (the Google TypeScript guide, tsguide.html, fetched, only calls aligned wrapped JSDoc description text "discouraged"), so the card relies on the cross-language statements. Formatter names stay out of the prose; the Go example's good half is gofmt output (gofmt -l clean, go vet and go build clean in a function scope, go1.24.7), and gofmt -d on the bad half changes only its padded first line.

Strict: Google Java Style §4.3, SonarSource S122, Pylint C0321 with `single-line-if-stmt` off by default, Ruff E701, and the Rust Style Guide's single-line-block rule. Tolerant: Google Python Style §3.14, the Google TypeScript Style Guide's `if` exception, and PEP 8 ("sometimes it's okay", although its examples of the form sit under "Rather not"). The separating condition is sourced on both sides and carried in Limits: the number of clauses decides, and the project's stated guide decides the single-clause form; arrow-style switch rules and match arms sit outside the multi-clause case · notes: confidence moderate. Every guide and checker cited for Java, Python and Rust states the core: two statements joined on one line, and a multi-clause statement on one line. The TypeScript and Go documents bear only on the exceptions. No empirical study was re-opened because the WebSearch budget was spent. The candidate readability papers (Buse & Weimer, TSE 2010; dos Santos & Gerosa, ICPC 2018) were neither searched nor carried, so the card states no number. The TypeScript guide's exception does not say whether a braceless if-else that fits on one line is allowed, so the card does not count that guide among the sources that reject multi-clause one-liners. The checker evidence covers Java (SonarSource, Checkstyle) and Python (Pylint, Ruff) only. Checkstyle is cited for the core and for the try-resources default, not for the single-clause form. The "single short result" bound on a one-line switch rule or match arm rests on Google Java §4.8.4.1's column-limit parenthetical and the Rust Style Guide's rule that a multi-statement right-hand side takes a block, both quoted here only. The Go spec's switch-header sentence, quoted here only, backs the Validator's skip of a switch header's init statement. rustfmt was run on the Example's bad half and printed exactly its good half; rustfmt is named here only. The triggers are revised from the spine's: (1) the first is broadened to typed declarations and a trailing terminator; (2) a jump-or-import-after-semicolon alternative is added to the first pattern; (3) `;\s*else\b` is generalised to `(;|\{[^{}]*\})\s*(else|catch|finally)\b`, so a one-line braced if-else or try-catch triggers in brace languages; (4) the clause-header pattern covers colon and brace clause headers (try, except, finally, else, elif, catch) followed by a body on the same line; (5) a single-clause-header pattern is added for the project-decided form. A declaration of several variables in one statement is not addressed
