(fetched; formulation and reception only); Software Engineering at Google ch. 10 "Documentation" § Reference Documentation (abseil/abseil.github.io `master`, resources/swe-book/html/ch10.html, fetched): "Implementation comments, on the other hand, can assume a lot more domain knowledge of the reader, though be careful in assuming too much: people leave projects, and sometimes it's safer to be methodical about exactly why you wrote this code the way you did." · reception: not contested as a rule. In the public discussion between the authors of A Philosophy of Software Design and Clean Code (aposd-vs-clean-code README, § Comments Summary), both agree that implementation code needs comments only where it is nonobvious. They disagree on how often that is the case ("Although neither of us argues for a large number of implementation comments, I'm more likely to see value in them than you do.") and on recasting comment content into code such as long names; the summary's "5-10x more lines of comments" counts all comments, interface comments included. The card meets the second point with the sourced first remedy, clearer code and then a comment for what clarification cannot carry (eng-practices handling-comments, Go and C++ guides). The topic as a whole stays contested on interface comments and on missing versus bad comments, which this card does not carry · notes: confidence moderate. The evidence is official style guides and code-review guidance (Google eng-practices; Google Go, Python, C++ and TypeScript style guides; LLVM; PEP 8; Linux kernel). It states the practice and its reasons but measures nothing, so the card carries no number. The one experiment reached (DOI 10.1007/s10664-018-9664-z, small tasks) found no significant effect of comment type on correctness, so the card claims no measured benefit and says so in its Source caveat. The candidate papers (Wen et al. ICPC 2019, Fluri et al. WCRE 2007, Tan et al. SOSP 2007, Steidl et al. ICPC 2013, Pascarella and Bacchelli MSR 2017, Woodfield et al. ICSE 1981) concern comment-code inconsistency, comment classification or comprehension in general, not missing why-comments; with web search exhausted, none was re-checked. Scope of the evidence: the workaround wording from the formulation is carried only as far as the fetched instances, which are code handling non-Error values a called API is known to throw (TypeScript guide) and a nuance of the language (Go guide). The broader "error or undocumented feature in a language or an environment" stays in the formulation. The brief's "ordering or delay that depends on a constraint outside the code" has no fetched source and is dropped from the Thesis. The delay case is left out of the Validator and the triggers as well. The brief's closing sentence that "both sides of the self-documenting-code dispute agree" rests only on the README, which is formulation and reception, so it moved to the reception above. Triggers: a cross-language regex-constructor pattern and a bitwise and/xor pattern, each matched by a line of the Example's bad half; regex-literal, shift, hex-literal and sleep patterns are left out because no bad-half line exercises them. Scope is file, because a comment at the head of the enclosing routine, which the Limits accept, and the usual form the Validator compares against both lie outside a -U0 hunk; the Rationale states the end()-loop signal only under a convention that evaluates the end once, as the LLVM source does, since in languages where the re-evaluating loop is the ordinary form it hints at no mutation. The Linux kernel coding style is promoted from formulation to fetched evidence for the placement limit, as official project documentation of the same class as the Google guides. Ownership: doc comments a declaration owes callers, restating or contradicting comments, TODO/FIXME markers, the stated reason for a silenced caught error, named constants and long names, and placement are each left to their own rules.

The backing is official conventions (PEP 257, Go Doc Comments, Rust API Guidelines, the Rust book, Google Python Style) and tool rules across Python, Rust, Java and JavaScript/TypeScript; clippy's errors and panics lints and the Ruff rules are pedantic and opt-in, Checkstyle's validateThrows defaults to false and require-throws is not in eslint-plugin-jsdoc's recommended set, while MISSING_SAFETY_DOC warns by default. No study measures what documenting side effects, errors or panics does for callers; Coelho et al. is about Android exception handling, and it reports that developers are unaware of undocumented exception behaviour, not what that costs. Go's doc-comment rule has no errors section; it backs the "what the caller needs to know" and special-cases parts. The statement's "preconditions on its arguments" is worded as PEP 257's "restrictions on when it can be called", because no fetched source states argument preconditions generally (clippy's "safety preconditions" covers unsafe routines only). The statement's two exemptions are narrowed to what their sources say. "Logic the caller supplies" covers panics only (Rust API Guidelines, which add "when in doubt, err on the side of documenting more panic cases"). "After the documented contract is violated" is one convention's position (Google Python Style); the Rust API Guidelines (Vec::insert "Panics if `index` is out of bounds") and Ruff DOC501 do not share it, so the card leaves it to the convention the code follows and does not flag a failure that enforces a stated restriction unless that convention or the project's linter asks for it. Exceptions propagated from callees that the signature does not declare are left to the convention (Ruff DOC501/DOC502). A write not relevant to the caller, such as a memo cache, a diagnostic log line or a metrics counter, is struck from the side effects, following Google Python Style §3.8.3's sentence that caller-irrelevant implementation details are better expressed as comments alongside the code. A routine with no doc comment is outside the card, since the topic's public-item doc-comment rule owns presence. A contradicting or drifted doc comment, assertions and deprecation notices are also outside it. Wen et al. ICPC 2019, Fluri et al. WCRE 2007 and Tan et al. SOSP 2007 bear on comment–code inconsistency, not on missing doc items, and are not used. What documentation tools read, where they attach a doc comment and which part they surface as the summary is stated directly in fetched compiler, linter and style-guide documentation for all five example languages. The Example was checked under rustc 1.97.0 (edition 2021, --emit=metadata): the good half, with a documented `pub struct Item { pub key: u32 }` and crate doc around it, compiles under `#![deny(warnings)]` and `#![deny(missing_docs)]`; the bad half raises unused_doc_comments (on by default) and, under `#![warn(missing_docs)]`, reports the `//`-commented `pub fn find` as undocumented. No study measures the cost of a misplaced, summary-less or mis-laid-out doc comment, so the card carries no number beyond a convention's own bound (Google Python's 80-character summary line). The brief's title said "one-line summary". The card says "the summary its convention prescribes" because Google Java's "brief summary fragment" and Go's first sentence are not bounded to one line; PEP 257 and Google Python bound it, and rustdoc calls one line good practice. The no-blank-line attachment condition is Go's alone (Go Doc Comments, Effective Go), so the Thesis carries it as "where the tool requires that". The attaching position includes the first statement of a body (PEP 257), and the Validator checks for it, so a correctly placed routine or class docstring is not read as dangling. The exemption for attribute docstrings follows PEP 257's scope (top level of a module, class or `__init__` method, rendered "constructor"). The file-consistency tier applies where the documented conventions for the language disagree or admit more than one form, because the only mood split in the Source is between PEP 257 (command form only) and Google Python §3.8.3 (either form, consistent within a file), not inside the language's own documents; because that tier reads the file's other doc comments, scope is file. A summary-less doc comment is one that opens with a block return tag; an inline return tag is a summary, because Google Java §7.2 gives `/// {@return the customer ID}` as a corrected form, the javadoc manual lets `{@return ...}` enclose the first sentence, the standard doclet writes it as "Returns {0}.", and MissingSummary does not fire on a non-empty first sentence. ST1020 is off by default, so it backs the starts-with-the-name clause only together with Go Doc Comments. The statement's list of per-language syntaxes moved to the Example and the Source because the Thesis names no language. The card does not carry whether a declaration needs a doc comment, what an interface comment must say (errors, panics and side effects as content), or whether a comment is accurate; the topic's other rules own those. Deprecation notices belong to api-evolution-and-deprecation, and the placement and spacing of ordinary comments to layout-and-coding-style

The card states the default (deny) reading of the tool rules and carries their configurable tolerances in Limits: PMD `forReassign: skip` (conditional increment), `foreachReassign: firstOnly` (first-statement normalization), Checkstyle `skipEnhancedForLoopVariable`. S127's stricter reading, which flags every call or property in a termination test as possibly varying, is carried as a project choice; the card flags a bound only when the body changes it, and its Limits and Validator skip list exclude only a variable the header neither advances nor compares the counter against, so a body write to the bound stays in scope. A change made through the loop variable to the element it holds — an in-place mutating method, a write through a reference the loop yields — is outside the card: PMD, Checkstyle and Ruff word their checks as reassignment or redefinition of the loop variable, and ES.86's enforcement covers only variables also updated in the iteration-expression, which a for-each variable never is; the Validator checks a hand-off by mutable reference or pointer only for a counted loop's counter. A new variable declared under the loop variable's name in a block-scoped language (a shadowing `let` or `:=`, an inner loop) is outside the card's check: no source covers shadowing, and Ruff's text restricts the nested-loop reuse to languages whose loops open no scope. The title broadens the topic's "A counted loop's control variable" to "A loop variable the loop header advances" since the card also covers the for-each variable, which the header advances to the next element, while a while loop and a header with no advance step stay outside, as the Limits state; the triggers extend the topic's set with `mut` and tuple patterns in a for-in header, a for-of or enhanced-for header, a Go range header, a prefix increment, and a counter write after `{`, `;`, `)` or `:`. Rewriting the loop as a pipeline, loop performance and asynchronous loops are left to their own topics. The Example's bad half compiles without a warning under rustc 1.94.1 and 1.97.0 and, run on the sequence "a\bc", emits "abbc", the escaped element twice; the good half compiles as written under rustc 1.97.0 and emits "abc".

Not carried: the original wording's demand that the comment name each participating type's role (the fetched abstracts state that the patterns, or the pattern instances, were documented in source comments, and none states what the comment said beyond that), so the card asks for the pattern's name only; nor does any abstract state where the comments stood, so the Thesis and the Validator accept a comment elsewhere in the file that names the pattern and lists the type as a participant; the formulation's participant-name convention (TeXLayoutStrategy) is carried only as the Limits' boundary — the two-experiment study contrasted pattern comment lines with a well-commented program without explicit reference to design patterns, and the four-experiment abstract does not describe its control code, so the boundary rests on the first study and a declaration that names the pattern lies outside its measured contrast — and not as a disclosure the evidence validated; whether a pattern fits its problem, and the reception's pattern-versus-simpler-solution question, belong to the topic's other rules. Step: `implement`, `refactor` and `document` — the rule applies when code that implements a pattern is added, a refactoring that introduces a pattern included; `review` is reserved for the shape and description of the change. Triggers: the orchestrator's `(self|this)[.]` forwarding-field pattern was widened to `[.]` so that a Go receiver (`s.inner`) also dispatches, and the type-name suffixes were extended with the remaining structural and behavioral catalogue names (Composite, Facade, Mediator, Bridge, Prototype, Flyweight, Memento); the routine-name patterns accept an initial capital (exported Go names) and a cls parameter, and the forwarding-field pattern an underscore prefix and the adaptee field name.

The Uber guide's count of three or more arguments, and the original wording's per-language mapping (keyword parameters in Python, a destructured options object in TypeScript, an option struct in Go, a builder in Rust or Java "which have no named or default arguments") are not carried: the card names no language, and the claim that Rust and Java lack named or default arguments rests only on formulation sources, so the card lists the named forms without tying them to languages. The Go guide's "consider" and the TypeScript guide's "prefer" are recommendation-strength; the card states the rule at minor severity and carries "may be unnecessary" for unexported constructors in Limits. `step` is design, implement and refactor: `review` is reserved for the shape and description of the change itself, and replacing positional optional inputs or a telescoping family with a named form changes structure while keeping behaviour. The card's scope is constructors and factories by topic ownership; long parameter lists of other routines, a method that configures an existing value among them, are left to the routine-shape topic. The TypeScript constructor trigger is widened from optional markers to default initializers. Example: the good half runs with python3 3.13 inside `class Client:`, and the bad call `Client("db", 5432, 30.0, 3, True)` raises TypeError ("takes 2 positional arguments but 6 were given") against it, as Pylint's R0917 good example states for a keyword-only signature; the bad half takes five optional inputs by position, the card's bar

SEI CERT MSC07-J (draft) counts classes with only static methods as good Singleton candidates. The Google Guice wiki holds that static state is what hurts and that static classes are fine, even preferred, for pure functions. typescript-eslint, the Google TypeScript and Python style guides, Checkstyle, PMD and SonarSource S1118 hold that a namespace class is unnecessary where modules exist and that a utility class should not be instantiable. The card's separating condition is state. CERT's sentence is unconditional on its own, so the card reads it within its paragraph, whose subject is a single instance whose fields occur once like static fields and which often controls a resource such as a database connection or socket. Guice's split between static state and the static keyword is the sourced side of the condition. · notes: confidence moderate. The evidence is analyzer documentation from four tools (one for TypeScript, three for Java), two official style guides (TypeScript, Python) and the TypeScript handbook, plus a framework wiki and a draft CERT rule for the contest; no empirical study of the cost is carried. The card narrows the tools' reach. Checkstyle, PMD and SonarSource also flag classes whose static fields hold mutable state, but the card reaches only a type whose static fields hold constants. It leaves static mutable state and resource-holding singletons to variables-scope-and-numerics, following the topic's ownership note. typescript-eslint's reasons about IDE suggestions and dead-code analysis ("IDEs can't provide as good suggestions for static class or namespace imported properties…", "It's more difficult to statically analyze code for unused variables, etc. when they're all on the class") are not carried, because they describe JavaScript and TypeScript tooling. The rule's original statement said Go and Rust meet the rule by construction. The card drops that sentence: a fieldless Rust struct whose associated functions take no receiver is the same namespace-only type, and the Rust example shows it. No Rust- or Go-specific source was found, so the reach to Rust rests on the module mechanism the TypeScript and Python sources describe, and the card states this as a caveat. Go has no static members, so the rule does not arise there. The Rationale's statement that a compiler-generated constructor takes the class's own access, and the Validator's skip of every enumeration where every function must belong to a class, rest on the compiler, because SonarSource's "implicitly generating a public parameterless constructor" holds only for a public class: OpenJDK javac sets a generated constructor's flags with `flags = (owner().flags() & AccessFlags) | GENERATEDCONSTR;` and comments "constructors of true enums are private" (fetched from `openjdk/jdk` master, `src/jdk.compiler/share/classes/com/sun/tools/javac/comp/TypeEnter.java`), and javap 21 shows `p.StringUtils();` for a package-private class, `private p.Outer$Helpers();` for a private nested class and `private p.HttpConstants();` for an enum. The card leaves out a type with no members, an enumeration that declares a value and a private class that declares no constructor, as the analyzers do: PMD `InstantiableUtilityClassRule` visits class declarations only and counts the default constructor only on a class that is not private, and SonarSource `UtilityClassWithPublicConstructorCheck` visits classes only and skips a private inner class (both fetched from `pmd/pmd` main and `SonarSource/sonar-java` master). Severity is minor, following the design facet, even though SonarSource defaults to Major: the evidence names a clarity cost, not a measured one. The triggers are two patterns, each spanning the languages: declarations (the class-name pattern with widened modifiers and the `struct` and `enum` keywords, a final class, a Rust unit or empty struct) and members (a static member, a static-method decorator, a private parameterless constructor, a Rust `pub` associated function without a receiver or associated constant). The private-parameterless-constructor alternative fires on Java classes that already comply, so the finder answers no unless a public constructor remains. Closing edits from the final skeptic verdict: the title says "hides its constructor", following Checkstyle's word "hide", because a protected or package-private constructor, which the Thesis and Validator accept, still leaves the class instantiable within its package or through a subclass (javac 21 reproduction). The skip of abstract types applies only where every function must belong to a class: that exclusion comes from the Java analyzers (PMD's "concrete class" criterion, Checkstyle's early return), while typescript-eslint's test suite lists `abstract class Foo { static property: string; }` as invalid (fetched from `packages/eslint-plugin/tests/rules/no-extraneous-class.test.ts`, main). The Thesis's statement that a private constructor can be called from a type that encloses the class rests on the compiler: javac 21 compiles `new Hidden()` inside `Outer` against `Hidden`'s private constructor (exit 0). The fix splits as SonarSource's `UtilityClassWithPublicConstructorCheck` does ("Hide this public constructor." / "Add a private constructor to hide the implicit public one.").

The card's title rewords the orchestrator's draft title ("rather than as a one-method interface with a class implementing it") because the single-operation interface stays as the function value's type in several languages; the defect is the implementing class. Ownership: a singleton used as a global goes to variables-scope-and-numerics, the inheritance a pattern rests on to inheritance-versus-composition, and pipelines and higher-order functions to functional-style-and-pipelines. The scope is `callers` because the test or mock that compares the value usually sits in a separate test file. The triggers are broad by design: an execute/perform/invoke call and the Java functional-interface names dispatch a finder whose Validator exempts non-strategy uses. A Python subclass of a strategy-family base, a Go empty struct type and a Rust unit struct are reached through the sixth pattern; another Go method or Rust impl is reached only when a name on its line carries a strategy-family suffix. Not carried: the hands-on run of this research round (rustc 1.94.1 E0004 non-exhaustive patterns; javac 21.0.10 "the switch expression does not cover all possible input values"; tsc 6.0.2 --strict TS2322 not assignable to never; go 1.24.7 go vet exit 0 and the unhandled variant silently returning 0; Python 3.11.15 match returning None), plus the drafters' mypy 1.19.1 / pyright 1.1.408 and, at revision, mypy 2.3.1 --strict / pyright 1.1.414 runs on the Example's good half (Python 3.13.16: compiles, both checkers pass; with a third variant added to the Shape alias, both report Triangle not assignable to Never), and the skeptic's reproduction that a void operation with no catch-all arm that misses a third variant passes tsc 6.0.2 --strict, mypy --strict and pyright at default settings while javac 21.0.12 and rustc 1.97.0 reject it — local scratch only, citable once committed under evals/fixture/. That reproduction is why the card asks for a final arm that asserts the matched value has no variant left, which the checker reports as an error once a variant can reach it, and allows a match with no catch-all arm only where the compiler or the project's checker reports every match that leaves a variant unhandled. Also not carried: Prechelt et al., IEEE TSE 27(12) 2001, and Krein et al., RESER 2011, both **relayed** and about patterns versus simpler solutions in general, not Visitor versus a match; the GoF footnote on double dispatch (formulation only). Trigger 3 was broadened from the research facet (adds impl, implements and extends, so `class Evaluator implements NodeVisitor<T>` and `impl Visitor for X` match); it is a superset of the original. Scope is `callers`, not `file`: a new visitor class often sits in its own file, and the Validator searches the repository for the set's declaration and the variants' accept methods. Ownership: the inheritance a visitor rests on → inheritance-versus-composition; a state machine dispatched by a match → table-driven-and-state-machines; pipelines over variants → functional-style-and-pipelines.

The mechanism rests on a relayed conceptual argument and a relayed standard definition. The measured evidence is associational: the 19-project result covers six anti-patterns together, with unstable interface and crossing contributing most, not modularity violations alone, and the developer study is twelve developers, 24 smell instances and four Java projects. The card says "other concerns" where the formulation says "unrelated", because no source requires unrelatedness. Not carried: Cataldo, Mockus, Roberts, Herbsleb, "Software Dependencies, Work Dependencies, and Their Impact on Failures", IEEE TSE 35(6):864–878, 2009, DOI 10.1109/TSE.2009.42 (**relayed** through the same note: "While all dependencies increase the fault proneness, the logical dependencies explained most of the variance in fault proneness"), because the relayed abstract does not define logical dependencies as co-change and so does not state the rule's claim. Also not carried is the formulation's "the answer should be one" module, because no source gives a count. Not carried: the detector's bound of more than δ = 3 classes (§2.2.2, Table 5, calibrated on Apache Xerces), because the paper's own §3.2.2 and Table 7 report a detection whose co-changes reach exactly three other classes, and because no source bounds one diff by a count. The paper's abstract says developers recognized "more than 75%" of the instances and its RQ3 summary says 71% (17 of 24); the card carries the RQ3 figure. The exclusion of renames, mechanical migrations and dependency upgrades is a scope bound drawn from the Thesis's condition (a change made for one requirement), not from a source.

the johnousterhout/aposd-vs-clean-code README, fetched, does not discuss the law), an Android frameworks-base developer in Palomba et al. 2015 (fetched; one developer, the only one in that evaluation who saw no need to refactor); the card states the rule at the tool's accessor-step threshold and carries in Limits two sourced separating conditions: what the chain passes through (PMD's degree rules) and a documented project tolerance (a raised trustRadius, or classes documented as one unit) · notes: confidence moderate for the rule as the tool documents it, low for its defect impact; the card follows PMD's operationalization (getter by the get/is name prefix, transformation by related types, java.util, Stream and array containers, String and primitive pure data, builders and factories by type-name suffix, static calls as construction) and generalizes the getter test across languages through the Go and Rust getter-naming conventions; evidence scope: one Java tool rule and two studies of Java open-source systems; the fault numbers concern Message Chain (chains of any calls longer than three, manually validated candidates) in 395 releases of 30 Java projects and show an association that the authors read as co-occurrence with intrinsically fault-prone code, not cause, and no source measures a single accessor step; the card does not carry two clauses of the computed rule: the "plain data record" exemption, because PMD's pure-data exemption covers only strings, string builders, primitives and boxed primitives and its field-access degree reports a field read on a field of any other type, and no admissible source states a data-structure exemption (Clean Code ch. 6 'Data/Object Anti-Symmetry' and 'Train Wrecks' state it, formulation only, **unfetched**); and "the remedy is not a forwarding method per hop", because PMD's own example remedy is a forwarding method (b.callDoItOnC()) and the 2018 study found Middle Man (classes delegating more than half their methods) in 30% of releases with a limited removal effect on change- and fault-proneness, so no admissible source states the cost of forwarding methods, which only the formulation names (PP 1st ed. §26, Refactoring 'Remove Middle Man'); the Handler quote concerns a Shotgun Surgery instance and is cited for the one-unit tolerance only; ownership: what a module hides yields to information-hiding-and-encapsulation, interface depth and pass-through methods to complexity-and-deep-modules, shared mutable state to mutable-state-and-immutability, inheritance coupling to inheritance-versus-composition; coupling between services over a network is outside the corpus

The mechanism (refusal by toolchains, load-time failure where cycles are accepted, the linters' treatment of type-only, deferred, dynamic and self imports) rests on fetched specifications, official guides and tool rules; the defect association rests on two correlational studies, one fetched only through its abstract and a review, one relayed, and neither isolates cycles from other coupling. The anti-pattern study measures six anti-patterns together, with unstable interfaces and crossings contributing most by far. The research note defines MacCormack and Sturtevant's Core as the largest cyclic group of files, but that is the note's commentary, not a quotation, so the quoted core figures do not tie defects to cycles and the card does not carry them. Verified hands-on: rustc 1.97.0 (editions 2018, 2021 and 2024, --crate-type lib --emit=metadata, each elision given the body `let _ = o.total;`) compiles both halves of the card's Example, so a two-module import cycle inside one crate is accepted by the compiler, which is why the Example shows a cycle no build refuses; pylint 4.1.2 reports "R0401: Cyclic import (pkg.a -> pkg.b)" when pkg/b.py closes the cycle with "from pkg import a" inside a function and reports nothing when that import sits under "if TYPE_CHECKING:"; import-linter 2.15 reports an acyclic_siblings contract BROKEN ("- .green -> .blue (1 import)") on a sibling cycle closed by a guarded import by default, and KEPT with exclude_type_checking_imports = True. The card leaves out the formulation's claim that a cycle fuses its members into one unit that must be understood, tested and released together: only the talk and the books state it, and they are formulation only. The card's nearest evidence is the relayed abstract's background sentence on understandability, testability, reusability, buildability and maintainability. The card also leaves out the draft's per-language list of which toolchains accept cycles: the card names no language, and no fetched fragment states that list for every language. The title is restated positively from the draft wording ("does not close a cycle"). Package-level cycles are checked only where the project's configured cycle check declares sibling packages acyclic, as an import-linter acyclic_siblings contract does. The subtree semantics rest on that one opt-in Python contract. Verified hands-on: the Go 1.24.7 standard library, whose package graph the spec keeps acyclic, links sibling directories both ways (go/build/read.go imports go/parser while go/parser/parser.go imports go/build/constraint; crypto/internal/fips140/aes/gcm/gcm_nonces.go imports crypto/internal/fips140/drbg while drbg/ctrdrbg.go imports crypto/internal/fips140/aes). Imports that only the type checker reads are outside the rule by the default of three cycle checks, and inside it where the project's build or configured cycle check counts them: import-linter counts guarded imports by default (docs/get_started/configure.md; src/importlinter/application/use_cases.py), and the Google Python guide's typing-smell sentence, with its build-system reason, covers guarded typing imports too. Ownership: removing an import through an interface the importing module declares is named here only as a way to break a cycle; a high-level policy depending on a low-level detail without a cycle belongs to the topic's dependency-direction rule.

(fetched) · reception: not contested · notes: confidence moderate — the rule rests on the documentation of five checkers in four ecosystems (import-linter, ArchUnit, eslint-plugin-import, go-arch-lint, go-cleanarch), which defines what a declared direction enforces, and on one project's architecture document (rust-analyzer), which covers the Rust case without a checker; no source measures the defect or maintenance cost of a breached direction, so the card carries no rate, and the only figure is ArchUnit's "hundreds or even thousands" of violations at rule adoption. The candidate research (Zimmermann and Nagappan ICSE 2008; ICSE 2019 multiple dependency structures; Briand et al. TSE 1999; Chidamber and Kemerer TSE 1994) measures coupling and dependency-graph structure in general, not a declared direction, and was not re-checked because the search budget was spent; it backs no sentence. The card states which module may depend on which only where the project declares it and does not decide policy against detail, since the checkers compare the code with the direction the project declares, written out in a contract or configuration or adopted as a checker's built-in layered or onion architecture whose layers the project assigns to its packages (go-cleanarch "assumes this files structure"; ArchUnit's onionArchitecture() has fixed semantics). The exception clause ("stated as a change to the rule") is the card's reading of the documented exception mechanisms (ignore_imports, except, -ignore-package, legalized entries, FreezingArchRule), which keep the check passing and are documented for violations present at adoption; ArchUnit frames the baseline as preventing "further deterioration" and ties adding current violations to the store to their being "consciously accepted"; no source requires the acceptance to be stated in the change, so the card frames a stated revision as a no-finding case rather than demanding approval. The planned "move the code" remedy was dropped because no fetched fragment states it; the rust-analyzer counterpart-and-conversion pattern takes its place. Between modules that may import each other in neither direction (an independence contract, independent siblings, two adapters) the card puts the interface in a module both may import, as ArchUnit's diagram does for two adapters (`Cli --> DomainRepository`, `NoSqlRepository --|> DomainRepository`, `Cli --> RestController #crimson`); the reason is limited to "an implementation that names the interface", since in Go, and for structurally typed values in TypeScript and Python, a type can satisfy an interface without importing the module that declares it. The indirect clause covers chains the added import completes in either direction, as import-linter's "chains of imports via other modules" does; the Validator reads the declaration's own diff because an entry added under an existing key or in a violation store may lie outside the triggered hunks. go-cleanarch's README sentence that names the practitioner book is not quoted in the card. check_kind is semantic: the finder reads the project's declaration, places both modules in it and, where the declaration counts indirect imports, traces chains of imports before it can decide.
- **DSN-12** · Go Wiki, "Go Code Review Comments", section "Interfaces" (golang/wiki, CodeReviewComments.md, https://raw.githubusercontent.com/golang/wiki/master/CodeReviewComments.md), fetched: "Go interfaces generally belong in the package that uses values of the interface type, not the package that implements those values. The implementing package should return concrete (usually pointer or struct) types: that way, new methods can be added to implementations without requiring extensive refactoring. Do not define interfaces on the implementor side of an API "for mocking"; instead, design the API so that it can be tested using the public API of the real implementation. Do not define interfaces before they are used: without a realistic example of usage, it is too difficult to see whether an interface is even necessary, let alone what methods it ought to contain. [...] Instead return a concrete type and let the consumer mock the producer implementation." · Google Go Style Guide, "Go Style Decisions", section "Interfaces" (google/styleguide, go/decisions.md, https://raw.githubusercontent.com/google/styleguide/gh-pages/go/decisions.md), fetched: "Avoid creating interfaces until a real need exists. [...] Keep interface types unexported if they are only used internally within a package. The consumer of the interface should define it (not the package implementing the interface), ensuring it includes only the methods they actually use. The producer package may export the interface if the interface is the product (a common protocol) to prevent interface redefinition bloat. The forwarding test is documented by Pylint and clippy for lambdas and closures; the card applies it to named routines by the same mechanism (a body that is a call on the same argument list), with the Go guide's "unnecessary levels of abstraction" as the general statement, and the Source caveat says so. Because a named routine can be reached in ways a closure cannot, the card also exempts routines that a subclass overrides or a test replaces, routines that a decorator, annotation or attribute wraps or registers, and entry points a runtime, framework or test runner calls by name (clippy's own `#[track_caller]` exclusion is the closure-side analogue), and it does not count a receiver the routine declares; a routine that calls an operation on an object its own instance holds is outside the forwarding case, the method PMD `LawOfDemeter` recommends adding in place of `b.getC().doIt()`. The README and APOSD give the wording only. Overrides whose body only calls the inherited version are left to the inheritance topic, and how far to split a longer routine goes to routine-size-and-parameters.

Scope: the card carries only the narrow case where tools converge — an override, a class's only constructor or an embedded-field forward to the parent's same member with unchanged parameters; the formulation's broader pass-through method (a method that forwards to a method of another class with a similar signature) and the "different layer, different abstraction" claim are not carried, since no openable source separates a useful delegating method from a useless one. Departures from the statement as handed in: "an annotation or decorator that a framework reads" became any annotation or decorator other than the override marker or a warning suppression, which is what PMD implements (Sonar's check also lets a warning suppression clear it, Pylint any decorator, ESLint any parameter decorator); "widens or narrows visibility" became a visibility different from the parent's member or, for a constructor, from the constructor the class receives when it declares none (PMD UnnecessaryConstructor), a constructor marked non-public (narrowing being sourced for constructors only: ESLint, typescript-eslint), or a protected-style visibility redeclared in a package other than the parent's (PMD `isProtectedElevatingVisibility`); the constructor clause is conditioned on the language giving a class that declares no constructor one that delegates to the parent's (ESLint's stated premise) and on the constructor being the class's only one, with the implicit constructor's visibility and declared exceptions (PMD UnnecessaryConstructor), so a forwarding constructor in a language whose implicit constructor does not delegate is outside the rule — no openable language-specification statement on constructor inheritance was fetched, and the Limits state this as the converse of the Thesis condition; the declared-exception-list exemption is sourced for constructors only (PMD UnnecessaryConstructor's throws check) and no source states it for a method, where it only narrows what the rule flags; the abstract-member exemption rests on the CPython abc documentation and departs from Pylint W0246, which reports such an override although removing it makes the class impossible to instantiate; a parameter that declares a field (ESLint parameter property), the member-name skips — equals, hashCode and toString (Sonar), clone (PMD), `__hash__` next to `__eq__` (Pylint), each attributed in the Limits to one tool and taken together by the rule — and Sonar's transactional-class skip were added from the tools. The Go clause rests on Effective Go's statement that a promoted method has exactly the same effect as the forwarding method; no Go linter for it was found. The Validator's handling of a parent declared outside the file (constructor visibility keyword, default value, parameter decorator or field-declaring parameter clear the member; method visibility and types taken to match, except that a protected-style method clears it when its class extends a parent declared in another package) is a line the card draws from ESLint's file-local behaviour and PMD's other-package guard, not one a source states for methods. Trigger changes: the handed-in `^\s*super\s*\(` was broadened to `(?:^|[{;])\s*super\s*\(` so that a one-line constructor body matches, and the handed-in fifth trigger `^\s*(?:return\s+)?\w+[.][A-Z]\w*[.][A-Z]\w*\([^()]*\)\s*$` was broadened to `(?:^\s*|[{]\s*)(?:return\s+)?\w+[.][A-Z]\w*[.][A-Z]\w*\([^()]*\)\s*[}]?\s*$` so that a one-line forwarding method, which gofmt leaves on one line, matches; the fifth trigger targets a forward through a capitalized embedded field and misses lower-case embedded types. Checked by running: pylint 4.1.2 with its default configuration reports W0246 on an override of an abstract method that has a body, and CPython 3 then refuses to instantiate the class once the override is deleted. Not verified: RSPEC-1185's membership in the Sonar way profile (the profile path answered 404).

These are the design note's locators; the book was not opened from the authoring environment. johnousterhout/aposd-vs-clean-code README.md was searched (fetched) and has no discussion of defaults or configuration parameters · reception: contested. On the 'require the caller to choose' side are construction-time validity advice (Effective Java 3rd ed. Item 2, required parameters in a builder's constructor; **unfetched**) and the same FSE 2015 study's default-value errors (17.5%–53.3% of configuration errors). The card resolves the dispute with the study's own separating condition. Parameters that are rarely set or set alike are defaulted or hidden (Finding 1(a), Guideline 1). Parameters most users must set to match their runtime environment stay required (Finding 1(b), §3.3, Table 9, Fig. 5), and the Rust builder and Swift 'essential parameters' clauses back that side. The .NET 'Member Overloading' page prefers overloads to default arguments ("Default arguments are not CLS compliant"); that is a choice of mechanism, and the card leaves it open · notes: confidence moderate. The study's numbers come from configuration of system software set by its users and administrators (a commercial storage system, Apache httpd, MySQL, Hadoop); the paper itself limits its findings to "configuration design as the users' interface". The card carries those numbers to a module's code interface, where the Swift, Go, .NET and Rust guides and the IntelliJ inspection state the rule, each for its own language. No openable study measures defaults of code parameters. The Validator's 'more than half' is the plain reading of the Thesis's 'most' and narrows the Swift guideline's 'single commonly-used value'; it is not the study's 'majority (50+%)', which counts users whose settings differ from the default (§3.1, Fig. 3, Table 6), the parameters the study's Guideline 2 promotes to first-class knobs. Stylos and Clarke, "Usability Implications of Requiring Parameters in Objects' Constructors", ICSE 2007, DOI 10.1109/icse.2007.92, fetched (abstract only; neverworkintheory/neverworkintheory.github.io, main, _posts/2011/2011-07-26-usability-implications-of-requiring-parameters-in-objects-constructors.html): "programmers strongly preferred and were more effective with APIs that did not require constructor parameters [...] causing undesirable premature commitment". It is carried in the Limits: it bears on when a required value is supplied, so the card's required side names no mechanism. The brief listed the FSE 2015 paper as relayed, but the full paper opened from the first author's GitHub Pages repository, so it is fetched. The security half of the .NET clause stays in the Thesis as a constraint on the default a fix chooses. The finding for an insecure default is left to a security corpus. Ownership: configuration files and their loading belong to runtime-configuration, and parameter count belongs to routine-size-and-parameters

The anchors are official style guides and language documentation for TypeScript, Python, Go and Rust, plus SWEBOK V3 and one peer-reviewed design-principles paper, and they agree. No Java official document stating the rule itself was fetched (the javac diagnostic carried backs only the implementing-method limit): the Java formulation, Effective Java Item 15, is unfetched. No empirical study of the cost of an over-wide public surface was found, and WebSearch was exhausted for this run. The package-wide clause rests on rustc's unreachable_pub explanation and on the TypeScript guide's general "Limit symbol visibility as much as possible"; the lint is allow-by-default because existing code would trip it widely. The interface clause is scoped to an interface a consumer declares for itself, as the Go guidance states it, and the producer-exported cases sit in Limits under the Go guide's "often makes sense" scenarios. Effective Go "Generality" is not carried. It covers a narrower case: the implementing type stays unexported and its constructor returns the interface. Its return-an-interface advice also runs against Google Go Style Decisions' "Functions should take interfaces as arguments but return concrete types". Not carried from the rule's wording: reflection and serialization hooks as a Limits item, since no fetched fragment states them (the Validator counts a framework or runtime the code hands the member to, or that finds it by its name, as an outside use; the Limits carry routines a test runner finds by name, on the Go testing and unittest documentation); the note that a richer return value is not added surface (no fragment); fields and representation details (information-hiding-and-encapsulation); widening a member only for its tests (left outside the rule as an information-hiding question). The Example shows only the visibility clause.

Construction for reuse is usually based on variability analysis and design." The card separates the cases by a deliberate variability analysis for planned reuse, documented and tested, against a developer's speculation about the future. Tensions recorded and not carried: A Philosophy of Software Design ch. 6 (**unfetched**) recommends a somewhat general-purpose interface over functionality that reflects current needs, which the review guidance's "more generic than it needs to be" does not carve out; the position that mocks force abstractions, recorded in an openable exchange (johnousterhout/aposd-vs-clean-code, main, README.md, https://raw.githubusercontent.com/johnousterhout/aposd-vs-clean-code/main/README.md, fetched) — "Generally the decoupling arises because the test requires a mock of some kind. Mocks tend to force abstractions that might otherwise not exist." against "In my experience, mocking virtually never changes interfaces; it just provides replacements for existing (typically immovable) interfaces." — which the card's mock clause does not reach because it keeps the implementing-side scope that Go Code Review Comments gives it; the same 1983 paper's corollary "Use procedure arguments to provide flexibility in an interface" (fetched) endorses a hook as a means of flexibility, which the card leaves alone because it limits only hooks no present caller uses · notes: confidence moderate. The core claim (no abstraction, option or generality ahead of a present need) is stated directly by language-neutral review guidance and a peer-reviewed design paper. The five needs that justify an interface come from Go guidance written as "could"/"may"; the card carries them to abstract types and to the other four languages as design reasons and leaves out the Go-specific placement advice (the consumer defines the interface). The only figures are the 1983 paper's line counts for one system and an association study over 30 Java systems. That study's operationalization of speculative generality (an abstract class with fewer than three children using its methods) is broader than a single-implementation interface, and its authors read smells as co-occurring with fault-proneness, not causing it. Dropped from the orchestrator's wording: "a dependency whose direction must be inverted", because no fetched source states it. The Go guidance names only breaking a circular dependency between two packages, and a project context that fixes a layer's dependency direction rejects the finding instead. "A material need to substitute an implementation" is carried as a material need for a test double and as a returned type whose provider must stay replaceable without a breaking change, the two forms the guide states. The orchestrator's carve-out for keeping an interface general over existing functionality has no openable source and is not carried. The wrapper prohibition keeps the guide's generated-RPC scope; a project-owned wrapper around another third-party library, doubled in unit tests and run against the real library in integration tests, is carved out on the Mockito wiki's recommendation. An interface that only names the shape of a data value (a TypeScript object type) declares no behaviour for an implementation to supply and is outside the rule, since every source speaks of interfaces whose methods implementations supply. The last trigger also matches a Go variadic options parameter (`opts ...Option`). Type parameters (generics) are left to the code domain. Neither DOI was opened (doi.org denied); both are confirmed by the GitHub-hosted pages cited above, and the Palomba paper's journal, volume and pages come from the author page's BibTeX (fpalomba.github.io index.html, fetched).

the card states the rule where the copies are meant to do the same thing and so must change together, and carries the accepted cases in Limits with each side's evidence · notes: confidence moderate. The fault link rests on one large-scale case study's abstract (Juergens) and the modification cost on one controlled experiment with 61 novices in Scratch (Hermans); the change-cost mechanism rests on CWE-1041, the CPD documentation and official Rust documentation; the floors are detector defaults, not measured thresholds. The four-line floor is Pylint's, a Python checker that counts textually identical lines after dropping blank lines, comments, docstrings, imports and signatures; the card applies it across languages and to parameterized copies, where the multi-language detectors default higher (jscpd 5 lines and 50 tokens, dupl 100 tokens on its CLI and 150 under golangci-lint, CPD a required token count). The routine-level floor follows S4144's documented exception ("only one line of code"), not "two statements". Kapser and Godfrey's pattern verdicts and the experimental-fork case are read through the paper's abstract and its conclusion as quoted in a review, and the platform-variation and language-idiom kinds through the reviewer's summary; the case study covers two systems (the Apache web server and Gnumeric). The duplicate_block signal compares only the diff's own added lines, so a copy of code already in the repository reaches the finder only through a comment trigger or through the finder's search for an added routine's body; the card adds a "copy of / duplicate of" comment trigger to the planned four, and the Example's bad half carries two comments ("copied from total(); keep in sync" and "copy of total(): same steps as total()") so that each of the four comment triggers matches a bad-half line and none matches the good half. Not carried: Charalampidou et al., XP '17 Scientific Workshops, DOI 10.1145/3120459.3120465 (fetched abstract: "interest probability of code clones seems to be higher than the other two examined code smells"), a hedged workshop result on change-proneness that adds nothing the fetched anchors lack; SonarSource S1871 (fetched; identical branch bodies, one-line branches exempt), whose remedy is combining the conditions, not extracting a routine; SonarSource S1192, since a repeated literal belongs to the variables and numerics topic; Wagner et al. arXiv:1803.10542, Roy, Zibran and Koschke arXiv:2005.01005 and arXiv:2409.08555 (**unfetched**: arxiv.org denied, WebSearch budget spent), none anchoring the card; the Rahman MSR 2010 abstract (bird.bib) was not re-opened because the EMSE 2012 abstract carries the claim. Both locators and quotations are carried from the topic research and were not re-opened in this run · reception: not contested · notes: confidence moderate. Four static-analysis checks (one of them documented for many languages, four of whose language rules are cited; RSPEC-1192 is also documented in sonar-php, sonar-kotlin, sonar-dotnet, sonar-ruby and sonar-scala) and one official language book agree on the remedy, a named constant in place of a repeated string literal; the SonarSource rules, goconst and the book name the mechanism, a change that must reach every occurrence, while Checkstyle says only that duplication makes maintenance more difficult and PMD names no mechanism. They disagree on the numbers (an occurrence floor from two to four, a length floor from one character (any non-empty literal) to ten characters) and on call arguments, which goconst leaves out by default under the linter runner while the SonarSource, PMD and Checkstyle checks count them, as the card does, so the card takes the three-occurrence and five-character defaults of the multi-language check and reports the others in its Rationale. No research is cited: none of the candidate clone studies (which cover code-block clones) states a claim about repeated literals, so none backs the card. Severity is minor although the SonarSource metadata rates the rule Critical with high maintainability impact, because no source ties repeated literals to failures or to a measured cost. The 'one purpose' condition narrows the tool rules to the case their own rationale names (a change propagated to all occurrences) and to the remedy two checks hedge ('can usually be improved', 'it can be better'); no tool implements it. The bare-word exclusion follows three of the four language rules of the SonarSource check. Its Java rule, PMD, Checkstyle and goconst count such literals. The sonar-python description's own noncompliant example ("action1", three times) contradicts its exception, and the implementation follows the exception. The existing-constant clause rests on the sonar-java implementation and goconst's match-constant default. Checkstyle and PMD state per-file counting, and the sonar-python, sonar-java, sonar-go and SonarJS rules implement it; goconst counts across a package. The card does not carry several things: the exclusions tied to one language's syntax (JSX attributes, require calls, object-literal property keys, type-level literals and member-access keys in the SonarJS rule; format patterns and colour codes in the sonar-python rule; arguments to fmt.Printf, Fprintf and Sprintf and redirect paths, which the sonar-go implementation leaves out and its description does not list); constants that duplicate one another's values (goconst find-duplicates, off by default); repeated numeric literals, which variables-scope-and-numerics owns; and knowledge duplicated across code, data and documentation, which other rules of the topic own.

It's better to make the length a calculated field"; the performance cache localized so that "only the methods within the class have to worry about keeping things straight", each setter recalculating the length; read in the third-party transcription `omarjazaa/The-Pragmatic-Programmer-Book`, `content/topics/topic-09.json`); 97 Things Every Programmer Should Know, thing_30 "Don't Repeat Yourself" (97-things/97-things-every-programmer-should-know `en/thing_30/README.md`, CC BY-NC-SA 3.0) — "DRY can be applied to structures, such as database schema, resulting in normalization." · reception: not contested. Denormalization for performance is the standing counter-practice. The same 97 Things essay admits it "only where it directly addresses an actual rather than an imagined problem". The card admits a stored copy wherever its source cannot change or a mechanism recalculates it on every change of its inputs, which covers a cache kept for speed when it is an input-keyed memo; a hand-maintained cache, which the formulation admits 'for performance reasons' when 'not exposed to the outside world', is not admitted, since no openable source states it and the UI guidance rejects it. The topic's other proposed formulation locators are not named as the card's formulation: Clean Code ch. 12 "No Duplication" (isEmpty returning 0 == size()), APOSD ch. 2 §2.2 (an emphasis shade specified apart from the colour it derives from) and TAOUP ch. 4 "The SPOT Rule" corollaries (caching as possibly premature optimization). The card follows none of their wording, and TAOUP's caching caveat is carried by the openable 97 Things essay. · notes: confidence moderate. The evidence is official documentation of three kinds. The first is one UI framework's normative guidance, with worked bug examples: the packing-list counter, the selected-item label and the mirrored prop. The second is one database's generated-column mechanism. The third is one language's cache documentation and FAQ. No empirical defect measure for stored derived values is carried. The run's search budget was exhausted, so no paper search was re-run; the topic's candidate papers concern code clones, not derived data. The guidance is written for UI component state. Its extension to objects, records and database rows rests on its own normalization analogy and on the generated-column and cached_property mechanisms, which the card's Source caveat states. The card's second accepted case is limited to a copy that a mechanism recalculates on every change of its inputs (a generated column, useMemo, an lru_cache keyed through `__eq__`/`__hash__`); a copy refreshed by hand in each write path is flagged, as the packing-list solution directs. Severity major rests on the documented bugs and the "less error-prone" statement, not on a measured rate. Two conditions are not carried. One is the "actual, not imagined, problem" condition on denormalization for speed, which is formulation only. The other is the framework's memoization threshold ("If the overall logged time adds up to a significant amount (say, 1ms or more), it might make sense to memoize that calculation."), a render-time measure for one framework; the card's two accepted cases hold whatever the cost. An emptiness flag computed from a size is not named as a case in the card, since no fetched source names it; the triggers still reach `is_empty`. `cached_property` itself "allows writes", so the card's "nothing else writes the copy" is stricter than the mechanism, and the finder treats a direct write to a cached attribute as one more write path. The triggers are wider than the topic spine's. They add any receiver name (Go receivers, field writes on other objects), compound assignment (`+=`), a `selected` name in field assignments (so a selected element copied out of a list, such as `self.selected_item = self.items[index]`, `this.selectedItem = this.items.find(...)` or `m.selected = m.items[i]`, reaches the card), the SQL `numeric`, `integer` and `bigint` column types, `pub(crate)`, `is_empty` in declarations, Go `sync.OnceValue`/`OnceFunc`, `memoize` and `@cache`/`.cache`. Look-arounds keep `account`, `discount`, `encounter`, `country`, `consumer`, `summary` and `assume` from firing. `useState` keeps every component file with local state in reach, which is where the evidence's examples live. Ownership: a duplicated code block, a repeated literal and a decision encoded in several modules belong to other rules of the topic. A value derived from data held in another table, module or service is outside this card.

(the implementation compares consecutive branches only, and asks for the same comments too) · topic: duplication-and-single-source-of-truth (research/software-craft/duplication-and-single-source-of-truth.md) · formulation: 97 Things Every Programmer Should Know, thing 30 "Don't Repeat Yourself" (Steve Smith; 97-things/97-things-every-programmer-should-know `en/thing_30/README.md`, https://raw.githubusercontent.com/97-things/97-things-every-programmer-should-know/master/en/thing_30/README.md, fetched): "Copy-and-paste *if-then* or *switch-case* logic is among the easiest to detect and correct." · reception: not contested · notes: confidence moderate. Five checkers across Java, Python, Go, JavaScript/TypeScript and Rust agree that identical branches are duplicate code or a probable copy-paste error, but no source measures a fault rate, so severity stays minor. The one-statement exemption comes from S1871 alone: its documentation says "single line of code", the sonar-java implementation counts statements, and the sonar-python check SameBranchCheck (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SonarSource/sonar-python/master/python-checks/src/main/java/org/sonar/python/checks/SameBranchCheck.java, `isOnASingleLine`) and the eslint-plugin-sonarjs check (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SonarSource/eslint-plugin-sonarjs/master/src/rules/no-duplicated-branches.ts, `hasRequiredSize`: `tokens[tokens.length - 1].loc.end.line > tokens[0].loc.start.line`) measure the lines a body spans, so the card's statement unit is sonar-java's. Error Prone, clippy and Ruff also flag one-statement duplicates, and the card's Limits record that other reading. The overlap, guard and binding-type conditions come from clippy's match_same_arms implementation. The fix's placement follows the same merge test: the later arm moves back when no arm between them overlaps it, otherwise the earlier arm moves forward. The card applies them to if chains by analogy, because an if chain also tests its conditions in order. The card does not flag branches that share only leading or trailing statements: the one check for that, branches_sharing_code, is nursery and allow by default, so the card names it only as a bound in its Limits. Consecutive identical conditions (clippy ifs_same_cond) are a control-flow defect and not this card's. The Finding output clause that keeps side-effecting conditions evaluated, joined in their original order with the short-circuit or, is the drafter's guard on the fix and has no source fragment; Error Prone's own suggested fix replaces the whole if with the else branch. Ownership: control-flow owns conditionals, and its evidence layer also opened S1871. If control-flow ships an identical-branch card, DSN-27 defers to it through a DEFER_TO entry. The design note's other formulation locators, Refactoring 2nd ed. §3.2 "Duplicated Code" and Clean Code ch. 17 G5, are dropped: they cannot be opened, and the openable essay carries the formulation. Example: java, good half compiled with javac.

Lampson, "Hints for Computer System Design", Proc. 9th ACM Symposium on Operating Systems Principles (SOSP '83), Operating Systems Review 17(5):33-48, 1983, doi:10.1145/800217.806614, §2.4 "Making implementations work", hint "Keep secrets of the implementation" (copy in papers-we-love/papers-we-love `comp_sci_fundamentals_and_history/hints-for-computer-system-design.pdf`, a version its p. 1 footnote calls slightly revised from the paper as published in Operating Systems Review, running header July 1983, p. 10, https://raw.githubusercontent.com/papers-we-love/papers-we-love/main/comp_sci_fundamentals_and_history/hints-for-computer-system-design.pdf), fetched: "Keep secrets of the implementation. Secrets are assumptions about an implementation that client programs are not allowed to make (paraphrased from [5]). In other words, they are things that can change; the interface defines the things that cannot change (without simultaneous changes to both implementation and client). Obviously, it is easier to program and modify a system if its parts make fewer assumptions about each other. On the other hand, the system may not be easier to design—it’s hard to design a good interface. And there is a tension with the desire not to hide power." / "There is another danger in keeping secrets. One way to improve performance is to increase the number of assumptions that one part of a system makes about another; the additional assumptions often allow less work to be done, sometimes a lot less. For instance, if a set of size n is known to be sorted, a membership test takes time log n rather than n. This technique is very important in the design of algorithms and the tuning of small modules. In a large system the ability to improve each part separately is usually more important." (its [5] is Britton et al., "A procedure for designing abstract interfaces for device interface modules", ICSE 1981); R. Mo, Y. Cai, R. Kazman, L. Xiao, Q. By directly exposing their internals, Data Classes break encapsulation, and therefore reduce the system's maintainability and understandability. Moreover, classes tend to strongly rely on their data representation, which makes for a brittle design. Refactoring a Data Class should focus on restoring a good data-behaviour proximity. In most cases, that means moving the operations defined on the data back into the class. The normative rule rests on a tool rule and on official guidelines (PMD DataClass, C++ Core Guidelines C.2 and C.4, Rust API Guidelines, clippy). The study corroborates only at method level and only as a co-occurrence: it covers Java-only projects, it counts read-only feature envy, and it found no change-proneness rise for that smell. The card narrows PMD's whole-class rule to write-back on a type with an invariant. A holder whose fields vary independently, and which outside code only reads or writes while keeping no condition on its members, neither a bound on one nor a relation among several, stays out of the finding, although PMD would flag it. An immutable record-style carrier is skipped even when its constructor validates, copies or normalizes; a carrier whose fields can be reassigned, such as a data class that is not frozen, is judged by its invariant. Three phrases of the drafted statement were dropped or replaced: "where the holder has a single user, move the data to that user" became PMD's unconditioned "in some other cases"; "a transfer object at a boundary" was dropped because no fetched source names it, and such an object is covered by the no-invariant property and by the skip for a default, clamp or normalization a caller applies to a member only for its own use, which rests on C.2's invariant as a condition a constructor establishes for the public member functions to assume and on C-STRUCT-PRIVATE's passive data structures whose public fields clients can mutate arbitrarily; "query methods that serve co-located behaviour stay allowed" was dropped for want of a fetched source and replaced by C.4's helper that needs no direct access to the representation, limited to a helper that calls only the type's own operations and reads no field or accessor to decide a write back into the object, so that the card's own bad half is not skipped. PEP 557 and C++ Core Guidelines C.2 and C.4 were added as fetched evidence; the PEP 557 `frozen` fragment backs the Limits sentence on carriers whose fields can be reassigned. Sjøberg et al., TSE 2013, DOI 10.1109/TSE.2012.89 (**relayed** only through Palomba 2018 §2: "smells do not always constitute a problem, and that often class size impacts maintainability more than the presence of smells") is not carried in the card. Trigger changes: the record-declaration trigger and `@Getter` were dropped, because a record's fields cannot be reassigned and a getter-only holder cannot receive a write-back. The annotation trigger `@(Data|Setter)\b|@dataclass\b` was dropped, because it names Java and Python annotations that the TypeScript bad half cannot show. Trigger 1 matches any read of the same object inside a setter's arguments, with `set` followed by an upper-case letter or an underscore, so `set_balance(acct.balance() - x)` and `SetBalance(acct.Balance() - x)` match while `cache.set(k, cache.get(k) + 1)` does not. Trigger 3 matches a read of any field of the same object on the right-hand side, such as `order.status = order.total > 100 ? ...`. All four triggers compile under Python re, and each matches one line of the bad half; none matches the good half or the negative lines `self.balance -= x`, `this.setBalance(this.getBalance() - x);`, `cache.set(k, cache.get(k) + 1)`, `if (a.x == a.y) {`, `x.a <= x.b`, `const total = order.total + tax;` and `@DataProvider`. The Example's good half compiles under tsc --noEmit --strict (tsc 6.0.2) with `declare const account: Account; declare const amount: number;` in scope and the elided body filled, and the bad half compiles under the same flags with `Account` declared with `getBalance`, `setBalance`, `withdrawnToday`, `dailyLimit` and `limitReached`.

For trivial accessors kept to keep the representation changeable: Code Complete ch. 6 and Effective Java Item 16 (formulation), SonarSource S1104's fix, Rust API Guidelines C-STRUCT-PRIVATE, Effective Go 'Getters', .NET 'Field Design', and the Lombok @Data practice (reception). Against them: C++ Core Guidelines C.131, Google Python Style §3.15 and §2.13.4, Google TypeScript Style 'Getters and setters', the TypeScript Handbook, PEP 8, A Philosophy of Software Design §5.1 and §19.6 and Clean Code ch. 6 (formulation), and A. Holub and Y. Bugayenko, who argue against accessors altogether (reception). The card ships because a sourced condition separates the cases: whether a public attribute can later gain behaviour behind the same access syntax (PEP 8; Google Python §2.13.1 and §2.13.2); where it can and the language's design guidelines admit a public instance field, the property-language guides agree that the pass-through pair goes, and where it cannot (S1104, C-STRUCT-PRIVATE, Effective Go, against C.131) the card does not reach · notes: confidence moderate — the rule rests on fetched official documentation and style guides for the two first-class languages with properties (the Google Python and TypeScript guides state it as a directive, PEP 8 as "it is best", the TypeScript Handbook as "very rarely useful" and "fine"), with C.131 for the definition of trivial and the examples of non-trivial semantics; no empirical measure of cost exists among the sources, so severity stays suggestion and the Caveat names a style cost, not a measured clarity or defect cost. The Thesis adds "whose design guidelines admit a public instance field" because the .NET Field Design guideline forbids public instance fields in a language with properties; there the replacement for a trivial property is not a public field, and the card does not carry that language's form; the Limits' statement of the documented guidance carries the same precondition. The Thesis reaches pairs only: the lone pass-through getter that the Google TypeScript guide also discourages ("consider making it readonly") stays a Limits note, since Google Python §2.13.2 counts a read-only property as a legitimate use. A pair forwarding to a collaborator's member is excluded because the Google TypeScript guide's own good example does that. The Limits and Validator exclude a pair that overrides an accessor or property a supertype defines, implements an abstract property of an abstract base class, or is overridden by a subtype's own accessor, because the fix fails to compile or run there: reproduced with tsc 6.0.2 --strict (TS2610 for a field overriding a base get/set pair, TS2611 for a get/set pair overriding a base field) and python3 (TypeError on instantiating a class whose field replaces an abstract property, AttributeError "property 'size' of 'After' object has no setter" when a field replaces a pair over a base's read-only property); the TypeScript 4.0 release notes, the Python Descriptor Guide and the abc documentation state each mechanism. The Validator skips a getter and setter method pair the change does not add or that code outside the change calls, matching the Limits, because replacing methods with a field changes every call site and PEP 8 ties a public attribute to a commitment to avoid backwards incompatible changes (the skeptic reproduced the gap this closes: a pre-existing `o.get_size()` caller raising AttributeError after an added pair was replaced); a property pair keeps its callers' syntax and stays in reach. The fix renames each use of the backing field in the class and in any subtype or other code that reads or writes it, and rewrites each method-pair call in the change, so that it compiles: the skeptic reproduced TS2339 when a subtype's `this.countValue += 1` was left behind, and the fixed form (`count` renamed in Base and Sub) compiles under tsc 6.0.2 --strict. The Example uses typescript, not the java the series assigned: the rule does not reach Java (no properties), so a Java pair would illustrate the Limits' opposite case; both halves compile with tsc --noEmit --strict --target es2022 (callers `c.count = 3` unchanged across the two). The fifth trigger was narrowed from any `get`/`set` call to a declaration at line start (optional access modifier, name, parameter list, optional return type, opening brace), so that the getter calls in every file of a language the rule does not reach do not dispatch the card; Python accessor methods are caught by the `def (get|set)_` trigger and properties by the decorator trigger; of the five triggers, the second and third match the Example's bad half. The card does not carry public fields in languages without properties, fields exposed wider than their callers need, or a data holder whose behaviour lives elsewhere, which the topic owns as separate rules, nor a mutable internal object returned by an accessor (SpotBugs EI_EXPOSE_REP), which belongs to mutable-state-and-immutability.

- **DSN-36** · J. Soto, J. McCall, "SE-0117: Allow distinguishing between public access and public overridability", Swift Evolution, status Implemented (Swift 3.0) (swiftlang/swift-evolution main, proposals/0117-non-public-subclassable-by-default.md, https://raw.githubusercontent.com/swiftlang/swift-evolution/main/proposals/0117-non-public-subclassable-by-default.md) §Motivation — "A subclass that overrides methods of its superclass is intricately intertwined with it. The two systems are not composed, and their behavior cannot be understood independently. For example, a programmer who changes how methods on a class delegate to each other is very likely to break subclasses that override those methods, as such subclasses can often only be written by observing the existing pattern of behavior. Within a single module, this can be tolerable, but across library boundaries it's very problematic unless the superclass has established firm rules from the beginning. It has frequently been observed that designing a class well for subclassing takes far more effort than just designing it for ordinary use, precisely because these rules of delegation do need to be carefully laid out if independently-designed subclasses are going to have any chance of working." (fetched; the proposal's later "within a single module, where the superclass and subclasses are co-designed, these problems are more manageable: testing both systems in conjunction is more reasonable" answers its "Moreover" paragraph on mocking the superclass and composing two subclasses, not the delegation dependency, so the card does not use it) · The Swift Programming Language, "Access Control" §Modules, Source Files, and Packages (swiftlang/swift-book main, TSPL.docc/LanguageGuide/AccessControl.md, https://raw.githubusercontent.com/swiftlang/swift-book/main/TSPL.docc/LanguageGuide/AccessControl.md) — "A *module* is a single unit of code distribution --- a framework or application that's built and shipped as a single unit and that can be imported by another module with Swift's `import` keyword." (fetched; the sense of SE-0117's "module", which is why the card draws its line at a library built and released as one unit rather than at a source-level module, a file in some languages and a namespace inside a crate in others) · Python Software Foundation, The Python Tutorial, "Classes" §9.5 Inheritance (python/cpython main, Doc/tutorial/classes.rst, https://raw.githubusercontent.com/python/cpython/main/Doc/tutorial/classes.rst) — "Derived classes may override methods of their base classes. The library-boundary condition and the within-library tolerance follow SE-0117 ("can be tolerable"), read with the Swift book's definition of a module as a unit of code distribution, and Checkstyle's library-only scope, so the Thesis keeps them rather than the unscoped wording of the formulation. The Thesis covers methods that already have an implementation; supplying abstract or required methods, which a skeletal class, an ABC and a trait ask for, goes to Limits. The trait clause applies the class mechanism to default methods on the Rust book's statement that defaults call implementor-supplied methods: an implementor that keeps a default overrides a method that default calls only under the documented-self-use condition, which is why the title names trait implementors. The Example is a trait-form case whose bad line names Sink as another crate's trait with a default write_line that the default write_lines calls undocumented: its good half compiles with rustc 1.97.0 --edition 2021 --crate-type=lib --emit=metadata, and run against two versions of the trait the bad half counted 3 and then 0 lines once the default write_lines stopped calling write_line, with identical output, while the good half counted 3 both times (a local reproduction, not evidence). The embedding clause rests on Effective Go's receiver statement only, and Deref-based delegation is not covered (no source). Triggers: the embedded-field pattern requires a pointer or package-qualified type, so it misses an unqualified same-package embedding; this keeps it from firing on NumPy-style docstring headers and JSX text lines. The impl pattern skips std derive-style traits. Because the pre-pass matches added lines only, the impl pattern also matches an indented method taking &self or &mut self, and the embedded-field pattern an exported method on an exported receiver type, so an override added to an existing impl or a shadowing method added to a type whose embedding is unchanged still dispatches the card (1 job on each test diff); neither matches a constructor without a self receiver, fn main, a free function or an unexported method. Ownership: a subtype's pre- and postconditions go to contracts-assertions-and-invariants, and the topic's other rules take hierarchy depth and width and the base author's design-for-extension or closing choice. The relayed inheritance-depth studies (Daly et al. 1996; Prechelt et al. 2003; Jabangwe et al. 2015) do not bear on self-use and are not cited
