the Deref documentation and C-DEREF state the dereference analogue · notes: confidence high for the rule — the standard library's own documentation of two shipped subclasses that are not kinds of their bases (Timestamp, Properties) states the failure, two C++ style standards state the is-a restriction and the member alternative, the Rust book states that inheritance exposes methods that do not apply to a subclass, the TypeScript handbook and a peer-reviewed definition (abstract) state the substitution premise, and Effective Go, the Go FAQ and the Rust Deref documentation state the embedding and dereference mechanisms; no source measures a failure rate, so the card carries no number and severity major rests on the documented failures (a non-symmetric equality, a store call that fails). Changes against the drafted statement: the drafted "Go embedding and Rust Deref create no subtype of the inner type, so the question there is only what the outer type exposes" is revised, because Effective Go ("it also satisfies all three interfaces") and the Go FAQ (a type "automatically satisfies any interface that specifies a subset of its methods") make an embedding type usable wherever an interface of the inner type is expected, and the Deref documentation ("Values of type `&T` are coerced to values of type `&U`") makes a dereferencing wrapper usable where a reference to the inner type is expected, so the card applies the same test to both; "the values it accepts" is carded as the Properties case — an inherited routine that admits values the subclass's own rules forbid — since a precondition narrowed on an override belongs to contracts-assertions-and-invariants; "the compiler checks only that signatures are compatible" is rewritten to what the sources state, the handbook's signature check (error 2416) and the shipped Timestamp class that passes it; the Liskov–Wing citation, unfetched in the draft, is fetched as its abstract from a GitHub-hosted ACM metadata copy and is quoted from that abstract only; the embedding clause rests on the Go FAQ's analogy to subclassing and Effective Go's mechanism, with no official Go page stating the every-gained-method test, whose wording comes from the Uber guide. Triggers: the three drafted patterns kept, the first with its type-parameter group widened from `<[^>]*>` to `<.*>` so that a class whose type parameters nest angle brackets (`public class SortedList<E extends Comparable<E>> extends ArrayList<E>`) matches, and the second also matching a class header whose base list starts on the next line (`class Foo(`); added a Go embedded-field pattern (an exported or package-qualified type name alone on a line, optionally behind `*`, with optional type arguments in brackets and an optional struct tag, before an optional trailing comment; it misses unexported embedded types such as `*node`, and it also fires on interface embedding and on a lone capitalised identifier in other languages, which the Validator dismisses) and a Rust `impl … Deref(Mut) … for` pattern, since none of the drafted patterns matched the Go example. Not carried: the inheritance-depth experiments (Daly et al., ICSM 1995 / EMSE 1996; Cartwright, IST 1998; Prechelt et al., JSS 2003), the CK metrics DIT and NOC, the Jabangwe et al. SLR (EMSE 2015) and the Refused (Parent) Bequest smell studies (Khomh et al., EMSE 2012; Palomba et al., EMSE 2018, whose detector flags a class that overrides more than half of its inherited methods) — they measure depth, breadth or an override-ratio smell, not whether a subclass is a kind of its base; the tool rules listed for the topic (Checkstyle DesignForExtension and FinalClass, PMD and Error Prone MissingOverride, Pylint R0901 and super-init-not-called, TypeScript noImplicitOverride, SonarSource S110) were not opened for this card and, by name, check override annotations, hierarchy depth, base-initializer calls or design for extension rather than substitutability. The design note's canon locators — The Pragmatic Programmer 20th anniv. ed. topic 31 "Inheritance Tax", Code Complete 2nd ed. ch. 6 §6.3 ("Implement 'is a' through public inheritance", "Adhere to the Liskov Substitution Principle"), Effective Java 3rd ed. Item 18, Refactoring 2nd ed. "Replace Superclass with Delegate" — state the same rule and are dropped as formulation because openable sources carry it. Ownership: pre- and postconditions of an override → contracts-assertions-and-invariants; hierarchy depth and breadth, self-use and the fragile base class, and designing a class for extension or closing it → the topic's other rules; type parameters → generics-and-parameterization; template method → design-patterns-in-construction.
- **DSN-41** · Soto, J.; McCall, J., SE-0117 "Allow distinguishing between public access and public overridability", Swift Evolution, Implemented (Swift 3.0), https://raw.githubusercontent.com/swiftlang/swift-evolution/main/proposals/0117-non-public-subclassable-by-default.md, Introduction, Motivation and Alternatives considered (fetched): "A `public` class will only be *usable* by other modules, but not *subclassable*. [...] A subclass that overrides methods of its superclass is intricately intertwined with it. The two systems are not composed, and their behavior cannot be understood independently. For example, a programmer who changes how methods on a class delegate to each other is very likely to break subclasses that override those methods, as such subclasses can often only be written by observing the existing pattern of behavior. Within a single module, this can be tolerable, but across library boundaries it's very problematic unless the superclass has established firm rules from the beginning. It has frequently been observed that designing a class well for subclassing takes far more effort than just designing it for ordinary use, precisely because these rules of delegation do need to be carefully laid out if independently-designed subclasses are going to have any chance of working. [...] within a single module, where the superclass and subclasses are co-designed, these problems are more manageable [...] The cost of getting something wrong within a module is very low, since it is easy to fix all of the clients."; Checkstyle check DesignForExtension, since Checkstyle 3.1, https://raw.githubusercontent.com/checkstyle/checkstyle/master/src/site/xdoc/checks/design/designforextension.xml, Description (fetched): "This check makes sense only for library projects (not application projects) which care of ideal OOP-design to make sure that class works in all cases even misusage. [...] ATTENTION: If the method which can be overridden in a subclass has a javadoc comment (a good practice is to explain its self-use of overridable methods) the check will not rise a violation. [...] The check finds classes that have overridable methods (public or protected methods that are non-static, not-final, non-abstract) and have non-empty implementation. [...] Rationale: This library design style protects superclasses against being broken by subclasses." (the page also quotes the formulation source, 2nd ed. Item 17, including "eliminate the class’s self-use of overridable methods entirely"; the card quotes only the page's own text); Scala 3 reference, "Open Classes", https://raw.githubusercontent.com/scala/scala3/main/docs/_docs/reference/other-new-features/open-classes.md (fetched): "An open class typically comes with some documentation that describes the internal calling patterns between methods of the class as well as hooks that can be overridden. We call this the _extension contract_ of the class. It is different from the _external contract_ between a class and its users. [...] However, they are on their own in this case. There is no documented extension contract, and future versions of the class might break the extensions (by rearranging internal call patterns, for instance). [...] for instance, to mock classes in tests, or to apply temporary patches that add features or fix bugs in library classes."; Dart language documentation, "Class modifiers", sections `interface` and `final`, https://raw.githubusercontent.com/dart-lang/site-www/main/src/content/language/class-modifiers.md (fetched): "Libraries outside of the interface's own defining library can implement the interface, but not extend it. This guarantees: [...] When one of the class's instance methods calls another instance method on `this`, it will always invoke a known implementation of the method from the same library. [...] Other libraries can't override methods that the interface class's own methods might later call in unexpected ways. This reduces the fragile base class problem. [...] This prevents subtyping from a class outside of the current library. [...] You can safely add incremental changes to the API. [...] You can call instance methods knowing that they haven't been overwritten in a third-party subclass."; Sullivan, M. J.; Levkivskyi, I., PEP 591 "Adding a final qualifier to typing", Final, Python 3.8, https://raw.githubusercontent.com/python/peps/main/peps/pep-0591.rst, Motivation and Specification (fetched): "A class wasn’t designed to be subclassed or a method wasn't designed to be overridden. Perhaps it would not work as expected, or be error-prone. [...] For example, you may want to prevent unnecessarily tight coupling between base classes and subclasses. [...] You want to retain the freedom to arbitrarily change the class implementation in the future, and these changes might break subclasses. Departures from the drafted statement: the TypeScript course "documents that it is not designed for extension" is dropped because no fetched source states it (the card keeps the private constructor, sourced by TS2675); "a framework or mocking library must subclass at run time" is narrowed to a class "a framework or library requires to be open" (Kotlin all-open) plus the Scala note that ad-hoc extension serves to mock classes in tests; "how their results are used" is rendered as how the method calls the overridable methods (once or repeatedly, order, condition), the forms the fetched JDK, CPython and Rust documentation show; a Dart-style modifier that admits implementation but not extension is added as a closing course. Traits: the Thesis holds a trait whose provided methods call other trait methods to the same courses, anchored on the Rust book's code-sharing analogy, the std write_all doc-comment and C-SEALED; default methods of interfaces in other languages are not named since no fetched source covers them. Ownership: a subtype's pre- and postconditions belong to contracts-assertions-and-invariants and a template method as a pattern to design-patterns-in-construction; this card owns only documenting or closing the self-use. Triggers: the Rust trait pattern is unanchored so it also matches the Example's bad line; the Java class pattern excludes final classes by lookahead; the protected-member pattern catches a hook added to an existing class; a self-call added to an existing public class with no matching line is missed, accepted for breadth control.

These are invoked on an incompletely constructed object and can be difficult to debug if overridden. This is because the subclass usually assumes that the superclass is completely initialized in all methods. If that is not the case, bugs can appear in the constructor, for instance, some fields that are still null may cause a NullPointerException or be stored somewhere else to blow up later. To avoid this problem, only use methods that are static, private, or final in constructors. Note that those methods also must not call overridable methods transitively to be safe." · PMD `ConstructorCallsOverridableMethodRule` implementation (pmd/pmd, main, pmd-java/src/main/java/net/sourceforge/pmd/lang/java/rule/errorprone/ConstructorCallsOverridableMethodRule.java, https://raw.githubusercontent.com/pmd/pmd/main/pmd-java/src/main/java/net/sourceforge/pmd/lang/java/rule/errorprone/ConstructorCallsOverridableMethodRule.java), fetched: `visit(ASTConstructorDeclaration)` returns early only when `node.getEnclosingType().isFinal()` or the class carries lombok's value annotation — "then cannot be overridden"; Drafter's checks with javac/java 21 and python3, checks of the card rather than sources: the bad half with a subclass whose override appends to a field initialized in its declaration throws a NullPointerException at Base.<init>; the good half compiles cleanly under `javac -Xlint:all`; a sealed class whose constructor calls `describe()`, with a final permitted subclass overriding `describe()` to add to a field-initialized list, throws a NullPointerException at Circle.describe from Shape.<init>, which is why the card treats only a final class as closed and keeps a class listing its permitted subclasses within the rule (CA2214's "unsealed" is the C# sense; PMD and SpotBugs skip final classes only); a `clone()` that calls an overridable `reset()` on the copy `super.clone()` returned lets a subclass's override clear the original's shared array, which is why the Validator follows the copy's reference; a `@staticmethod` called through `self` in a Python base `__init__` dispatches to the subclass's static method, which is why the Thesis qualifies static and private where every method is effectively virtual. The TypeScript handbook states the order for a field read in the base constructor; the card applies that order to an override reading a derived field, which the handbook does not show. The C# standard (dotnet/csharpstandard, draft-v9, standard/classes.md §15.11.4 Constructor execution, fetched) runs variable initializers before the base constructor — "Variable initializers are transformed into assignment statements, and these assignment statements are executed *before* the invocation of the base class instance constructor." — which is why the Rationale makes the declaration-initializer clause depend on the order. In Python, where every method is effectively virtual, no class is closed at run time, so the rule reaches every class not marked final for the type checker; the card carries the class-private alias (the tutorial's own `__init__` example) and PEP 591's final as the closed forms. The Go embedding statement is limited to calls through the embedded value's receiver: an embedded type that stores a back-reference to the outer value as an interface and calls through it can reach the outer type's method on a half-built value, which the skeptic reproduced with go 1.24.7 and the card does not claim to exclude. Not carried: SonarSource's OOP50-CPP reference (C++ is outside the corpus's five languages); SpotBugs's "insecure" framing of the clone case (the card keeps the partially initialized state, a correctness concern); PEP 8 "Designing for Inheritance" (double leading underscores for attributes a class intended to be subclassed does not want subclasses to use), which corroborates the alias but is conditioned on that intent; the javac `-Xlint:this-escape` lint (openjdk/jdk jdk-21-ga src/jdk.compiler/share/man/javac.1, fetched by the skeptic), an official compiler statement of the mechanism whose warning follows a module-boundary policy rather than closure. Out of scope for this card: the leak of the object under construction to other code beyond the one-sentence mention, and the pre- and postconditions an override must keep.

The Thesis's "user id and order id" illustrates the playground's "User Identification Numbers" and the typing documentation's UserId. The alias clause covers an alias of the primitive; an alias of the primitive intersected with a unique marker, the FAQ's own spelling of a brand, names a distinct type. Java has no type alias and its mechanism (a record or a class) is distinct by construction; the java.lang.Record javadoc (openjdk/jdk jdk-21-ga `src/java.base/share/classes/java/lang/Record.java`) was opened and states only "A record class is a shallowly immutable, transparent carrier for a fixed set of values", not the distinction, so it is not cited, and JEP 395 is not openable. The sixth trigger catches an alias written by plain assignment, which the typing documentation allows, and a line of a grouped Go type block. The Mars Climate Orbiter loss appears in essay 65 and as C-NEWTYPE's link target; the card carries only C-NEWTYPE's wording "averting certain catastrophic bugs". SWEBOK Guide V4.0 ch. 3 §5.10 is not openable; the V3 transcription's design chapter (ligurio/swebok-v3 `2_software_design.md`) was opened and has no passage on distinct types for units or identifiers. Ownership: identifier spelling and single-name consistency stay with naming-identifiers, boolean parameters with routine-size-and-parameters, and validation of a value crossing a trust boundary with security-hygiene-in-ordinary-code; this card asks for distinctness, not validation.

(golang/website master, _content/doc/faq.md, #variant_types), fetched: "Variant types, also known as algebraic types, provide a way to specify that a value might take one of a set of other types, but only those types." / "We considered adding variant types to Go, but after discussion decided to leave them out because they overlap in confusing ways with interfaces." / "The error example is easy to express using an interface value to hold the error and a type switch to discriminate cases." go-check-sumtype README (alecthomas/go-check-sumtype master, README.md; a fork of BurntSushi/go-sumtype, enabled in golangci-lint as `gochecksumtype` per golangci/golangci-lint main, .golangci.reference.yml), fetched, § "Details and motivation": "Sum types are otherwise known as discriminated unions. That is, a sum type is a finite set of disjoint values. In type systems that support sum types, the language will guarantee that if one has a sum type `T`, then its value must be one of its variants. Go's type system does not support sum types. A typical proxy for representing sum types in Go is to use an interface with an unexported method and define each variant of the sum type in the same package to satisfy said interface. This guarantees that the set of types that satisfy the interface is closed at compile time. [...] The downside of this approach is that Go's type system is not aware of the set of variants, so it cannot tell you whether case analysis over a sum type is complete or not."; § "Usage": "Adding either a `default` clause or a clause to handle `*VariantB` will cause exhaustive checks to pass." The fetched anchors are official documentation from four languages' type checkers (TypeScript, Rust, Python through mypy, Go), plus one pedantic (allow-by-default) clippy lint and one golangci-lint linter. They document the mechanism: what the checker can and cannot verify under each encoding. None measures the defect or comprehension cost of the flat encoding, which is why the severity is minor. Java has no fetched anchor in the card. Records and sealed interfaces enter only through the amber design note, a formulation. The javac diagnostic `compiler.err.not.exhaustive`, "the switch expression does not cover all possible input values" (openjdk/jdk master, src/jdk.compiler/share/classes/com/sun/tools/javac/resources/compiler.properties), was fetched but does not name sealed types, so it is not carried. The card's Example uses a payment only as an illustration. clippy words its remedy "consider a custom `enum`", and the Thesis states that remedy as the rule under the lint's own condition: the three states are distinct cases. Not carried: Wlaschin's limit of 15 combinations ('Designing with types: Discovering new concepts', **unfetched**) and the clause that a better domain concept replaces an exploding enumeration, since no openable source states either. A local rustc 1.97.0 run (`--crate-type=lib --edition=2021 --emit=metadata`, the good half wrapped in `fn refund(receipt: String, reason: String) -> Payment`) confirmed that the Example's good half compiles and gave E0063 ("missing field `reason`") on `Payment::Refunded { receipt }`. The Go standard library uses the closed-interface form itself (golang/go master, src/go/ast/ast.go: "exprNode() ensures that only expression/type nodes can be assigned to an Expr.", fetched). Ownership: clippy `struct_excessive_bools` ("Excessive bools in a struct is often a sign that the type is being used to represent a state machine, which is much better implemented as an enum.") covers state machines, which yield to table-driven-and-state-machines. A boolean argument yields to routine-size-and-parameters. A tag typed as a free string and a bare primitive standing for a domain value are neighbouring rules of this topic, not this card. The Kosar et al. DSL comprehension studies (relayed) bear on the topic's domain-language rule, not on this card.

We would have to keep in mind that `width` is the tuple index `0` and `height` is the tuple index `1`. This would be even harder for someone else to figure out and keep in mind if they were to use our code. Because we haven’t conveyed the meaning of our data in our code, it’s now easier to introduce errors."; "We use structs to add meaning by labeling the data. We can transform the tuple we’re using into a struct with a name for the whole as well as names for the parts"; "Our function signature for `area` now says exactly what we mean"; "This conveys that the width and height are related to each other, and it gives descriptive names to the values rather than using the tuple index values of `0` and `1`. The same design note records that "some users would surely prefer we expose this ability via structural tuples, rather than via a nominal mechanism"; the TypeScript Handbook keeps tuples for convention-based interfaces and the Go wiki leaves unnamed the results whose meaning is clear from context, and the card carries both as Limits rather than as a contest · notes: confidence moderate. The evidence is official language documentation from four ecosystems (Rust, Python, TypeScript, Go) that states the mechanism (parts without names, access by index, mix-ups easier to introduce) and measures no defect rate. No empirical study of positional tuples could be reached through the open channels. The domain-specific-language experiments the topic lists (Kosar, Mernik, Carver, EMSE 17(3) 2012, DOI 10.1007/s10664-011-9172-x; Kosar, Gaberc, Carver, Mernik, EMSE 2018, DOI 10.1007/s10664-017-9593-2; Kosar et al., ComSIS 7(2) 2010) compare a DSL with a general-purpose library and say nothing about this rule, so they are not carried. The Amber note states the claim most directly ("less error-prone") and could be opened, but the topic assigns it to the formulation layer as a language designer's design note, so it is named here and not in the card. The Rust book's case is a tuple passed as a parameter and the CPython case is tuples returned as results. The Thesis extends to a value stored in a field or variable on the same mechanism, and no source restricts the mechanism to parameters or results. The Thesis's instances (width and height, the fields of a returned row) come from the Rust book and from the CPython namedtuple section's csv and sqlite3 result tuples; the Go wiki's latitude and longitude, whose remedy there is names on the results, stays in the Limits; the Example's minimum and maximum follow the formulation. The Limit on named results rests on the Go wiki and keeps its hedge ("may be useful in some contexts"); accepting such names as a fix is the card's scoping on the wiki's clarity claim, and a caller still binds named results by position; it states the trait without naming the language. Grouping a routine's separate parameters into an object belongs to routine-size-and-parameters. Triggers cover: Python tuple annotations, return and variable; TypeScript tuple return types, plus tuple aliases and annotations with primitive elements; Rust tuple return types, parameters and fields, with a lookahead that skips an arrow-function property value such as `sort: (a, b) => ...`; Java pair and triple types; Go signatures with two or more unnamed results of one repeated type, matched by a back-reference so that `(lat, long float64, err error)` and `(*Node, error)` do not match; and a bare return of two values that excludes `nil`, `err`, `ok`, `true` and `false`, so the Go returns `x, nil`, `nil, err`, `x, err` and the comma-ok forms do not dispatch; a return of a sentinel error such as `return 0, ErrNotFound` still dispatches and the Validator skips it as a value and its error. TypeScript labelled tuple elements (`[min: number, max: number]`) do not match. The first bad line of the Example matches the Pair trigger. The good half compiles under javac 21 inside a class that declares `record Range`, `bounds` and a method with `values` in scope. The candidate sources C-NEWTYPE, C-CUSTOM-TYPE, Narrowing, NewType, the clippy bool lints and SWEBOK §5.10 concern other rules of the topic and do not state this one.

(2019), Item 28 'Avoid More Than Two Control Subexpressions in Comprehensions' · reception: not contested in the canon; the sources differ on the iteration-clause threshold (the Google Python guide forbids a second `for` clause, WPS224 allows two and flags a third, and the Effective Python 2nd-ed. item's title draws the line above two control subexpressions); the card states the stricter official-documentation bound and carries the two-clause bound in Limits as a project tolerance · notes: confidence moderate. The rule rests on official documentation (CPython HOWTO, Google Python guide, Rust and OpenJDK API docs, the Rust book) and static-analysis rules (WPS224/WPS307, sonar-java S5612, clippy needless_collect); no study measures the comprehension or defect cost of nested or long pipelines. The clause limits are stated for comprehensions; the card extends them to a flattening step whose function runs its own pipeline by the flatMap definition, and says so in its caveat. The drafted wording "chains several non-trivial steps" is carried as "a step whose inline function exceeds the documented bound", because no source sets a step count and an inline function's length is the only sourced measure of a non-trivial step. The bounds come from two languages: the one-line/60-80-character bound is the Google guide's preference ("might be better") for Python's expression-only lambdas, and the ten-line bound is sonar-java's default for every Java lambda, expression- or block-bodied (its fixture java-checks-test-sources/default/src/main/java/checks/LambdaTooBigCheckCustom.java, https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SonarSource/sonar-java/master/java-checks-test-sources/default/src/main/java/checks/LambdaTooBigCheckCustom.java (fetched), flags the seven-line expression lambda c3 at Max 6), extended in the card to the inline functions of other languages whose inline functions can take a statement block. A chain's length alone is not a finding. The inspect/peek docs show that developers need to see values inside a chain; they do not state the naming remedy, which rests on the HOWTO's interface-point and intermediate-inputs-and-outputs passage and on the style guides' rewrites. The HOWTO's lambda section also reproduces Fredrik Lundh's lambda-to-named-def refactoring rules, a further formulation of named step functions that the card does not name. The relayed papers from the candidate list (Khatchadourian et al., FASE 2020; Mazinanian et al., OOPSLA 2017; Rosales et al., SPE 2023) describe stream and lambda use and misuse but say nothing about naming intermediate results, so the card does not cite them. Ownership: side effects in a step, lazy pipelines whose effects are deferred or skipped, folds, closures over mutable state, loop-versus-iterator cost, failure propagation and parallel pipelines are left to their own rules.

The fetched evidence is official documentation from four ecosystems (OpenJDK streams, MDN for the array methods, the Rust standard library and book, the CPython functional HOWTO) plus one research paper's statement of the evaluation-order mechanism. No source measures a defect rate, so severity major rests on the documented failure modes rather than on measured cost: effects elided or never run, effects cut short by short-circuiting or repeated by a sort, and exceptions or incorrect answers from modifying the source. Hughes caveat: the quoted sentences are the paper's summary of how the advantages of functional programming "are often summed up", which it then calls a catalogue that "says a lot about what functional programming is not (it has no assignment, no side effects, no flow of control) but not much about what it is"; the card carries only the evaluation-order mechanism and not "eliminates a major source of bugs". Sequential scope: the Java section's thread-safety, visibility and ordering clauses and its statelessness example are parallel-pipeline hazards and are not carried, because parallel pipelines belong to concurrency correctness. The "more safely and efficiently" and "safer, more efficient, and more amenable to parallelization" reasons for reduction are left out for the same reason. For-each gathering: the claim that a terminal for-each does not add the pipeline's result to an outside variable or collection (the spine's folded foreach-reports-only, severity minor) is not carried. Within sequential scope its only documented ground is the Side-effects example on `forEach(s -> results.add(s))`, "This code unnecessarily uses side-effects. If executed in parallel, the non-thread-safety of ArrayList would cause incorrect results [...] Furthermore, using side-effects here is completely unnecessary; the forEach() can simply be replaced with a reduction operation that is safer, more efficient, and more amenable to parallelization", whose only failure is a parallel one and whose remaining reason is a design cost, so it belongs on its own minor card or in pending-evidence rather than in this major card. The comprehension clause rests on two things in the HOWTO: its framing of comprehensions as map and filter notation borrowed from a functional language, and its general statement on side effects. No fetched source names a side effect inside a comprehension specifically. Go has no stream library in its standard library; the rule reaches Go code through callback-taking helpers and user-written map and filter functions, and no Go source is carried. Not carried: Khatchadourian, Tang, Bagherzadeh and Ray, 'An empirical study on the use and misuse of Java 8 streams', FASE 2020 (DOI 10.1007/978-3-030-45234-6_5, **relayed**: 34 projects, 5.53 million lines, 719 patches, performance the crosscutting concern of most fixes); Mazinanian, Ketkar, Tsantalis and Dig, 'Understanding the use of lambda expressions in Java', OOPSLA 2017 (**relayed**: lambda adoption growing, mostly used for behaviour parameterization); Rosales, Basso, Rosà and Binder, 'Large-scale characterization of Java streams', SPE 2023 (DOI 10.1002/spe.3213, **relayed**: title and venue only). None of the relayed statements says anything about side effects in a stream callback. clippy `suspicious_map` (fetched, clippy_lints/src/methods/mod.rs) is recorded as the one fetched counter-position on observation steps and is not carried: it flags a map followed by a count ("Maybe `map` was confused with `filter`") and advises "If the `map` call is intentional, this should be rewritten using `inspect`. Or, if you intend to drive the iterator to completion, you can just use `for_each` instead."; the card flags the first remedy and follows the second, resting on the observation steps' own documentation ("This method exists mainly to support debugging"; "It's more common for `inspect()` to be used as a debugging tool than to exist in your final code") and on the documented skipping of an observation step's action for elements a short-circuiting step or a count optimizes away. Ownership: shared mutable state between components goes to mutable-state-and-immutability, a lazy pipeline that nothing consumes is that topic's own concern beyond the callback, and failure propagation goes to error-and-exception-handling. A terminal for-each step's change to the source it traverses stays in this rule, because the forEach and forEachOrdered parameters are declared non-interfering and non-interference applies to sequential pipelines. Triggers: the first matches a step call, including a sort or sort_by call, a Go Sort or Slice call and a helper whose name ends in Func, that has on the same line a compound assignment, an increment, a field assignment, an assignment inside a one-line callback block, an append, a method reference to a mutating method on a lower-case receiver such as seen::add, a mutating call or a print (the Example's bad line); its inc alternative excludes includes. The second matches a for-each whose function calls add, push, append, put, insert, extend, remove, splice, delete, clear, pop or shift, the shapes of a change to the source it traverses; the validator sets aside such a call on another collection. The third matches every peek or inspect, so the finder can tell debugging output from another effect. The fourth matches a step, including a Go ForEach, Sort, Slice or Func helper, whose callback block opens at the end of the line, which reaches multi-line callbacks. The fifth matches a comprehension or generator whose expression calls a mutating method or print. The sixth matches a comprehension or generator whose condition, after its for clause, calls a mutating method or print, such as the seen.add dedupe idiom. A function passed by name, other than a mutating method reference handed to a non-for-each step, is reached only when another pattern matches its line, so a for-each handed items::remove is not reached on its own; with scope hunk the finder reads a named function's body only when the hunk shows it.

The backing is official documentation (MDN for arrays and the return statement, the JDK `Iterable` API, the Rust standard library and Reference, the Go `iter` package, CPython `itertools`) plus four lint rules, one of them (`checkForEach`) off by default; Ruff SIM110 and Clippy manual_find anchor the Thesis's choice of a short-circuiting step when the stop yields the result; no source measures how often an emulated stop causes a defect, so the card carries no number. The throw-only stop is stated for JavaScript arrays (MDN) and Java iterables (the JDK); the impossibility of break and continue in a callback is stated for Rust closures; the card generalizes these to any routine that calls a callback once per element and carves out, in its Limits, protocols whose callback return value stops the iteration (the Go `iter` yield returning false, Rust `try_for_each` with `ControlFlow::Break`). The original wording also covered work that must skip an element; the card does not carry that part, because a bare return in the callback ends only the current call and the step goes on with the next element (MDN `return` and `forEach`), and ESLint's `checkForEach` lists such a bare return among its correct examples; eslint-plugin-unicorn `no-for-each` prefers `for…of` over every `forEach` and lists continue among the benefits, a broader preference than this card's defect, which the card does not carry either. A captured flag that only gathers a result across all elements, with no stop, is a side effect in a callback rather than an emulated stop and is left to that topic's own rule. Python's built-in `any` and `all` documentation (`Doc/library/functions.rst`) answered 404 on raw.githubusercontent.com at `main`, `3.13` and `3.14`, so short-circuiting in Python is anchored only by `itertools.takewhile`, and find, any and all rest on the Rust and MDN statements. Python has no for-each step in its standard library. Go has `container/ring` `(*Ring).Do` (golang/go `src/container/ring/ring.go`, https://raw.githubusercontent.com/golang/go/master/src/container/ring/ring.go, fetched: "Do calls function f on each element of the ring, in forward order.") and `sync.Map.Range` (golang/go `src/sync/map.go`, fetched: "If f returns false, range stops the iteration."), whose stop protocol the Limits carve out. The rule reaches these, a project helper or library routine that calls a callback per element, and a function iterator called directly with a callback; the Example uses such a helper (`for_each(items, send_fresh)`). The relayed candidate papers (Khatchadourian, Tang, Bagherzadeh and Ray, FASE 2020, LNCS 12076; Mazinanian, Ketkar, Tsantalis and Dig, OOPSLA 2017, PACMPL 1(OOPSLA) art. 85; Rosales, Basso, Rosà and Binder, SPE 2023, doi:10.1002/spe.3213) characterize stream and lambda use, and their relayed statements say nothing about stopping an iteration from a callback, so the card does not cite them; the WebSearch budget was exhausted in this session and no relayed item was needed. Severity stays minor as the spine set it; a return whose value the step discards changes what the enclosing routine computes, which the verifier may raise. All eleven sources the card cites, and the two Go files named in these notes, were opened with curl and every quoted fragment was matched against the fetched text. The good half compiled with python3 `compile()` inside a function scope defining `send`, and the bad half, completed with a `for_each` helper, ran on the same input and sent the same items. Both triggers compile and each matches a line of the bad half.

The topic's canon locator, PP topic 30 'Transforming Programming', frames pipelines in general and supplies no wording for this rule · reception: contested. Replace reduce: What's New In Python 3.0 and the Functional Programming HOWTO (an explicit loop more readable '99 percent of the time'), eslint-plugin-unicorn no-array-reduce (recommended config; by default it allows only simple arithmetic), and clippy unnecessary_fold (for folds that a named method expresses). Keep reduce: the java.util.stream package documentation (a reduction preferred over a mutative accumulation as 'more abstract' and parallelizable), MDN (summing, promise sequencing and function piping are acceptable uses; naming mitigates the readability cost), Hughes 1989 (reduce as glue from which named functions are defined), and, as formulation, clean-code-javascript, Airbnb §11.1 and Rust Design Patterns. Unicorn itself is disabled in its unopinionated config and tells users who prefer functional programming to disable it. The card flags only the two cases where the sources on both sides point the same way: a named operation exists (clippy, the HOWTO, MDN's 'better alternatives', Hughes's named folds), or the accumulator is mutated or a growing accumulator is copied (MDN's 'much clearer' and its Description's 'In such cases [...] it's better to use a for loop instead'; the HOWTO and unicorn prefer the loop for reduce in general). It leaves unflagged a fold that has no named equivalent and neither mutates its accumulator nor copies a growing one, and the project context decides that case · notes: confidence moderate. The evidence is official documentation and tool-rule rationale, so it records judgment, not measurement. The quadratic costs are analytic bounds: MDN states O(N^2) worst case and cites one real-world instance, and the Java documentation states O(n^2) in characters. MDN words its mutated-accumulator advice as 'you may want to convert [...] which is much clearer'. The card states it as the rule because every source that addresses the case points to the loop and none defends the mutating fold. Scope: reduce and fold calls only, as the title says. Three sources were fetched but are not carried: Ruff SIM110 reimplemented-builtin (for loops replaceable by any or all), the Go modernize analyzer slicescontains (golang/tools `go/analysis/passes/modernize/doc.go`: 'replace loops with slices.Contains or slices.ContainsFunc'), and SonarSource S4034 (stream chains such as filter().findFirst().isPresent() to anyMatch). They concern hand-written loops and call chains, not folds, and are candidates for a sibling rule. The chain triggers (findFirst().isPresent(), filter().length compared with 0 or 1) were dropped with them. 'join' is in the named-operation list on OpenJDK Collectors.java (jdk-21-ga, lines 332-333) and CPython Python/bltinmodule.c (line 2880), both fetched. The condition 'names its accumulator' became a Limits mitigation (MDN: naming 'can help mitigate'), because no source makes an unnamed accumulator a defect of its own. The relayed Java-stream studies are not carried (Khatchadourian et al., FASE 2020, LNCS 12076; Mazinanian et al., OOPSLA 2017; Rosales et al., Software: Practice and Experience 2023, DOI 10.1002/spe.3213). Their relayed statements concern stream and lambda adoption, parallelism and performance fixes, not reduce against named operations or loops. The triggers were rewritten. The given patterns wrote literal dots as backslash-dot, which the validator rejects. The reduce-with-spread/push pattern only matched lines the reduce-call pattern already matches, so it was dropped. Added: capitalized helper names (Reduce, Fold), explicit type arguments, the reducing collector, and reduce.call/apply as an optional suffix of the one pattern, so that the pattern matches the Example's bad half. Go's standard library has no reduce, so the Example's bad half calls a package-local generic helper. Both halves compile and pass go vet and gofmt with go 1.24.7.

SPE 2023) do not state this claim and are not cited; the lazy case (a discarded lazy map whose effects never run) overlaps the neighbouring rule on unconsumed lazy pipelines and is kept here because the Rust map documentation and the rustc lint name it as the canonical instance of a map used for effects, so the review workflow's ownership table decides which card reports it; severity stays minor per the facets though the lazy case loses the effect and the verifier may calibrate it up; side effects inside a map whose result is used, failure propagation through a pipeline, folds and parallel pipelines are outside the card; the triggers carry no pattern for a comprehension standing alone as a statement, so such a comprehension is checked only inside a hunk another trigger matched; Go has no map or comprehension in its standard library, so the rule reaches Go only through a mapping helper a codebase defines.

The wording follows the fetched documentation: the OpenJDK non-interference requirement and the Python Tutorial's copy-or-new-collection advice. The topic's canon locator, The Pragmatic Programmer, 20th anniversary ed., topic 30 "Transforming Programming" (ch. 5 "Bend, or Break"), frames a program as a pipeline of transformations and did not supply this rule's wording · reception: not contested · notes: confidence high for the mechanism. The specification or official documentation of each of the five languages says what a structural change during traversal does: an exception or a best-effort fail-fast error, a skipped, repeated or newly visited element, a run-to-run variation, or a compile error. One recommended linter rule reports the pattern. No source measures how often the defect causes failures, so the card states the mechanism with no frequency. The candidate papers (Khatchadourian et al., FASE 2020; Mazinanian et al., OOPSLA 2017; Rosales et al., SPE 2023) are not cited: their relayed statements cover stream adoption, parallelism and performance, not modification of a traversed source. Authoring check, not evidence: the card's Java bad half, run on JDK 21, threw ConcurrentModificationException for [done, done, pending] and finished silently for [pending, done, done], leaving a done task in the list. Scope: the card covers additions and removals only. MDN's warning also covers changing the values of unvisited elements, which the card leaves outside as a non-structural change. A counted loop that reads the collection by position and holds no iterator is outside the rule when every position it reads stays valid (removing from the last position down, or a work queue whose bound re-reads the length): the cited sources cover iterators, iteration methods, for-each and for...of loops and a for loop that holds a vector reference, and MDN admits special cases; a counted loop that removes at its current position and then advances stays inside, by MDN's already-visited deletion clause. A change to a lazy pipeline's source made before its terminal operation starts is made by no loop body or pipeline step, so the card says nothing of it; Java's late-binding sentence is not carried because it is one library's property. Modification by another thread belongs to concurrency correctness, per the topic's ownership note; a parallel pipeline's own step stays inside the rule, since non-interference applies to all pipelines. The allowance for deleting the current map or set entry rests on the unicorn rule, the ECMAScript Map/Set notes and the Go spec's removal clause; Python dicts and Java fail-fast collections keep that deletion inside the rule. Triggers: the proposed patterns are rewritten with [.] to satisfy the validator's backslash-dot rule and broadened (removeAll, retainAll, delete, discard, popitem, flatMap, find, reduce, inspect). One pattern is added for removal from a slice by append(s[:i] or slices.Delete/Insert. A bare add/push/append is not a trigger because it would fire on nearly every diff.

The sides separate on whether the step supplies any argument beyond those the function means to take. The card narrows two exceptions to the cases its sources show: the built-in exception to functions that need no receiver (MDN's Number, unicorn's Boolean), and unicorn's type-predicate allowance to predicates that take only the element, since a predicate with an optional second parameter receives the index as parseInt does.

The cause of this kind of bug can be difficult to track down after the fact, especially when the second piece of code changes the value only sometimes. The Rust compiler guarantees that when you state that a value won't change, it really won't change, so you don't have to keep track of it yourself. (2021), §19.6 "Getters and setters"; Fowler, Refactoring, 2nd ed. (2018), ch. 11 "Remove Setting Method"; Bloch, Effective Java, 3rd ed. (2018), Item 17 "Minimize mutability"; Kimchi, "Coding with Reason", 97 Things Every Programmer Should Know (2010), essay 15 · reception: not contested for a field private to its type, where PMD, Error Prone, typescript-eslint, IDE0044, the Google TypeScript guide and the Kotlin conventions agree. For a field visible outside its type that holds a mutable object, the .NET Field Design guideline ("DO NOT assign instances of mutable types to `readonly` fields") disagrees with the Google TypeScript guide (readonly on every property never reassigned outside the constructor, "these need not be deeply immutable") and the Kotlin conventions (`val` for every property not modified after initialization). The card leaves the declaration half out of that case and keeps the setter half there, which .NET Property Design supports. Effective Go calls getters and setters "often appropriate", so the card flags only a setter that no code calls. · notes: confidence moderate. The evidence is four analyzer rules, all four checking private fields only (Error Prone reports a field only when `canBeRemoved` holds, that is when the field or an enclosing element is private), and the Error Prone check is disabled by default. Alongside them are official style guidance for TypeScript and Kotlin, the .NET design guidelines, and language documentation for the mechanisms (TypeScript readonly, Python Final and frozen dataclasses, Rust immutability, Go's getter/setter idiom). No empirical measure is carried. The Rust passage on why a fixed value helps is about variable bindings, and the card applies its mechanism to fields. The orchestrator's three relayed papers are not carried: Coblenz et al., ICSE 2016 (ResearchGate link only); the Glacier paper, ICSE 2017; and Weber et al., SecDev 2017 (a cmu.edu PDF on a denied host). Their relayed statements are about whole-object and transitive class immutability, and about references reused instead of immutable copies, not about a field's no-reassignment declaration, and no DOI or arXiv id was relayed for them. Scope was changed from the orchestrator's `file` to `callers`. To decide that a field is never reassigned after construction, and that a setter has no caller, the finder must grep the whole repository, because a Go unexported field is visible package-wide and a public or protected member is visible to callers and subclasses. A fifth trigger, a data-class decorator without `frozen=True`, was added for Python. The title changed from "never reassigned after construction ... gets no setter" to "set only while its object is constructed ... has no setter". The Example is Go and shows only the setter half, because Go fields take no no-reassignment modifier.

Coblenz, Sunshine, Aldrich, Myers, Weber, Shull, "Exploring language support for immutability", ICSE 2016, https://www.researchgate.net/publication/303099366_Exploring_language_support_for_immutability, **relayed** (the orchestrator's search snippet): "interviews with professional developers in which participants stated that incorrect state mutations are a major source of bugs, for example an object thought to be immutable changed by some other object because references were reused instead of immutable copies"; DOI 10.1145/2884781.2884798 is from memory, **unfetched**, and is not in the card. · topic: mutable-state-and-immutability (research/software-craft/mutable-state-and-immutability.md) · formulation: SonarSource RSPEC-2384 ("Instead use an unmodifiable Collection [...] or make a copy of the mutable object, and store or return the copy instead."), PMD MethodReturnsInternalArray ("violates object encapsulation since elements can be removed or replaced outside of the object that owns it", the Rationale's encapsulation sentence) and SpotBugs EI_EXPOSE_REP ("exposes the internal representation of the object"), each fetched and quoted above; the topic locator PP topic 34 'Shared State Is Incorrect State' for the design claim that shared mutable state is a cost · reception: contested. Sonar S2384 states without condition that private mutable members "should never be returned to a caller". The Go standard library hands out the owner's storage on purpose and documents the terms: `bytes.Buffer.Bytes` returns a sub-slice of its unexported `buf` whose doc comment says it "aliases the buffer content at least until the next buffer modification", and `bufio.Scanner.Bytes` returns `s.token`, whose underlying array "may point to data that will be overwritten by a subsequent call to Scan. It does no allocation." The JDK's `Map.keySet` (a documented, backed, removal-supporting view) and Rust API Guidelines C-GETTER (`first_mut` returning `&mut self.first` as the conventional getter) corroborate the deliberate side. PMD ("It is safer to return a copy"), SpotBugs ("better approach in many situations") and Uber ("be wary of scenarios when they need to be copied") stop short of Sonar's "never". Separating condition, stated in the Limits, the Validator's skip and the bold question: a routine whose documentation declares that its result shares the owner's storage, and states until when the result stays valid or what a change made through it affects, hands out that storage by design and is outside the rule. The rule covers storage handed out without that declaration. The undeclared side rests on S2384, PMD, SpotBugs, Uber and the JDK view semantics, and the declared side on the two Go standard-library doc comments · notes: confidence high for undeclared exposure of a private mutable collection, array, map, slice or buffer. The declared-alias exception rests on two fetched Go standard-library doc comments, and its "typically to avoid a copy" rests on Scanner.Bytes's "It does no allocation" alone. Scope: the three analyzer rules check Java, and the reach to the other four languages rests on their documented semantics. Severity major follows the drafting facets and the evidence that ties exposed mutable state to bugs and unexpected state changes. Sonar ships S2384 at default severity Minor with maintainability impact LOW, so the verifier may calibrate it down. `step` is [design, implement, refactor] instead of the proposed [design, implement, review], because the controlled vocabulary reserves `review` for the shape and description of the change; refactor is the taxonomy's "changing structure while keeping behaviour". Skeptic revisions applied: (1) the separating condition above, together with the two Go standard-library Source items; (2) the Rationale's assignment clause is scoped to assigning the returned result, since the Python copy documentation states it of Python and Effective Go says arrays are copied on assignment; (3) the Validator's passive-data-structure skip now applies to the owner type, as the Limits do. C-GETTER shows the `_mut` getter as a convention and does not say when to provide one. The Example's bad half has that shape with no doc comment declaring the share, so the card flags it. A verifier who reads Rust's `&mut` return type as that declaration may move the Example. Not carried, and why: the receiving side (storing a caller's collection without a copy: Sonar's "accepted and stored directly", PMD ArrayIsStoredDirectly, SpotBugs EI_EXPOSE_REP2, Uber 'Receiving Slices and Maps') belongs to the topic's accept-side rule. Dates and other non-collection mutable objects, and mutable elements inside a returned collection, fall outside the card's subject; the Limits state what a shallow copy shares. Concurrency is left out under the topic's reserved-specialty bound: Uber's mutex and data-race framing of the Snapshot example, the Rust book's data-race motivation, and Scanner's and Buffer's validity windows read only as documentation terms, never as synchronization. Refactoring ch. 7 "Encapsulate Collection", Effective Java Item 50, Program Development in Java ch. 5 and The Pragmatic Programmer Tip 45 "Tell, Don't Ask" are not named as formulation: S2384, PMD MethodReturnsInternalArray and EI_EXPOSE_REP carry the copy-or-view, encapsulation and exposed-representation wording the card follows, and no sentence of the card states Tell, Don't Ask. Triggers: `Date` was dropped from the proposed Java signature pattern, which was widened to any public or protected method returning a collection type. Python and TypeScript result-type forms and the Rust `&mut self.field` tail expression were added. A Java `return field;` with no receiver is left untriggered so that dispatch does not fire on every return; it is reached when the hunk carries the signature. Dropped evidence: the Go Blog 'Go Slices: usage and internals' (fetched; it states the same slice sharing as the Go specification, but a blog is not named in a card); the relayed Glacier (ICSE 2017) and Weber et al. (SecDev 2017) statements, which are about immutability in general and make no claim specific to returning internal collections.

The mechanism (an assigned reference shares one object, so an in-place change reaches every holder, and a holder that assumes the value never changes can then misbehave) is stated by fetched official documentation (CPython FAQ, Rust book, React, Error Prone, OpenJDK); the bug-source claim rests on a relayed interview study whose snippet carries no counts, and no source measures a defect rate, so the card states no number. The separating condition (another holder can observe the change) is sourced by React's local-mutation passage, Error Prone's unobservable internal state and the CPython FAQ; the mutation side's evidence (create-then-set APIs preferred, mutability as the author's call) is accommodated by the fresh-object exclusion. Scope: an object its holders use for the data it holds, whether or not its type compares instances by that data, held by more than one component; a fresh object not yet handed out, internal state no caller can observe and entities its holders track as one particular thing are outside; thread safety is a reserved specialty and is left out. Not carried: Coblenz, Nelson, Aldrich, Myers, Sunshine, "Glacier: transitive class immutability for Java", ICSE 2017, DOI 10.1109/ICSE.2017.52 (**relayed** snippet without a URL: about twenty hours of refactoring found two previously unknown bugs, one in a copy method, one in improper cache use), because its bugs do not show an in-place change to a shared value; Pylint W0102 and Ruff B006 (the mutable default argument, one language's semantics), carried in no part of this card; PMD ImmutableField and MutableStaticState, SpotBugs EI_EXPOSE_REP and MS_MUTABLE_COLLECTION, typescript-eslint prefer-readonly, which check field finality, module-level state and representation exposure and belong to neighbouring rules; frozen dataclasses, java.lang.Record and TypeScript readonly, language mechanisms for the immutable form, left to the fix. Triggers: two of the four given patterns (the @dataclass and @Data/@Setter patterns are dropped: each is one language's declaration marker and matches no in-place change), with the setter pattern widened from [.]set[A-Z] to [.]([sS]et[A-Z]|set_) so it also matches the exported SetX and snake_case set_x setter spellings, plus a one-dot field-assignment pattern that skips this./self. and an Object.assign/setattr pattern, so the card dispatches in languages that change fields directly rather than through setters; the assignment lookahead is widened from (?!=) to (?![=>]) to skip arrow tokens. Ownership: an in-place change to a value passed in as an argument, or to private state handed out, also meets the argument-mutation and representation-exposure rules of this topic; the workflow's defer map settles a shared span. The Example's good half compiles with javac 21 against a Money record and Catalog and Cart stubs.

The shallow semantics of read-only and final fields, records, frozen data classes, tuples and unmodifiable collections, and the remedy (a copy on receipt down to every mutable element, or receipt by a move or a by-value copy that leaves the sender no reference; handing out only a copy or a view that yields no mutable element), are fetched normative text from the official documentation of all five languages and from four Java tool rules. The cost rests on two relayed statements: an interview study's qualitative finding and one case study's two bugs. Neither search could be re-run in this session because the WebSearch budget was exhausted. No GitHub-hosted copy of either paper was found: raw paths under mcoblenz/Glacier and mcoblenz/mcoblenz.github.io answer 404, and neither paper appears in the neverworkintheory bibliography. Severity major rests on those relayed bug reports and on Error Prone's ERROR severity for an @Immutable type that is not deeply immutable; Sonar rates S2384 Minor. Scope: the card narrows S2384 and the EI patterns, which reach every class, to types that present themselves as immutable. Returning or accepting a private mutable object in an ordinary class, a mutated argument, module-level state and the no-reassignment declaration of fields are left to the topic's other rules. The presentation list (record, frozen data class, tuple or named tuple whose elements cannot be reassigned, read-only or frozen whole type, immutability annotation, documentation or name) is the card's own scope definition; a class whose fields are merely all read-only is not counted, to keep service classes with collaborator fields out. A shallow copy of a container whose elements are mutable does not satisfy the rule, since the Collection Javadoc calls such a collection mutable; an object received by a move or a by-value copy is not flagged, since the sender keeps no usable reference to it. A date counts as mutable only where its type has setters: the Python date types are immutable. The step facet is design, implement and refactor, since the rule applies when a refactor turns a class into a record, a frozen data class or a read-only type; review is reserved for the shape and description of the change itself. Not carried: the formulation's exemption that a trusted caller with documented responsibility may stand in for a defensive copy, since no openable source states it; the project-context tolerance is the card's path for such a type. Also not carried: "Immutable objects are inherently thread-safe", because the topic reserves concurrency. The Weber et al. SecDev 2017 relayed snippet is not used, because it states a general positive effect of immutability, not this mechanism. Dispatch: the triggers fire on every record header, frozen data class, named tuple, Readonly wrapper, const assertion, freeze call and line containing the word immutable, by design. A type in a language without a read-only modifier is dispatched only by the word immutable on an added line. A mutable field added to an existing record or frozen type is dispatched only when the header or a read-only field pattern (a readonly property, or a final field of a collection, array, map or date type) is on an added line. The Rust pattern covers only Rc- or Arc-wrapped interior mutability. Example: the good half compiles with tsc 6.0.2 --noEmit --strict and rejects stops.push. The bad half compiles; at runtime its stops change through the caller's array (["x","y"] against ["x"] for the good half).

Three Java static-analysis rules and one CERT rule state the rule directly. Official documentation from five languages states the mechanism and the limits: the aliasing on assignment, read-only views and types that still change, shallow copies that share elements, documented hand-overs, and moves and borrows. The cost rests on one relayed interview finding, which reports what developers stated and gives no measured defect rate. The Thesis keeps SpotBugs' condition ("unchecked changes ... would compromise security or other important properties") and drops its untrusted-code condition, because S2384 and PMD state the rule for any caller; the Source caveat records the narrower framing. S2384 offers an unmodifiable collection as an alternative remedy. For a stored input, the OpenJDK Collection Javadoc shows that such a view still shows the caller's changes, so the card counts a read-only view, and a read-only type, as no copy. The card takes only two things from CERT OBJ06-J (tagged draft, framed by time-of-check-to-time-of-use races and untrusted code): its statement that a value which passed validation can change before use, and its deep-copy statement; its validate-the-copy ordering is not carried, because CERT gives it as the remedy for a write that races the check, and concurrency correctness is outside the corpus. It makes no race, lock or memory-model claim, since concurrency correctness is outside the corpus. Not carried: Weber et al., SecDev 2017 (relayed: immutability had positive effects on security and usability) and Coblenz et al., "Glacier", ICSE 2017 (relayed: two previously unknown bugs, one in a copy method), because both concern immutability in general rather than storing a received object, and the Glacier snippet came without a URL. Also not carried: the mutable default argument, which is one language's semantics and appears in no example here. Ownership: returning the component's own mutable state and mutating an argument without keeping it fall to the topic's other rules; exposure of representation apart from mutation belongs to information-hiding-and-encapsulation. Triggers: the orchestrator's field-assignment pattern and its struct-literal pattern, widened to one-line literals, are kept; both compile and each matches a line of the Example's bad half. The orchestrator's `void set…(List…)` setter pattern is not carried, being a Java-only spelling, and no record-header, constructor-parameter-property or class-level-annotation pattern is added, since each is one language's spelling; the Validator's grep step still names those forms. The Example's good half, a constructor and a setter, passed `gofmt` unchanged and `go vet` (go1.24.7) in a package declaring `Item` and `Registry` and importing `slices`. The corpus validator reports 0 errors; its only warning is the DSN numbering gap for 01–07.

Four ecosystems' official documentation state the mechanism: a shallow copy shares nested objects, and a change through either holder reaches the other. The rule rests on the clone convention ("By convention … should", "Typically", "usually"); the style guide supplies the aliasing mechanism of a by-value struct copy. The only defect evidence is one relayed case study whose copy-method bug is not characterized, and no source measures a rate. The wording given to the drafter was narrowed: "every mutable object the copied value refers to" became the mutable objects that make up the value's internal ("deep") structure, after the Javadoc's "deep structure" and copy.rst's warning about data intended to be shared. The Go guide's pointer-receiver clause ("In general, do not copy a value of type T if its methods are associated with the pointer type, *T") is not carried. It is one language's semantics, and as a finding it flags the by-value copy that a deep copy method starts from, as net/http's (*Request).Clone does (*r2 = *r, then URL, Header, Trailer, TransferEncoding, Form, PostForm, MultipartForm, matches and otherValues replaced with copies, while Body stays shared as the doc comment states: "Clone only makes a shallow copy of the Body field."; golang/go master src/net/http/request.go, lines 383-418). A by-value copy that shares a slice's backing array fails the card's field check. A nested object the code treats as immutable and only replaces may stay shared; the Limits exempt it, after the React state-update guidance, whose handleNameChange spread keeps the nested artwork object shared. The React line-376 quote runs on to its second sentence, which states that updating a nested property takes the spread more than once; it pairs the Limits' "copies only the nested level it changes". The card does not carry: Item 50's untrusted-subclass clone point (a security concern with no fetched source here); the Go guide's sync.Mutex copying (concurrency is reserved outside the corpus); copy.rst's recursion and memo mechanics (a detail of the fix); McConnell's "until proven otherwise" cost trade-off (the Rust book's "Deep copies of data can take a lot of time" states the cost but no tolerance). Ownership: this card owns a copy that exists but is shallow. A mutable object passed in or returned with no copy at all belongs to the topic's defensive-copy rule.

Six fetched documents state it for Python and TypeScript: an evaluate-once default, a class-body attribute, and a per-call initializer that names a stored mutable field; the seventh, MDN, states the per-call evaluation the Limits rest on. Carrying the rule over to an overload or constructor that supplies the omitted argument rests on that mechanism and on the Google Python guide's equivalence of defaults and overloading. That form is the only one a language without default parameters has, and it is the form of the Java example. No source names it directly. Ruff B006 also skips parameters with immutable type annotations. Google §2.12.4 rejects `b: Mapping = {}` because the object "Could still get passed to unchecked code", so the card judges the object, not the declared type, and carries no annotation exemption. The drafted statement made the cache exemption depend on the cache being documented. The card keeps that condition only as the Validator's heuristic (a default named or commented as a cache), because the sources state the intentional cache but say nothing about documenting it. The cache exemption rests on the FAQ's memoizing passage; B006 lists the intentional cache under Known problems and prefers a memoizing decorator for it, so B006 is not cited as support for the exemption. The shared-on-purpose exemption (RUF012's ClassVar) covers only a class-level field that no instance takes as its own default and that no routine, overload or constructor supplies for an omitted argument. A static or class-level mutable object used as a default therefore stays inside the rule, as the Thesis's class-body clause requires. The triggers arrived as five patterns. Two remain, both language-neutral, and they match the Example's bad half (the overload call and the field initializer) but not its good half. The two Python-only spellings (a `def` signature with a mutable literal, an annotated class attribute) and the `??`/`or` fallback pattern were dropped. The facet arrived as `scope: hunk` and is set to `file`, because a named default's declaration and initializer usually lie outside the hunk. Concurrent access to a shared default is outside the corpus and is not carried. The candidate immutability studies (Coblenz et al., ICSE 2016 and ICSE 2017; Weber et al., SecDev 2017) state the general cost of unintended mutation, not of shared defaults, and are not cited.

The anchors are normative: five SEI CERT Java rules (each tagged draft in the repository's front matter; OBJ05-J rated severity High, OBJ01-J Medium), the Rust API guidelines and official book, one SonarSource rule (a Minor code smell), the contract model of a deferred PEP, and the class-invariant definition a peer-reviewed study adopts; no study measures defects caused by a broken class invariant, and the same ECOOP 2017 study finds class invariants rare in practice (Table 5: 3,793 class-invariant constructs over all versions, 100 in the latest versions, in 5 programs, against 786,723 precondition constructs in 160 programs) — a usage count, not carried in the card. Severity major rests on the CERT rules' statements that exposed fields and leaked mutable references let a class's invariants be violated and its state corrupted, and on ERR03-J's documented incorrect results after a failed method left the object modified. The CERT rules are written for Java and motivated by security; the card carries only their invariant statements, which hold for any type with non-public state, and Python marks non-public members by a naming convention, as PEP 316's definition of public shows. The Go zero-value bound rests on Effective Go, which accepts types whose zero value needs an initializing constructor. The card does not carry: the callback problem (an operation that calls out while the invariant is suspended lets the callee observe the inconsistent state), located only in an abstract with no confirmed identifier ("The dependent delegate dilemma", in the same Google Scholar export); loop invariants and the subtype substitutability rule, which are separate rules of the topic; invariants of state shared between threads, reserved to concurrency correctness; checking a precondition and failing fast, owned by defensive-programming; the assertion form of an invariant check and its removal in optimized builds, judged by their own rules. SWEBOK V3 ch. 3 §4.4 (ligurio/swebok-v3 transcription, fetched) states design by contract with preconditions and postconditions only and does not mention class invariants, so it is a formulation locator, not evidence here; the assertion-density studies (Kudrjavets et al. 2006, Casalnuovo et al. 2015, Catolino et al. 2019) measure assertions, not invariants, and are not cited. The ERR03-J case overlaps the error-handling rule that a handler leaves the program in a valid state; this card owns the type's own public operations, that one the handler.

Official language documentation, three tool and weakness entries (Ruff S101, Bandit B101, CWE-617), Guava's and Chromium's coding guidance and Google's Python guide agree, but no study measures the defect. CWE-617 is about assertions an attacker can trigger, and the card keeps that scope. The stripping cost holds only where the build or the runtime disables assertions (Python under -O, Java without -ea, Rust debug_assert! in release builds). Rust's assert! is always checked, so for the always-on case the card relies on the reporting cost and the stop. Chromium's checks guide, which the topic's candidate list classes as reception, is cited as a project coding standard in the same class as the Google style guides. It is the only anchor for the Limit on a deliberate non-assertion stop, for the "bad server-side rollout" clause and for the closing sentence of the Rationale (invariant failures triaged as bugs). The card leaves out "the environment" from the original wording, and the operating-system, driver and hardware failures that only Chromium names, so that the Thesis rests on the official sources. The Example follows the Google Python guide's own No/Yes pair. Ownership: a precondition on a public routine's arguments and the fail-fast check inside the trust boundary belong to defensive-programming; validation at a trust boundary belongs to security-hygiene-in-ordinary-code; reporting the expected failure belongs to error-and-exception-handling. ERR-12 owns a panic, exit or abort on an expected failure; this card owns the assertion forms, including the ones a build strips.

Ownership: whether a condition is checked by an assertion or by an error the caller handles belongs to defensive programming and error handling, not to this card.

The card narrows the orchestrator's wording, which said every test configuration keeps the assertions on. The criterion asks for "at least some dynamic analysis", so the card asks for at least one run: a run with assertions off follows the rule while any other test, fuzzing or dynamic-analysis run keeps them on, not only a run of the same tests, and the Validator question and the Finding output use the same threshold. The criterion asks for a configuration "which enables many assertions", so the Thesis forbids only a switch that strips or disables assertions throughout the code under test, and the Limits let a run disable them in named packages, classes or dependencies (java(1) -da with a package or class argument; a Cargo per-package profile override). The step facet is test only, since the rule is about how runs are configured, not the shape or description of the change. Not carried: Casalnuovo et al. (ICSE 2015) and Catolino et al. (ICSME 2019), both **relayed**. They are about assert density and defects, or test-class assertion density, and say nothing about running tests with assertions enabled. Go and TypeScript have no assert statement of their own, so the Go example shows a harness that launches the code under test. Scope file cannot see a sibling run in another file, such as tox.ini beside a CI workflow, so a false positive there is left to the verifier. Ownership: whether a test states its own checks with an always-enabled assertion library (Error Prone UseCorrectAssertInTests) belongs to test quality, and whether assertions stay on in production is left open.

The obligation case rests on documented duties in three ecosystems: Go cancel functions, Java closeable resources and Python asyncio tasks. The explicit-discard clause for obliged values rests on the lostcancel report and the let_underscore_lock lint, and a binding that holds the value keeps it whatever its name, following the same lint and MustBeClosedChecker's acceptance of a try-with-resources initializer; the deliberate unused-named discard is accepted only for the no-effect case, following Error Prone. The TypeScript example's `subscribe` is a stand-in API, and its comment states the documented obligation. The card does not cover a returned error or failure status, which error-and-exception-handling owns; the design-side rule of marking an API's result as must-use (`#[must_use]`, `@CheckReturnValue`), which this topic may card separately; or release of a kept resource on every path, which resource management owns.

The evidence is official design guidance from two ecosystems (the Rust API Guidelines; the Google Go Style Guide), official language documentation from three (the TypeScript Handbook, the Python `typing` reference, the Go specification), one tool rule (Error Prone) and the SWEBOK Guide; no controlled experiment or measured defect rate is carried. Rice, Aftandilian, Jaspan, Johnston, Pradel, Arroyo-Paredes, "Detecting argument selection defects", OOPSLA 2017 (DOI 10.1145/3133928) and Pradel and Gross, ISSTA 2011, on equally-typed argument order, are **unfetched** (no GitHub-hosted copy, no relayed snippet, WebSearch budget spent) and are not cited; the relayed API-usability papers in the candidate list (Piccioni, Furia, Meyer, ESEM 2013; Stylos and Myers, FSE 2008; Ellis, Stylos, Myers, ICSE 2007; Myers and Stylos, CACM 59(6) 2016, DOI 10.1145/2896587) state nothing about parameter types and are not carried. Scope as the rule was proposed, with two narrowings: the swap clause covers two or more parameters of one primitive representation that differ in meaning or unit, although C-NEWTYPE's own example is a single `Miles` parameter; and the closed-set clause covers a fixed set of named alternatives (an enumeration or a union of literals), leaving a range-checked wrapper type such as C-VALIDATE's `Ascii` to contracts and defensive programming. C-CUSTOM-TYPE's own example is two boolean arguments; boolean flag parameters stay with routine-size-and-parameters and parameter count with the same topic. The named-argument alternative rests on the Go option-structure guidance alone, which frames it for long signatures and says the techniques "may be unnecessary for your use case"; the card offers it as one way to satisfy the rule, never as a requirement, and names no language mechanism for it (keyword arguments, builders and functional options stay out of the prose). The Thesis states the alternative's effect as the guidance states it, harder to swap: the Go specification, Struct literals, allows a literal without keys whose "element list must contain an element for each struct field in the order in which the fields are declared", so an options value alone does not make every caller name each field. The Limits carry five language traits sourced from official documentation: an alias that the checker treats as identical gives no distinction (TypeScript, Python), a distinct type checked only by a static type checker holds only where that checker runs (Python), a checker that compares types by their members accepts one same-shape wrapper for another unless each declares a private member (TypeScript), a defined type still accepts any representable untyped constant (Go), and an enumeration over numbers is compatible with numbers (TypeScript). The role-only exclusion (width and height) rests on the Error Prone page's own legitimate-swap example. The Example's good half was compiled with `rustc --emit=metadata`, and a swapped call against it fails with E0308, while the bad half compiles. The triggers widen the proposed set: the C-family pair pattern also matches a pair after the first parameter, the Go pattern also matches `a T, b T`, the closed-set pattern is case-insensitive, matches a suffix (`sortMode`) and the Java and Go forms, and the unit pattern matches Java and Go declarations as well.
