The evidence is official documentation across five ecosystems (Go, Rust, .NET, Java, TypeScript, plus Kotlin), one analyzer rule and one misuse-detection study's abstract; it states the mechanism and the designs, and none of it measures how often an unenforced call order causes a defect. The detector figures come from the reviewer's summary on the It Will Never Work in Theory page, not from the abstract, and they cover API misuses of every kind, not call-order misuses alone. Compared with the original statement: "an error that names the missing step" became an error that says the object is not in an appropriate state, because the Java and .NET exception guidance says only that; the Kotlin lateinit text backs only the Rationale's "can identify" and the Finding output's fix. The Rust book sentence became the Limits' trade-off sentence, and the book's encapsulated workflow, where a call out of order has no effect, became a Limits case so that the finder does not flag it. Invariants and preconditions are left to the contracts topic, named in the card only as "a precondition … is outside the rule". The relayed API-usability papers (Piccioni et al. ESEM 2013, Stylos and Myers FSE 2008, Ellis et al. ICSE 2007, Myers and Stylos CACM 2016) are not cited because none of their relayed statements is about call order. A controlled study comparing required constructor parameters with create-set-call (Stylos and Clarke, ICSE 2007, from memory, **unfetched**) could not be searched this run. The card's any-order-properties branch keeps create-set-call admissible, so the study would not contradict the rule. Triggers differ from the computed facets: capitalised first letters for exported set-up methods, a declaration-form trigger that catches set-up methods taking parameters (the Example's bad half matches through it), with a second alternative for a method declared without a keyword, as in TypeScript classes, a state-flag trigger that accepts any receiver name, and `(?i)` on the doc-comment and message triggers.

Official guidance from three ecosystems agrees on keeping non-public what only the module itself uses: PEP 8 and the Google TypeScript and Go style guides. PEP 8 also states the uneven cost of narrowing a public name later, and the Rust book states privacy by default as the way to hide implementation details. None of them measures a cost, and no API-usability paper could be confirmed this run because the WebSearch budget was used up. The in-doubt clause is stated for a class's attributes and the Go clauses for interface types; the card reads both for every name a module exposes. No Java source on access modifiers was opened: the dev.java language tutorial is not in the public `java/devjava-content` repository, and docs.oracle.com is denied. The Java reach therefore rests on the shared mechanism. The test clause keeps the Go guide's own terms (back door, test double) and leaves it to the finder to judge what a back door is. It does not exclude test uses in general, because the TypeScript guide's "used outside of the module" admits them. Module depth and interface width belong to their own topic. Narrowing a surface that is already published also belongs to its own topic, and the card's Limits confine the rule to names the change adds or makes public. The trigger set is broad and matches the common declaration heads of exported or public names in the five languages; a Rust or Go struct field, a TypeScript class field without a modifier, a Python module-level variable, a Java interface member and a restricted Rust visibility such as pub(crate) reach the finder only in a hunk another trigger selects. The Validator narrows it to names added to the public surface.

(2004) §7.5. None of the three was opened here. · reception: not contested (the TypeScript declaration-files guidance and the .NET page differ on whether to overload rather than use optional parameters, not on parameter order) · notes: confidence moderate. The evidence is one official guideline page, a reprinted 2008 book text marked as possibly out of date, plus one tool rule that Error Prone ships disabled. No study measures the cost of inconsistent overloads: the WebSearch budget was spent, and none of the topic's relayed papers states the claim (Piccioni et al. ESEM 2013; Stylos and Myers FSE 2008; Ellis et al. ICSE 2007; Myers and Stylos CACM 2016). Scope: the evidence covers .NET members and Java methods that share one name. The card reads it for TypeScript overloads and Python typed overload declarations by the same mechanism. It does not extend the rule to differently named related functions in Go and Rust, because only the formulation sources state that. Variadic parameters: the position requirement and the append-at-the-end fix leave a variadic parameter out and keep it last, as ParameterTrie does; javac ('varargs parameter must be the last parameter') and tsc (TS1014 'A rest parameter must be last in a parameter list.') reject the alternative. Similar-type clause: where no reordering separates two meanings at one position, the fix is a separate operation name, following the DO NOT clause and the page's ref/out sentence. Not carried: the page's other overloading guidelines (descriptive names for the defaults of shorter overloads, only the longest overload virtual, no ref/out overloads, null for optional arguments, overloads rather than default arguments). The title adds the guideline's "similar types" qualifier; the analyst's "never give one position different meanings" overstated the DO NOT, which covers similar types only. Triggers: the analyst's four facets are joined into one alternation, so that the pattern matches bad lines 1 and 2 of the TypeScript example; the Java method branch takes one or more parameters ('\([^)]*\w[^)]*\)' in place of the comma form), and a TypeScript constructor-overload branch and a Java constructor branch are added, since the guideline names constructors first. Tested: it matches '@overload', '@typing.overload', a TypeScript member overload signature, Java methods with one and with several parameters, a Java constructor, a TypeScript constructor overload and a Java varargs method, and none of 'return take(arr, 5, 2);', 'super(a, b);', 'this.take(a, b);', 'Take t = new Take(a, b);' or 'const x = foo(a, b);'. A branch for Java interface and abstract methods with no access modifier (ends in a semicolon, has at least one typed parameter, excludes return/throw/new/else/await/yield/assert/case) and a TypeScript call/construct-signature branch are added, because the Validator names a signature that ends in a semicolon with no body; tested against the lines listed above. The Example's overloads differ in return type, so the good half also meets the TypeScript declaration-files guidance (microsoft/TypeScript-Website v2 `packages/documentation/copy/en/declaration-files/Do's and Don'ts.md`, fetched: "Don't write several overloads that differ only in trailing parameters" and "Note that this collapsing should only occur when all overloads have the same return type."). The good half compiles under tsc 6.0.2 --noEmit --strict --target es2020 once its body is filled.

The Google Go guide records the in-band string functions of the Go standard library as a deliberate trade-off; the card carries this as a limit, not as a contest. The Google TypeScript guide treats null and undefined as legitimate absence markers on a return type, so the rule reaches only a null that the declared result type does not mark. An exception for a no-result outcome belongs to failure reporting, and a default value is accepted only where it means the same to every caller as a real result, which the evidence states for a zero value in a set held as a map to booleans. · notes: confidence moderate. The evidence is official and style documentation for Go, Java, TypeScript and Rust, the mypy type checker's documentation for Python, and two SpotBugs patterns written for Java; no source measures a defect rate, and the card carries no number. severity major follows the evidence tying in-band values and unchecked nulls to bugs ("can lead to bugs", "a major source of bugs", "will most likely break client code"). The search-comparison trigger leads the finder to the called routine; the card does not flag a caller's misuse of a library string function's sentinel, because the rule judges the operation's declaration. An unannotated Python routine has no declared result type, so the finder flags its unmarked None for a no-result outcome and the fix adds the `| None` annotation. Return types divide: the Go style guide's adage returns concrete types, while PMD LooseCoupling's preferred example declares a returned set with its interface, so the card leaves return types out and states the split in Limits. The evidence is official design guidance from four ecosystems (.NET, Rust, Go, Python typing) and analyzer documentation for Java (PMD) and Rust (clippy); none is empirical and none gives a measured cost, hence severity minor (PMD priority 3, clippy group style). No API-usability study measuring parameter-type generality was reachable: the relayed Stylos and Myers (FSE 2008) and Ellis, Stylos and Myers (ICSE 2007) studies concern method placement and factories, and Piccioni, Furia and Meyer (ESEM 2013) and Myers and Stylos (CACM 2016, DOI 10.1145/2896587) concern API usability in general, so none is carried. No TypeScript source states the rule (the Google TypeScript style guide's "Use structural types" concerns declaring types, not parameter generality) and no trigger targets TypeScript specifically. The card leaves out local variables and fields, which PMD LooseCoupling also flags, because the topic owns operation signatures; changing the type of an existing public parameter is owned by api-evolution-and-deprecation, so the card skips a parameter whose declared type the hunk leaves unchanged. Like both analyzers, the Validator skips an operation that overrides or implements an inherited declaration, because the language makes it repeat that declaration's parameter types and the fix would not compile; the rule then applies to the inherited declaration, which clippy lints through `check_trait_item`. Because the card's scope is the hunk, the Validator also skips a body that passes the parameter to a codebase operation whose declared parameter type the hunk does not show or stores it in a field or variable whose declared type the hunk does not show, and it counts among what the body requires the declared type of a field or variable the parameter is stored in and the declared result type when the operation returns it, the uses for which `ptr_arg.rs` keeps the owned type (clippy 0.1.97 lints `fn longest_len<'a>(a: &'a Vec<i32>, b: &'a Vec<i32>) -> usize` but not the same parameters returned as `&'a Vec<i32>`, nor a `&Vec` stored in a struct field). The check reaches concrete implementation types only: a parameter typed with an interface wider than the body uses (the .NET example's IList where IEnumerable suffices) breaks the Thesis but is not flagged, and the Limits say so. The triggers extend the candidate set with more concrete Java collection classes, Rust references with a lifetime, a parameter line of a multi-line Python signature, and `bufio.Writer`; a nested generic such as `ArrayList<List<String>>` is matched by a greedy `<.*>`.

Python Programming FAQ, "How do I write a function with output parameters (call by reference)?": "Remember that arguments are passed by assignment in Python. Since assignment just creates references to objects, there's no alias between an argument name in the caller and callee, and consequently no call-by-reference."; "By returning a tuple of the results"; "This is almost always the clearest solution."; "By passing a mutable (changeable in-place) object"; "By passing in a dictionary that gets mutated"; "Or bundle up values in a class instance"; "There's almost never a good reason to get this complicated."; "Your best choice is to return a tuple containing the multiple results." (fetched from `python/cpython` main, `Doc/faq/programming.rst`); the FAQ's own examples read and change the passed object, so it reaches further than this rule, which keeps in-out parameters · topic: api-design-and-use (research/software-craft/api-design-and-use.md) · formulation: Rust API Guidelines C-NO-OUT "Functions do not take out-parameters" with its exception for data the caller already owns, and the Google C++ Style Guide's "Prefer using return values over output parameters" (both cited above, openable); Clean Code ch. 3 "Output Arguments", named by the rule spine and not among the design note's locators for this topic, dropped as a formulation because these carry the same wording in openable form · reception: not contested · notes: confidence moderate; six official-documentation sources across five ecosystems (Rust, Go, C++, .NET, Python) agree, and none is a measurement: the "reduces the likelihood of bugs" claim is the Abseil tip's expert judgement. The Rust, Go, C++ and .NET sources are written for languages with pointer or reference parameters; for a language that passes object references, the Python FAQ names a mutable object, a dictionary and a class instance passed to receive results as its ways to get output parameters, and the card treats an array or holder object created by the caller only to receive a result as the output parameter in Java, Python and TypeScript, on that FAQ, on the style guide's role definition of a parameter (input, output or both) and on the tip's list of questions, and no Java- or TypeScript-specific source was found (the WebSearch budget was exhausted, so no paper was searched for this rule; the relayed API-usability papers in the candidate list, Piccioni et al. ESEM 2013, Stylos and Myers FSE 2008, Ellis et al. ICSE 2007 and Myers and Stylos CACM 2016, DOI 10.1145/2896587, state nothing about output parameters and are not cited). The Rust guideline's reason that tuples and structs "do not require heap allocation" holds where they are values and is not carried into the Rationale: a returned tuple, record or object is a heap object in Python, Java and TypeScript. The .NET guideline's reasons (experience with pointers, the out/ref distinction, an out parameter "initially considered unassigned") describe by-reference parameters that none of the five example languages has, and its ref half reaches the in-out parameters the card keeps, so they are not carried into the Rationale. The statement's named exception "decoding into a value the caller supplies" is not carried, because no fetched fragment states it; such a decoder is reached only where it modifies data the caller already owns. The Abseil tip's advice to resist std::pair and std::tuple for multiple returns rests on the style guide's "Structs vs. Pairs and Tuples" (a meaningful field name reads more clearly than .first, .second or std::get<X>), a readability preference among return forms that the Rust guideline's tuples and the Python FAQ's tuple do not share; the card admits a tuple, a struct or a record and leaves the choice among them outside the rule. The .NET Try-Parse pattern (`docs/standard/design-guidelines/exceptions-and-performance.md`, fetched: "returns false if parsing is unsuccessful and returns the result of a successful parsing using an `out` parameter", for "extremely performance-sensitive APIs") sanctions an out parameter tied to failure reporting, which belongs to error-and-exception-handling; the card's evidence-of-cost limit and project-context tolerance cover it, and the five example languages express the same contract with an optional or a value-and-flag return. The style guide's use of non-const pointers for optional outputs is not carried. Parameter count is left to routine-size-and-parameters and failure reporting to error-and-exception-handling. The good half of the TypeScript Example compiled with `tsc --noEmit --strict` (tsc 6.0.2) in a scope declaring `text: string` and `pos: number`; the fifth trigger matches the bad half's signature line, and the other four were tested against Rust `&mut`, Go pointer, Java array, generic and holder, and Python typed-list output parameters.

The evidence is seven fetched official documents: style guides for Go and Python, PEP 8, the .NET property guideline and the CA1024 analyzer rule, the Kotlin conventions and the Rust conversion-naming guideline. They agree, but each is a recommendation ("can be used", "Avoid", "AVOID", "should probably", "Prefer", "preferable"), none measures a cost, and CA1024 is off by default, so the severity is minor. The relayed API-usability papers among the topic's candidates (Piccioni et al., ESEM 2013; Stylos and Myers, FSE 2008; Ellis, Stylos and Myers, ICSE 2007; Myers and Stylos, CACM 2016, DOI 10.1145/2896587) do not state this claim and are not cited. The card does not carry the following. (1) "Blocking input or output" in the orchestrator's wording became "a time-consuming operation perceivably slower than reading a field" (CA1024) together with "complex computation or remote call" (Go), because no fetched fragment names file or database input or output; the Validator lists those as instances. (2) "load" was dropped from the work-naming words, because only compute and fetch are sourced. (3) The Swift remedy of documenting the complexity of a non-O(1) computed property is formulation only, and no admissible source in the five languages makes documentation sufficient. (4) Kotlin's same-result condition is quoted in the Rationale but is not a Thesis clause. CA1024's conversion, side-effect, order, differing-results and array criteria are left out, because state changes belong to the query-naming card and the rest lie outside the rule's statement. (5) The no-failure and no-precondition clauses rest on the .NET property guideline and the Kotlin "Does not throw", both written for properties, and hold for properties and getter accessors only. In a language that has properties, the Kotlin conventions ("Prefer a property over a function when the underlying algorithm: Does not throw. Is cheap to calculate"), CA1024 ("In these situations, a method is preferable to a property"; "The method performs a time-consuming operation") and Google Python Style Guide §3.15 ("they should be used when getting or setting the variable is complex or the cost is significant"; "such as `get_foo()`") place costly or throwing work in a method, including a get-prefixed method with no arguments, so that shape is set aside. In a language without properties, the getter clause rests on the Go Style Guide §Getters alone, at its threshold of a complex computation or a remote call. The indexer exception follows the .NET text. (6) A get-named routine that takes arguments is left out, although the Go guidance covers any function, because the card holds a routine called as a method to the getter clause only where the language has no properties, and there it takes the no-argument shape the Go guidance names (a noun in place of Get). (7) The Validator sets aside a lock held only around a field read. This follows from the trivial-work condition, not from a fragment. (8) The input-output vocabulary trigger runs on any added network, file, database or sleep call by design, to reach a body changed under an unchanged accessor name. The accessor shapes of the five languages share one alternation, which takes any Rust &self method and any Go method with no arguments, because their getters carry no prefix. The good half of the Example compiled under go vet (go1.24.7) in /tmp/craft-research/api-design-and-use/api-accessor-shape-promises-cheap-access/fix/work/ex.

(fetched); Daniel Venturini, Filipe Roseiro Cogo, Ivanilton Polato, Marco A. (fetched); Shaikh Mostafa, Rodney Rodriguez, Xiaoyin Wang, "Experience Paper: A Study on Behavioral Backward Incompatibilities of Java Software Libraries", ISSTA 2017, DOI 10.1145/3092703.3092721 (from memory): an empirical study of behavioural backward incompatibilities between versions of popular Java libraries, found by running client tests against the newer library version (**unfetched**; this run had no GitHub-hosted copy and no relayed snippet, so the card does not carry it) · topic: api-evolution-and-deprecation (research/software-craft/api-evolution-and-deprecation.md) · formulation: Software Engineering at Google (Winters, Manshreck, Wright eds., O'Reilly 2020), ch. 1 "What Is Software Engineering?", § Hyrum's Law ("With a sufficient number of users of an API, it does not matter what you promise in the contract: all observable behaviors of your system will be depended on by somebody"); ch. 21 "Dependency Management", § The Limitations of SemVer › Motivations ("SemVer version bumps should be applied to semantic changes just as much as syntactic ones; changing the behavior of an API matters just as much as changing its structure"); Michael Feathers, "The Golden Rule of API Design", 97 Things Every Programmer Should Know (O'Reilly 2010), thing 35 (when an API class calls one of its own overridable methods, the subclasses that override it fix the class's future implementation choices) · reception: not contested. The compatibility policies of Python, Go and .NET, the semver specification and the Griffe check agree that these changes break callers. The bug-fix exemption meets a stricter reading in two places: the .NET rules count a correction to the intended value as breaking, and the semver FAQ says a major release may be best when a huge audience is drastically impacted. The Limits carry both. Whether callers are protected in behaviour the documentation and the declaration leave unstated (Hyrum's Law) is the contested case undocumented-behaviour-is-protected: the .NET parsing rule and PEP 387's unqualified 'Given a set of arguments' item protect it, while Rust RFC 1105 § Behavioral changes permits behaviour outside the documented contract to change in minor revisions. This card reaches only behaviour the documentation or the declaration states, records that divide in its Limits without taking a side, and keeps properties the documentation declares unspecified or undefined outside it (Go 1 compatibility) · notes: confidence high for the classification, since the official compatibility policies of four language ecosystems, the semver specification and one tool check all state it. Confidence moderate for the cost: the one number comes from a single npm study that counts breaking changes of every kind, not behaviour changes alone, as the Source caveat says. The evidence is Python, Go, .NET and Rust policy text, applied as the compatibility promise of any published element in the five corpus languages. The Go compatibility article sits under the Go project's official blog path on go.dev and is cited as official documentation. The card leaves out: the Mostafa et al. study (unfetched); the Raemaekers et al., Ochoa et al., Xavier et al. and Brito et al. studies (their relayed statements concern removals and structural breaking changes, so they back the deprecation and versioning rules, not this one); SEG's remark that tooling cannot feasibly detect semantic changes (formulation only); and Griffe's sentinel-default deprecation hint (deprecation mechanics belong to the deprecation rules). Triggers: six patterns: the plan's five, written as four by folding the Go error constructors into the panic/Err pattern, with the two quote characters written as `\x22` and `\x27` so the inline YAML list needs no doubled quotes; a fifth for enumeration and constant values (`NAME = n` and `NAME(n)` lines); and a sixth for a return of a literal or a named constant. All six compile with Python `re`, and they match the Example's bad half on the `Err(` line. The Example's good half compiled with rustc 1.97.0 `--edition 2021 --crate-type lib --emit=metadata` in an enclosing scope that declares `PortError` and `DEFAULT_PORT`, with the elisions filled by a `parse` call.

Bogart, C. Kästner, J. Herbsleb, F. Thung, "When and how to make breaking changes", ACM TOSEM 30(4), 2021, doi:10.1145/3447245, reviewed in neverworkintheory (main, `_posts/2022/2022-03-25-breaking-changes.html`, fetched): Eclipse's "prime directive" of "never permitting breaking changes", while npm accepts breaking changes "but signaled clearly through version numbering" — the card's major-version set-aside follows the latter, not cited in the card · notes: confidence high for the required-parameter break and the old-behaviour default (seven fetched documents across Python, Go, Java/Eclipse, .NET and the semver standard); moderate for the separating condition, since the function-value break is shown for one statically typed language with a variadic parameter and the override break for one language with overloading, neither of which has default arguments. The unfetched hands-on tests show that in the two example languages with default arguments a value of the old function type still accepts the defaulted function, so the card conditions the function-value case on "where that type no longer accepts the function" rather than stating it for every defaulted parameter, and states the override case as the Eclipse document does only where methods are told apart by their parameter lists, with PEP 387 placing the conditions under which overridden methods are called in the public API; a further local test (tsc 6.0.2 --strict, unfetched) shows `Promise.all(urls.map(fetchPage))` failing with TS2345 once an options parameter with a default is added, and compiling while passing the index as the timeout once `timeoutMs: number = 30_000` is added, while a value of the old function type still accepts both; the callback clause of the Thesis, Limits and Validator rests on the Go blog's general statement "call compatibility is not enough for backward compatibility", with that test as corroboration only. The des Rivières direction (new method's default implementation calls the old one, for overridable methods) and the Go blog direction (old function forwards to the new one, for plain functions) are kept apart deliberately; for an interface that cannot carry a default implementation the card follows the Go blog's §Working with interfaces (a new interface and a run-time check). Scope base-compare: the routine and its body at the base are needed to tell a new parameter and a changed default from a new routine. The triggers fire on an added signature line with at least one parameter; a field added to an options type with no signature change in the same file does not dispatch the card, because no vocabulary separates an options field from any other field. The card leaves out: the Go blog's struct-comparability exception behind "almost always" (a non-comparable field breaks comparison of the options type); the .NET allowance "Adding `params` to a parameter" (one-platform detail); Rust's private-field and non_exhaustive future-proofing of an options type and the first design of an options type (owned by the variants-and-fields rule and by api-design-and-use); Griffe's sentinel-based deprecation of a changed default (deprecation rules); codebase-wide caller migration (large-scale-changes-and-migrations); Hyrum's Law and observable-behaviour changes (another rule of this topic). The relayed papers of the topic (Raemaekers et al. SCAM 2014 / JSS 2017; Ochoa et al. EMSE 2022, arXiv:2110.07889; Xavier et al. SANER 2017; Brito et al. SANER 2018; Sawant et al. ICSE 2018) carry no relayed statement about adding parameters or defaults and are not cited; WebSearch was unavailable this run. Example good half (a new function fetchPageWith that the unchanged fetchPage forwards to) compiled with `tsc --noEmit --strict --target es2020` (TypeScript 6.0.2), exit 0, and `Promise.all(urls.map(fetchPage))` keeps compiling and the old timeout; the bad half fails with TS2554 "Expected 2 arguments, but got 1"; the five pattern triggers compile, the export-function trigger matches the bad half's signature line, and 14 positive and 5 negative sample lines across the five languages were checked; `validate-craft-cards.py` reports 0 errors (a numbering-gap warning only, run on the card alone).

The rule sets differ in degree on the default-implementation remedy. The Eclipse table marks "Add default method" to a client-implementable interface "Breaks compatibility" for the name-clash case, yet allows "selected default methods" where the clash risk is low. Rust RFC 1105 classes a defaulted item as a minor change that is "technically a breaking change". The .NET rules list it as allowed. The card states the default as the remedy for existing implementations that inherit from the type and carries the clash in Limits. The sources disagree on releases below 1.0.0: semver.md ("Anything MAY change at any time"), RFC 1105 §Scope ("de facto stable after the library reaches 1.0.0 (per semver)") and golang/website _content/doc/modules/version-numbers.md (v0 "carries no backward compatibility or stability guarantees") give them no compatibility promise, while the caret-range ecosystems treat the left-most non-zero component as the breaking-change indicator: Cargo's semver crate makes `^` the implicit default with `^0.J.K` equivalent to `>=0.J.K, <0.(J+1).0`, node-semver's caret allows changes that do not modify the left-most non-zero element, and the cargo-semver-checks README counts 0.5.2 to 0.6.0 as a major version bump. The card carries the condition between them in Limits and Validator: a release below 1.0.0 is outside the rule unless the ecosystem's default version ranges accept every release that keeps its left-most non-zero component, and there only a bump of that component declares the break · notes: confidence high. The official compatibility documentation of five ecosystems agrees on the break, the default-implementation remedy, the new-interface remedy and closure: Eclipse for Java, the Go blog and the apidiff checker, Rust RFC 1105 and the API Guidelines, the .NET rules, and the Ember RFC for TypeScript. The cargo-semver-checks lints state the break and that sealing a published trait is itself major, and the CPython abc documentation states the instantiation failure. PEP 544 limits the default-implementation remedy to implementations that inherit from the type: one that satisfies the type by its shape alone inherits no default, so the card sends the member to a new interface there, and the Ember RFC's "the type side of classes" keeps a returned concrete type from closing the type unless outside code can neither implement it nor match it by shape. No study measures how often interface-member additions break clients. The relayed breaking-change studies (Raemaekers et al. SCAM 2014 and JSS 2017; Ochoa et al. EMSE 2022, arXiv:2110.07889; Xavier et al. SANER 2017; Brito et al. SANER 2018) classify breaking changes in general, and none of the relayed snippets states the interface-member case, so the card carries no number and cites no paper. The statement's "Sealing costs callers the ability to substitute the type in their own tests" is rewritten to what the Ember RFC states: a type closed by a mechanism leaves users no safe way to provide their own mocks ("cannot safely provide their own mocks"), short of embedding it where the language allows, which the apidiff README states for an interface with an unexported method, mitigated by test helpers or sanctioned mocks; a type documented as non-constructible still lets users mock it and update the mocks. The statement's "a new interface that extends the old one" is widened by the Go form: a new interface holding the new method alone, checked for at run time. The card does not claim that an optional member is safe for implementers, because the Ember RFC lists "a new optional property" as non-breaking only for non-user-constructible types; it scopes the rule to members every implementation must supply instead. RFC 1105's further defaulted-item exceptions appear only as "some type systems list further cases", with object safety as the example. The defaulted-associated-type case and the .NET boxing caveat for default methods with update semantics are left out as single-language mechanisms. Effective Java 3rd ed. Item 21 "Design interfaces for posterity", given in the design note as a formulation, is not named as one: under the repository rule an unopenable formulation is dropped where an openable source carries the same formulation, and the Eclipse document does. That item's distinct claim, that a default method can compile yet break an existing implementation's invariants at run time, has no openable source here, and the card does not carry it. The triggers are wider than the design note's header-only facets. A member added to an existing type adds only the member line, so they also cover bodyless member signatures (Go interface methods, Rust trait fns, Java interface methods, TypeScript method and required-property signatures) and Python abstract-marked and stub methods. They were tested against 25 positive and 26 negative lines, including Rust Ok/Some tail expressions, Go call statements and TypeScript optional members. They also cover TypeScript abstract members, which carry no return type before the name, TypeScript function-typed required properties (`name: (args) => T;`, the form typescript-eslint method-signature-style enforces by its default option "property", packages/eslint-plugin/src/rules/method-signature-style.ts `defaultOptions: ['property']`) and Go interface methods with unnamed parameters, as in slog.Handler's `Enabled(context.Context, Level) bool`. Over the 2,511,616 lines of the Go 1.24.7 standard library the widened Go pattern matches 52 more lines and loses none, and a recheck against 17 positive and 9 negative lines, the Example's bad half among them, gave no miss and no false hit. The TypeScript pattern also matches semicolon-free method signatures and function-typed properties: over prettier --no-semi output of TypeScript's lib.es5.d.ts it matches all 340 required method-signature lines, where the semicolon-only form matched none, at a cost of at most 20 extra matched lines in any of the Go and Python standard libraries and the npm, eslint and prettier packages. The Source item for node-semver also quotes its "left-most non-zero element" sentence, which states the condition the Limits name.

(fetched); semver crate, crate documentation and Op::Caret (dtolnay/semver, src/lib.rs, https://raw.githubusercontent.com/dtolnay/semver/master/src/lib.rs) — "A parser and evaluator for Cargo's flavor of Semantic Versioning."; "Caret requirements allow parts that are right of the first nonzero part of the semver version to increase."; "^0.J.K (for J>0) — equivalent to >=0.J.K, <0.(J+1).0" (fetched); node-semver README, §"Caret Ranges ^1.2.3 ^0.2.5 ^0.0.4" (npm/node-semver, README.md, https://raw.githubusercontent.com/npm/node-semver/main/README.md) — "Allows changes that do not modify the left-most non-zero element in the [major, minor, patch] tuple. In other words, this allows patch and minor updates for versions 1.0.0 and above, patch updates for versions 0.X >=0.1.0, and no updates for versions 0.0.X."; "Many authors treat a 0.x version as if the x were the major "breaking-change" indicator." (fetched); local hands-on reproduction, rustc 1.94.1 via cargo --offline, a lib crate holding a #[non_exhaustive] enum and struct (the struct built through a constructor) beside a plain enum and an all-public struct, and a client crate matching and building each, built before and after adding one variant and one field to every type (**unfetched** — a scratch test, not openable by a reader) — "error[E0063]: missing field `b` in initializer of `Plain`"; "error[E0004]: non-exhaustive patterns: `Closed::C` not covered"; the marked enum (matched with a wildcard arm) and the marked struct compiled unchanged · topic: api-evolution-and-deprecation (research/software-craft/api-evolution-and-deprecation.md) · formulation: Rust RFC 1105 "API evolution" §Structs and §Enums, and The Rust Reference, `non_exhaustive` (both fetched, cited above) · reception: not contested · notes: confidence high for the break mechanism, which the Rust RFC and Reference, Go's compatibility document and its go vet check, the TypeScript handbook and the Python typing guide state directly, and which the local test reproduces; moderate for the design half (declare a type open when it is first published), which the sources give as an option and a trade-off (clippy keeps its exhaustive-type lints in the off-by-default restriction group) rather than as a measured cost. Scope: compile-time breaks under a compiler's or type checker's exhaustiveness check, under literals or constructor calls that have to give every field, by name or by position, and under patterns that have to name every field; a positional call that may omit a defaulted parameter and a pattern that may omit fields are not covered. A positional literal is flagged only where the language offers a keyed form that may leave fields unset: Go's keyed literal is one, while a Rust struct literal has to give every field (RFC 1105: adding a public field "breaks existing uses of such literals"). The keyed-literal policy counts whether the record's package or its language publishes it, so a field added to an exported struct in a Go module at v1 or above is no finding, as the Go blog and apidiff state. At major version zero the card follows the caret requirements of Cargo and npm, under which the leftmost nonzero component plays the part of the major version; Cargo's semantics rest on the semver crate, which describes itself as Cargo's flavor of Semantic Versioning, because the Cargo book's reference/semver.md and reference/specifying-dependencies.md answer 404 on master. The open marker is documented for one compiler only, and the keyed-literal policy only in Go's compatibility promise. No fetched source covers Java's switch exhaustiveness or the binary compatibility of a new enum constant, because the JLS is on a denied host. The card carries no rule on the new field's default value: it appears only as context in the Rationale and a scope bound in Limits, and that rule belongs to the topic's new-input-has-old-behaviour-default. None of the relayed candidate studies (Raemaekers et al.; Ochoa et al.; Xavier/Brito et al.; Sawant et al.) has a relayed statement about variant or field additions, so the card cites none of them. Triggers: the spine's anchored Rust enum pattern was dropped because the unanchored enum pattern covers it; the card carries four patterns, with added alternatives for one-line struct declarations, Java record headers, semicolon-terminated typed members and a positional literal qualified by a package name (the caller-side clause) beside the struct and field pattern, and for enum-member lines with a value (Python, TypeScript) and union-member lines (TypeScript) beside the variant-line pattern. All four compile, each matches at least one line of the Example's bad half, and the merged alternatives still match `p := pkg.Point{1, 2}`, `  | { kind: "closed" }` and `  | "closed"`. Both Example halves compile under rustc 1.97.0 with --edition 2021 --crate-type=lib --emit=metadata.

Further reception: Bogart, Kästner, Herbsleb, Thung, "When and how to make breaking changes", ACM TOSEM 30(4), 2021, doi:10.1145/3447245 (fetched as the review neverworkintheory/neverworkintheory.github.io _posts/2022/2022-03-25-breaking-changes.html, whose review text quotes these sentences from the paper; the abstract it reproduces does not contain them): ecosystems differ — "long-term stability is a central value of the Eclipse community, achieved by their "prime directive" practice of never permitting breaking changes", while "the Node.js/npm community values ease and simplicity for upstream developers and has a technical infrastructure in which breaking changes are accepted, but signaled clearly through version numbering" · notes: confidence moderate. The rule rests on the published compatibility policies of five projects or standards (SemVer FAQ, PEP 387, NEP 23, Rust RFC 1270, Eclipse), all fetched, plus one relayed study of the Maven repository; no source measures how much breakage a deprecation release prevents, and the periods are policy rather than measurement. The card's threshold "at least one release" is the minimum across the policies (SemVer); the longer periods are carried as the project policy the removal waits for. The orchestrator's "changed together with every caller in one commit" is narrowed to "fixed up at the same time", which is what the Linux text states. Abseil's live-at-head promise (about/philosophy.md §Upgrade Support, a refactoring tool for well-behaved code) is not carried: it states no removal without deprecation, and Abseil's own tool workflow deprecates first (abseil/abseil-cpp, master, absl/base/macros.h, ABSL_REFACTOR_INLINE, https://raw.githubusercontent.com/abseil/abseil-cpp/master/absl/base/macros.h, fetched: "will mark `OldFunc` and `OldType` as deprecated, and the go/cpp-inliner service will replace calls to `OldFunc(x)` with calls to `NewFunc(x, 0)` and `OldType` with `NewType`. Once all replacements have been completed, the old function or type can be deleted."). The in-repository side rests on the Linux text. Added beyond the given evidence: .NET Breaking Change Rules (renaming listed with removal), java.lang.Deprecated (compiler warnings at use; since and forRemoval in the Example), the Linux note on the stable userspace interface (both sides of the separating condition in one project), the Abseil compatibility guidelines (internal elements), SemVer item 4 (0.y.z), PEP 387's exceptions and NEP 23's bug-fix exemption. The Rationale's compiler-warning sentence opens with "in some languages", since java.lang.Deprecated and RFC 1270 each state it for one language only. The statement's "state how long the deprecation period lasts" is carried as waiting for the period the project's policy states; the notice's content (replacement, since-version, planned removal release), the caller-site warning, delegation from the deprecated element, the no-new-use rule and the version-number signal belong to the topic's other rules. Not carried: Ochoa et al. (arXiv:2110.07889), Xavier et al. (SANER 2017), Brito et al. (SANER 2018) and Sawant et al. (ICSE 2018), for which no relayed statement on deprecation before removal was available, with WebSearch exhausted in this run and not re-run for the Maven study either; Hyrum's Law (SEG ch. 1), which formulates the topic's behaviour-change rule. Example: Java, good half compiled with javac 21 -Xlint:all (the elision given a body), and a caller of parse received the [removal] warning; triggers tested with Python re against the bad half (the public-member pattern matches); the changelog pattern matches "### Removed", "- Removed `Config.parse(String)`; use `Config.load(String)`." and "Renamed `load` to `read`.".

(fetched from `SonarSource/sonar-java` master, `sonar-java-plugin/src/main/resources/org/sonar/l10n/java/rules/java/S1123.html` and `S1123.json`). Checkstyle `MissingDeprecated`, since 5.0: "The @Deprecated annotation is used for compilers and development tools. The Rationale claims only that a tool can quote the text. Verified hands-on: javac 21 ("warning: [deprecation] parseDate(String) in Dates has been deprecated") and the TypeScript 6.0.2 checker (6385 "'parseDate' is deprecated.") give the generic message whatever the notice says, so their callers read the text in the editor's hover and in the generated documentation. Gleison Brito, Andre Hora, Marco Tulio Valente, Romain Robbes, "Do Developers Deprecate APIs with Replacement Messages? A Large-Scale Analysis on Java Systems", IEEE SANER 2016, **unfetched** (no GitHub-hosted copy, neverworkintheory post or relayed snippet found; WebSearch budget exhausted): from memory, a large-scale measurement of how often deprecated Java API elements carry a message naming a replacement; it anchors nothing in the card · topic: api-evolution-and-deprecation (research/software-craft/api-evolution-and-deprecation.md) · formulation: Software Engineering at Google, ch. 15, section "Deprecation Warnings" ("A warning is actionable if the user can use the warning to actually perform some relevant action ... In each case, the warning provided the next steps that an engineer can perform to no longer depend on the deprecated system.") and section "Why Is Deprecation So Hard?" ("a one-to-one match between the old system and the new system is rare, and every use of the old system must be evaluated in the context of the new one"), read from `abseil/abseil.github.io` master, `resources/swe-book/html/ch15.html` · reception: not contested · notes: confidence high for the convention, which the fetched Java, Go, Rust, NumPy and TypeScript sources state in near-identical terms, while PEP 702 leaves the content to the author ("The content of deprecation messages is up to the user") and backs only the message shown at the use site; no study of its effect on callers was fetched or relayed, so the card carries no number. The validator checks the floor shared by the Java apiNote (reason strongly recommended, replacement if applicable), RFC 1270 ("and/or") and NEP 23 ("or a reason ... if no clear alternative"): replacement or reason; the drafting statement's "why and what to use instead" conjunction is recorded in Limits as one convention, not as the rule. Dropped from the drafting statement: "when no replacement exists, the notice says so", since no source asks the notice to state the absence, only to give the reason. "What to use or do instead" counts the change to make at the call site as well as a replacement element, as the Go Doc Comments and RFC 1270 ("what to use instead"), NEP 23 ("information on alternatives") and the Google TypeScript Style Guide ("directions for people to fix their call sites") put it; a run-time warning often deprecates a way of calling rather than an element. The Thesis names the body of a documentation directive among the notice texts, paired with the NEP 23 item "A ``.. deprecated::`` directive can be used for this." The link clause comes from the Java apiNote and is narrowed to documentation formats that support links, because a runtime warning message is plain text. The Go standard-library timing rule ("not added until Go 1.N+1") is kept in Limits as one standard library's documented policy, named without its language, and the validator does not check timing. SonarSource S1123 and Checkstyle MissingDeprecated are Java-only rules and back only the reason-and-alternative wording; S1123's exception for the members of a deprecated class belongs to its annotation-and-tag pairing check, not to the notice text, and is not used. The Limits check a member's own marker even inside a deprecated type or module, verified hands-on: rustc 1.97.0 reports a bare `#[deprecated]` function inside a module deprecated with a note as "use of deprecated function `legacy::own_bare`" with no note while its unmarked sibling gets the module's note, and does the same for a method in an `impl` block deprecated with a note; the TypeScript 6.0.2 language service reports a bare `/** @deprecated */` method of a class whose notice names its replacement as 6387 "The signature '(): void' of 'o.ownBare' is deprecated." and shows an empty deprecated tag on hover; javadoc 21 shows "Deprecated." with no text on a member of a deprecated class. Not cited: Sawant, Aniche, van Deursen, Bacchelli, ICSE 2018 (the relayed URL carries no statement on notice content); the neverworkintheory review of "A First Look at the Deprecation of RESTful APIs" (service APIs, outside the corpus). Triggers: the drafted `@deprecated\(` alternative was dropped because `@[Dd]eprecated\b` already matches it, and the reStructuredText `.. deprecated::` directive was added; `util.deprecate(` and `process.emitWarning(` are Node.js runtime deprecation calls, used for dispatch only and backed by no fetched source. `[.]deprecated\(` admits the module-qualified decorator (`warnings.deprecated(`, `typing_extensions.deprecated(`), and `(?:version-)?` admits the directive's current name: Sphinx 9.0 renamed `deprecated` to `version-deprecated` and keeps the old name as an alias (sphinx-doc/sphinx master, doc/usage/restructuredtext/directives.rst, fetched). '#!?' admits the inner attribute on a module; FutureWarning is the warnings module's category 'for warnings about deprecated features when those warnings are intended for end users' (python/cpython main, Doc/library/warnings.rst, fetched). The good half of the Example compiles with `tsc --noEmit --strict`.

The per-routine count of levels rests on Ruff's "higher number ... higher up the stack", the decorator's "further up the stack" and NumPy's stacklevel=3 examples, none of which says "one per frame" verbatim; the decorator's numbering from the direct caller rests on its documented "If it is ``1`` (the default), the warning is emitted at the direct caller" and on CPython's "stacklevel=stacklevel + 1". The Validator flags a level set too high as well as too low, because the cited documentation asks for "``deprecated_api``'s caller" and "the correct place", an exact line, and in the local run a stacklevel=3 warning called from the module level of __main__ is reported at "<sys>:0", which the default filters hide. The link between emitWarning's ctor and captureStackTrace's constructorOpt is not stated in the Node.js documentation; it is stated in lib/internal/process/warning.js and confirmed by the local run. util.deprecate is left out of the triggers, which the plan listed: its documented signature takes no stack level, cut function or skip list, and its implementation already passes the returned wrapper as emitWarning's ctor, so no finding on it could carry a fix; util.md does not document where its stack starts, so the Limits' documented-default skip does not cover it. The hiding of a deprecation warning by its nominal location is one runtime's default filter, so the card states it under that condition. applies_to drops the dynamic-types facet the plan proposed, because the Rust Example shows a statically typed language raising a run-time warning; the rule depends on a warning raised at run time, not on when types are checked. The card does not carry what a deprecation notice says (the replacement named, the removal period), compile-time deprecation markers, the choice of warning category beyond the audience fact in its Rationale, or adding no new use of a deprecated element, which the topic's other rules own; the formulation's relevance property is served here by attributing the warning to the line the engineer is writing.

Dropped from the drafted statement because no fetched source states them: "the forwarding code adapts ... results" (only argument supply is sourced: context.Background(), Pow(x, 2)) and "where it cannot be expressed in terms of the replacement, the notice says how the behaviour differs" (that case is now outside the rule). Ownership: automated migration of callers by inlining belongs to large-scale-changes-and-migrations, the notice, the warning and the deprecation period to this topic's other rules, and duplication in general to the design domain; this card judges only the deprecated element's body.

Scope is file: the entry point, an initializer and a boundary recover in another function of the same module are not visible from the added lines alone. The broken-invariant stop is the opposite pole, owned by ERR-06; this card defers it to Limits. Retries and fallbacks go to fault-tolerance-retries-timeouts-fallbacks. The breadth of a catch-all that aborts goes to ERR-08. The card leaves out: the Uber guide's preference for `t.Fatal` over panic inside tests (a test-quality point); the Google Go guide's note that a recovered request-handler panic is a historical mistake (a recovery rule, not a stop rule); an Erlang-style supervised crash of a lightweight task (no admissible source fetched; out of the five example languages). The card narrows the original statement where the evidence did: the original's "its declared type admits null, None, nil or undefined" becomes a declared type that marks the value as possibly absent (an optional or nullable type, a union with null, None or undefined, or a nullable annotation), and a bare reference or pointer type, where every such type admits absence, does not on its own make a value possibly absent, since NullAway assumes every unannotated parameter, return value and field non-null and asks for @Nullable where one may be null, nilness reports only where the control-flow graph shows nil, SA5011 only a pointer also checked against nil elsewhere, and SpotBugs a null that reaches the dereference on a branch or a return value that should generally be checked; the title says a null test elsewhere "says" the value can be absent, since SA5011 says such a test "suggests" it; a dereference before a later null test is carried as SpotBugs' disjunction (the test is redundant or the dereference is erroneous), decided by the declared type and the producing call, not as a defect outright; an operation the language defines on the absent value (ranging over or taking the length of a nil slice or map, indexing a nil map) is set aside from the Go specification; and the original's handling clause "a value the caller can tell apart from a real result" is left out of the Thesis, which no fetched fragment states, and handed to the rules on substitute values. The Rationale keeps the Handbook's subject, "the lack of checking", rather than making it the programmer's omitted test, since the Handbook sentence sits under §"strictNullChecks off" and may mean the language's checking, and keeps NullAway's "a series of type-based, local checks" rather than confining the checks to dereferences, since its example also reports a call site that passes null. "Throws" among the ways an absent branch leaves the path generalizes SA5011's "will not continue execution after a call to panic or log.Fatal". Osman et al., SANER 2016, DOI 10.1109/SANER.2016.57, was not opened (no GitHub-hosted copy, search budget spent) and is not cited. Scope is file: the finder reads the enclosing routine, because a check more than three lines above the change lies outside the hunk context, and at hunk scope the Validator flagged a guarded lookup whatever its stated reason. Java coverage: SpotBugs anchors downcasts, and the Optional javadoc documents only that get() and orElseThrow() throw. Triggers: six patterns — postfix `!` followed by a member access, a closing parenthesis, a comma, a semicolon, a closing bracket or brace, an index other than a `vec![` macro, or the end of the line; unwrap/expect including `_err` and `_unchecked`, `orElseThrow()`, and `.get()` on an optional-named receiver or on the result of a find…, max, min or reduce call (such as `repo.findById(id).get()`); the single-value type assertion; `as` to a capitalized or primitive type; `cast(`; and a parenthesized cast to a capitalized type. A bare `.get()` is left out because it would dispatch the card on nearly every Java diff (Future, Supplier, atomics), so an Optional.get() on a receiver neither named as an optional nor returned by such a call is missed. A definite-assignment assertion (`x!: T`) is not matched either. The triggers compile, parse through cardlib, and the type-assertion pattern matches the bad half's assertion line. Ownership: a stop on an expected, recoverable failure belongs to the error-handling card on returning recoverable failures (shipped ERR-12); trust-boundary validation to security-hygiene-in-ordinary-code; an unchecked dereference with no forced form written, and assertion statements and their removal in optimized builds, to their own defensive-programming and contracts cards

Three Go tool rules (revive, go-critic, Staticcheck) and Effective Go agree that a release deferred to routine exit inside a loop does not run per iteration. The per-step half rests on PEP 8 and the Google Python Style Guide, with the AutoCloseable Javadoc and the Rust book for block-scoped release. No fetched source measures a failure rate, so the card carries no number. The leak studies named as candidates (Weimer and Necula, OOPSLA 2004, DOI 10.1145/1028976.1029011; Ghanavati et al., EMSE 2020, DOI 10.1007/s10664-019-09731-8, arXiv 1810.00101; Kellogg et al., ESEC/FSE 2021, DOI 10.1145/3468264.3468576) had no openable or relayed text in this run and back nothing in the card. The mechanism was reproduced locally but is not cited. In Go, 50 files opened in a loop with a deferred close held 50 extra descriptors until the routine returned, and none once the body moved into a routine. In Rust, a value bound at routine level was dropped after the following step, and one in an inner block before it. The exhaustion and blocked-move statements come from Python-specific guidance, but the mechanism (an open handle holds an operating-system resource until released) does not depend on the language, so applies_to stays universal. The deferred-release half covers languages whose deferred release is routine-scoped, Go among the five, and the card names none. Triggers differ from the topic's proposal in three ways. The acquisition pattern's path prefix is broadened from [.] to [.:] so that path-qualified calls such as File::open( match the Rust bad half. `defer cancel()` is added to the defer pattern. A pattern for opening a scoped-release block (with … as, try (, using) is added, because such a block can enclose work after the resource's last use. The hand-off exemptions in Limits follow OS_OPEN_STREAM's escapes (returned, assigned to a field, passed on), narrowed to a callee that takes over the release, so that a helper which only reads the resource does not exempt it. The card does not carry release on the exceptional paths, release order, ownership transfer, or finalizers, which belong to other rules of the topic. Locks and release across threads lie outside the corpus.

no source measures how often a release operation that stops at its first failure or releases twice leaks or faults, and the candidate papers (Weimer and Necula, OOPSLA 2004, DOI 10.1145/1028976.1029011; Kellogg et al., ESEC/FSE 2021, DOI 10.1145/3468264.3468576; Ghanavati et al., EMSE 2020, arXiv 1810.00101) were neither opened nor relayed in this run and state client-side leaks rather than release-operation design, so the card carries no number. The idempotence half rests on contracts that range from required (Closeable) through strongly encouraged (AutoCloseable) to undefined at the interface (io.Closer), which the Limits carry; the "report after releasing" half rests on the AutoCloseable/Closeable advice, the FilterOutputStream implementation, DisposableStack and close(2); the destructor half rests on Rust documentation and is stated conditionally on a language whose failing destructor during unwinding aborts the program, and its separate operation follows C-DTOR-FAIL's "e.g. a close method" together with File's sync_all and BufWriter's flush. The rule covers the resources the object owns: the Checker Framework treats unannotated fields as non-owning, and gzip.Writer.Close and TarFile.close leave a writer or file object the caller passed in open, which the Limits carry. The close(2) retry hazard is quoted as the man page states it ("from another thread"); release across threads stays outside the corpus. The card leaves release order, the catch-and-propagate structure around a call to the release operation, a blocking destructor (C-DTOR-BLOCK) and retry or timeout of a connection to their own topics; it overlaps the owning-type card of the same topic on "releases every owned field on every path", which an ownership note in the review workflow resolves.

The card names no language API in its prose ("a destructor hook the collector runs" stands for the Python `__del__` hook) and its triggers name each runtime's finalizer and cleanup hooks, since the hooks have no shared vocabulary. Not carried: FIO04-J's starvation while waiting for a finalizer to release a Lock or Semaphore (concurrency is a reserved specialty); the Go finalizers' dependency order (the card says only that a runtime may run cleanups in any order); release on every path of the acquiring routine, the release operation an owning type provides and ownership transfer, which other rules of this topic own. The id ERR-26 was assigned by the orchestrator in topic-local order and collides with the shipped ERR-26 of error-and-exception-handling, so it is renumbered at merge.

Thirteen fetched sources state the rule's parts: four tool rules (go vet httpresponse and Staticcheck SA5001 for the release before the error check; Infer RESOURCE_LEAK and CodeQL java/input-resource-leak for the nested constructor), a secure-coding standard (CERT FIO04-J, ERR05-J), official documentation of Go, TypeScript, Python and Rust, and the TC39 Explicit Resource Management proposal. No source measures how often the defect occurs, so the card carries no number. Scope: the nil-dereference half rests on Go tool rules, and on CERT and Infer for a cleanup block. The Rationale says "a registration or release that reaches through it" for two reasons. `defer resp.Body.Close()` on a nil response dereferences at the defer statement itself. Go's `(*File).Close` returns ErrInvalid on a nil receiver (golang/go, master, `src/os/file_posix.go`, `if f == nil { return ErrInvalid }`, read from the skeptic's download, not cited in the card). So the card does not claim that every release dereferences. The nested-constructor half is documented by two tools for Java stream wrappers only, and the TypeScript example reproduces it (see below). The card names no allocation among the intervening steps, because only C++ Core Guidelines R.12, a formulation outside the five languages, states that case. It names "an operation on the resource" (Infer's fos.write) under "any other call that can fail". The replaced original failure rests on ERR05-J (lost in Java, kept as `__context__` in Python, hence "propagates in place of") and is scoped to a cleanup block, where a raised dereference ends the protected block abruptly. The wrapper clause carries the condition "a wrapper that can fail" from CodeQL ("if the constructor of the outer expression may throw") and from Infer. The Validator's default carries the same condition: where signatures declare the errors they raise, a standard-library wrapper whose constructor declares none, such as a buffering wrapper's, is treated as unable to fail. This follows CodeQL's CloseType.qll (an outer closeable "whose constructor does not have a throws clause" is safe), CodeQL's own good example (CloseReaderGood.java, a one-statement `new BufferedReader(new FileReader(...))`), and Infer's list of constructors that can throw, which names no buffering wrapper. So the Validator no longer flags that nesting. TypeScript signatures declare no errors, so the Example's RecordParser is still treated as able to fail. Infer's note that an argument that is not a resource causes no nested leak goes to Limits. A shared cleanup that null-tests each release in its own nested cleanup is CERT FIO04-J's compliant solution, so Limits declare it correct, and the card flags only the release with no existence test (CERT, Infer). A shared cleanup whose null-tested releases are not nested is still marked. The Finding output's `rationale` names an earlier release's failure as its cause (CERT FIO04-J's third noncompliant example; Infer's fis.close). Infer's "Two Resources Fix 1" (swallowing the close exception) is not carried. Infer's "when you don't want to return the resource to the surrounding context" bounds the standard acquire-then-protect idiom to a resource the routine does not hand back. For a resource that is handed back, Limits follow contextlib's cleanup in `__enter__` and TC39's `move()`: a release registered on a cleanup stack right after the acquisition, and moved out once nothing before the hand-back can fail, meets the rule. The Validator skips only the path on which the routine hands the resource back, so a returning routine that registers its stack release after a step that can fail is still marked. The formulation field drops three trade books (The Pragmatic Programmer topic 26 "An Exception Antipattern", The Go Programming Language §5.8, Effective Python Item 13 / 2nd ed. Item 65), which were relayed and cannot be re-checked here, because the fetched sources named in it carry the same formulations. Not carried: the candidate papers (Weimer and Necula, OOPSLA 2004, DOI 10.1145/1028976.1029011; Kellogg et al., ESEC/FSE 2021, DOI 10.1145/3468264.3468576; Ghanavati et al., EMSE 2020, DOI 10.1007/s10664-019-09731-8). The WebSearch budget was spent, no GitHub-hosted copy was opened for this card, and the papers measure leaks along all paths rather than when the release is registered. Ownership: a release made by hand with no registration, release on every path, release order and ownership transfer belong to the topic's other rules; the catch-and-propagate structure around the release goes to error-and-exception-handling. Example: the good half, in a module that declares Disposable FileReader and RecordParser classes, compiled with `tsc --noEmit --strict --target es2022 --lib es2022,esnext.disposable` (TypeScript 6.0.2), exit 0, on the drafter's run and again on the closing pass. On the closing pass it also matches `try (BufferedReader br = new BufferedReader(new FileReader(path))) {`, which the Validator now skips. `rs` sits in the whole-name list of trigger 3, so `if (users != null)` and `if errors != nil` do not match, while `if (rs != null)` and `if rs is not None:` do. On the drafter's run, 20 positive and 10 negative lines were checked, with 0 failures. (Goodliffe); Amazon Builders' Library "Avoiding fallback in distributed systems" (Gabrielson); Netflix Hystrix wiki "How To Use", "Fallback" and "Common Patterns" · reception: contested. One position is "a substitute may be returned without a signal" (SWEBOK V3 ch. 3 §4.5; Hystrix wiki "Fail Silent" and "Fallback: Static"; .NET Microservices guide "Provide fallbacks", formulation). The other is "the failure stays visible and a fallback never fails open" (OWASP ASVS 5.0 16.3.4 and 16.5.3; CWE-636; Liu et al. HotOS 2019; Dai et al. IC2E 2018; Software Engineering at Google ch. 14 and the AWS "Avoiding fallback" article, formulation). The substitute's effect and the record of the failure separate them: silence toward the caller is accepted where the substitute only removes a feature or returns an empty response with a benign effect (SWEBOK "benign effect", ASVS 16.5.2, Hystrix "Fail Silent"), provided the failure is recorded (Hystrix metrics "updated to indicate the command failure" whether or not a fallback runs; ASVS 16.3.4). On the permissive point the sides do not agree: Hystrix "Fallback: Static" defaults a credential-based true/false command to true, which CWE-636 and ASVS 16.5.3 treat as fail-open. Where the answer grants access or passes a check, the card follows the security sources and carries the Hystrix example in Limits · notes: confidence moderate. The fail-open half rests on two fetched security standards (ASVS 5.0, CWE-636). The record half rests on official library documentation, ASVS 16.3.4 and two cloud-system studies whose counts are of fault-handling and timeout bugs, not of fallbacks as such; no source measures how often a silent or permissive substitute causes a failure. No fetched source states an unconditional rule for writes, so the original statement's "a write or payment reported as done" and the title's "never substitutes a success the call did not give" are narrowed to the hedged Hystrix wording ("probably", "usually") in the Rationale, and the title reads "never grants access or passes a check the call did not". The original statement's "A non-transient failure such as data loss is surfaced, not absorbed" is not carried: its one source, Google AIP-194 "Automatic retry configuration" (aip-dev/google.aip.dev master aip/general/0194.md, fetched), governs whether a client retries an RPC automatically and says a DATA_LOSS error "must immediately be surfaced to the application", not what the application's own handler does with the error once it arrives. The topic's retry, timeout, deadline-propagation and idempotency discipline is outside this card. The local catch, wrap and propagate of the failure belongs to error-and-exception-handling, and the log record of the fallback to logging-and-diagnostic-output.

the IC2E figures are the paper's own counts out of 156 (42 missing, 65 misused; 83 no error message, 16 misleading, 40 correct), since its percentages are shares of the 137 bugs it classifies by root cause and the 139 it classifies by diagnosability; zero counts as unbounded only where the client documents it so, since the Java request builder and the Rust socket setters reject a zero duration; a bound on connecting alone does not meet the rule, since the wait for the response stays unbounded; the Limits carry the finite 5-second default of one client together with the checker that therefore flags only its explicit None, the per-read versus total timeout distinction, and the "nearly all production code ... nearly all requests" qualifier of one client's guide as a project tolerance; the card does not carry deadline propagation to callees, retry, backoff, idempotency or fallback (other rules of this topic), the handling of the timeout error (error-and-exception-handling), the timeout value as a setting (runtime-configuration; the IC2E study's 65 of 156 bugs from misused values), or timeouts on synchronization within one node (the IC2E study counts 16 missing-timeout-for-synchronization bugs, file system and process/thread synchronization among them; concurrency is a reserved specialty); the triggers follow the topic's computed set with two broadenings, `\bcreate_connection\s*\(` in the first pattern and `So|Write` in the timeout-setter alternation of the last, so that a socket opened with no timeout and a socket read timeout set to zero dispatch; the triggers name client APIs per language because a missing argument has no language-neutral vocabulary; the Example's good half compiles with python3 compile().

The exemption for a retry of a whole transaction block is limited to a transaction abort or another failure documented as meaning the transaction was not committed, following AIP-194's ABORTED guidance; a retry after a commit whose outcome is unknown is judged like any other retry, following AIP-194's UNKNOWN guidance and the lost-acknowledgement case in Saltzer et al. The transparent retry of a request that never reached the server's application logic is stated in A6 for the gRPC client library, so the card says only that a client library may retry it. The study shows the defect with one case (Cassandra-6427) and gives no count for the incorrect-retry category, so the card carries no rate. Not carried: the draft's callee-side mechanics (fingerprints, the 409 for a retry that overlaps the original, the 422 for a reused key), and attempt bounds, transient-failure classification, backoff, per-call timeouts and retry layering, which the topic's other rules own

All three compile, and each matches one line of the Example's bad half (routine-at-error, failure-at-debug, detail-at-info) and no line of the good half. The good half compiles and passes go vet (go 1.24, log/slog). The card carries S1166's tolerance in Limits as a project tolerance, not as a dispute over the practice. Ruff files TRY400 in its pedantic category ("too opinionated or are too prone to false positives", off by default), and its fix-safety note names false positives on logger-like calls outside the `logging` module. The evidence is one telemetry convention, facility documentation (Log4j, Python logging, Go slog, Rust log) and tool rules (Sonar, Ruff); no empirical study measures the diagnostic cost of a message-only record. The candidate studies (Yuan et al. ICSE 2012, Fu et al. ICSE SEIP 2014, Chen and Jiang ICSE 2017, Hassani et al. EMSE 2018) were not used: the openable copies in reach say nothing about passing the exception value, and the WebSearch budget was used up. The facility condition limits the rule to facilities that accept the value; OTel's instance-passing sentence ("When language implementations support passing exception instances to the [Emit a LogRecord](…) API") governs records emitted through its Logger API ("This document does not apply to logging bridges."), and the Rationale states it at that scope. The card claims only that a record "can hold" a stack trace. The card leaves these to their own rules: whether to log or propagate, logging once at the handling layer, the level (OTel's severity guidance), the identifiers in the message, a stack trace printed in place of a log statement (diagnostics-through-logging-facility), and the sensitive-information remarks of OTel and Log4j (security hygiene). Clean Code ch. 7 "Provide Context with Exceptions", a second formulation the orchestrator named (**unfetched**), is dropped: its wording about context in exceptions belongs to the content rule, and the openable SLF4J FAQ carries this rule's wording. ICSE 2012, Fu et al. ICSE SEIP 2014, Chen and Jiang ICSE 2017, Hassani et al. EMSE 2018) was used, since none was reached stating this claim. PMD GuardLogStatement's own point is that an unguarded method call in a log argument runs whatever the level; the card cites it for the guard it asks for, which is the later change that would skip a side effect, not as a check that flags side effects. The qualifier "that later code relies on" narrows the log crate's unconditional "Avoid writing expressions with side-effects in log statements" for finder precision; a side effect nothing reads is outside the card though the crate's advice covers it. Extending the rule to statements inside a level guard that wraps the log call is the drafter's reading of the CPython guard example, where the skipped calls are arguments of the guarded call; a statement of its own in the guarded block is skipped by the same branch. The Thesis's state changes, the assignment among them, are limited to state that code after the log call or its guard relies on, and the Limits exempt a name declared or assigned inside a level guard and read only there. Both follow the log_enabled! doc example, which computes the costly value inside the guard for the debug! call it encloses; without them the card would flag the guard idiom its main source recommends. The triggers merge the method, generic-call and macro log forms into one pattern, so the increment, channel, compound-assignment, assignment-expression and consuming-call spellings apply to every form; a second pattern catches level guards. Go's slog evaluates plain arguments at every level, so the Example shows the guarded form, where the pop is skipped at a disabled level; its good half compiled and ran with go1.24.7 (gofmt clean, go vet ok) and popped one item at both info and debug level. Not carried: the cost of building a message the level discards (the topic's lazy-formatting rule), and side effects inside a type's own string-conversion or log-value method, which the hunk scope cannot reach.

The anchors are two tool rules, a mocking library's own annotation contract, a style guide and the client owner's documentation that contests it, all fetched except the AWS v2 guide, which is relayed. No measured study backs the rule: a search for Spadini et al. (MSR 2017) relayed only its abstract, which states no preference, so the card carries no number and no frequency claim. Scope was narrowed on review. The preference for the owner's testing library and the real client is kept only for a component reached through a client over a transport, which is the scope the style guide gives. The general preference for an owner's or the repository's fake over a mock, for any dependency, is not carried; it is recorded as a pending entry with SEG ch. 13 "Faking" as its formulation. The narrowing also leaves out mocks of first-party wrappers, which the Mockito wiki "How to write good tests" (fetched, https://raw.githubusercontent.com/wiki/mockito/mockito/How-to-write-good-tests.md) recommends in place of mocking "a type you don't own"; the card's Limits state that bound. A second review found the transport condition contested by the client's owner: the AWS SDK for Go documents stubbing its service client through an interface it publishes (v1 `s3iface`) or one callers define (v2 guide), so the Limits exempt a stub built the way the client's owner documents and keep the condition for a client whose owner documents no such pattern. grpc-go's own Documentation/gomock-example.md (fetched at tag v1.30.0, https://raw.githubusercontent.com/grpc/grpc-go/v1.30.0/Documentation/gomock-example.md: "Idea: Mock the client stub that connects to the server."; 404 at v1.40.0) once documented the same pattern for generated RPC clients; it was removed, so it is not cited in the card. SEG ch. 13 "When Is Stubbing Appropriate?" also calls stubbing a credit-card-server client appropriate; it is a formulation source and stays out of the card. The all-methods condition carries S5969's bound of more than one non-private method, counted on one instance, so the Example's one-method `Doer` is flagged under the transport condition only; net/http's owner documents no interface for stubbing its client (src/net/http/client.go, fetched, has no such pattern) and ships net/http/httptest. S5969 is a Java rule on mocking-framework mocks, both do-not-mock markers are Java annotations and the style guide is written for Go; the card carries each to other languages, as the Source caveat states. The formulation's "those duplicates tend to break the API's contract" is carried only as the mechanism the style guide states ("the complexity of imitating client behavior correctly"), without the "tend to". The Example's good half (an httptest server with the real client, net/http's own testing library) was checked with gofmt, go vet and go test under /tmp/craft-research/tst-02-draft3/goex. The bad half's stubbed `&http.Response{StatusCode: 200}` has a nil Body, which the `http.Client.Do` contract ("the Response will contain a non-nil Body") excludes, so a Fetch that closes the body panics on it. The title says "type" rather than "class" so it holds in languages without classes. The card bundles three conditions with separate evidence; splitting it into three cards is left to the orchestrator.
