The card flags only a verification of a call the same test stubs with argument matching at least as narrow as the verification's, which is the scope in which the documentation's argument holds. The card states the broader principle (verify only calls made for their side effects) in the Thesis's first sentence as guidance for the developer, but the Validator does not flag it, because deciding whether an unstubbed call is a query and whether its effect is observable needs semantic tracing. The Rationale states the redundancy only for an outcome the code under test reaches only with the stubbed value: when a path that skips the call yields the same outcome, the outcome assertion passes on the skip and the verification is the only check, so the fix asks for a stubbed value no skipping path yields. The Rationale states the study's population as one language and one mocking framework (§ 3.1 admits only Java projects that declare Mockito). The Limits carry the cases where the documented argument does not hold: count and order checks; a call made for its side effect whose returned value only reports whether the effect succeeded and which the code under test checks, where the stub keeps the code under test on its success path, a skipping path can end in the same outcome and the verification is the only check of the effect (the study's § 6.1 observes side-effect calls whose return value is checked only to confirm success; the SEG formulation draws the line at state-changing functions); specific-argument checks on an any-argument stub; and whole-double strictness checks. The Rationale lays the redundancy on the verification only where an asserted outcome needs the stubbed value, and on the stub where the code under test does not use the value (the second branch of the Mockito argument: "it should not be stubbed"). Where the test also checks that the double received no other calls and that check counts stubbed calls, the fix sets it to ignore them (Mockito's `verifyNoMoreInteractions` and `ignoreStubs` Javadoc). Triggers are refined from the plan: `AssertExpectations` is dropped because it is a whole-double check that the Limits exclude; `\bverify\(` is widened to `\b(co)?([Vv]erify)\s*[({]` so it also matches block, capitalised and coroutine verify forms (mockk/mockk README.md `coVerify`); the BDD `should(`, `call_count`, `assert.called*` and `AssertNumberOfCalls` forms are added; the awaited (`assert_awaited*`, `await_count`) and `been.called*` forms are added; after review, the mock attribute reads `called`, `call_args`, `call_args_list`, `await_args*` and `mock_calls` (cpython Doc/library/unittest.mock.rst), the `toHaveBeenLastCalledWith` and `toHaveBeenNthCalledWith` matchers (jestjs/jest docs/ExpectAPI.md) and the `mock.calls` array (jestjs/jest docs/MockFunctionAPI.md), and the spy `calledOnce`, `calledTwice`, `calledThrice`, `calledWith*` and `callCount` forms (sinonjs/sinon src/sinon/proxy.js), the testify `.Once()` count (stretchr/testify mock/mock.go, where `Once` returns `c.Times(1)`) and the NSubstitute `.Received(` check (nsubstitute/NSubstitute docs/help/received-calls/index.md) are added, all fetched from raw.githubusercontent.com; every backslash escape that followed a word is placed behind a group or written as a character class, so the audit's backslash-path check (R-42 in static-audit.py) passes, and the patterns match the same lines. The Example's good half compiled with javac against a minimal stand-in of the mocking API, since no mocking-framework jar could be reached.

Scope: the defect is live in dynamically typed mock libraries and in statically typed code where a cast via an unchecked type or an untyped module factory bypasses the compiler; a double created from the class or interface in a statically typed language already meets the rule. The card does not carry behavioural fidelity of a double (a double that returns what the real type never returns) — speccing checks shape only and no fetched source states a checkable behaviour rule; nor the @DoNotMock theme of type owners forbidding doubles, which belongs to mocking what you own. The "misspelled assertion helper" claim is hedged in the card because the Python library has raised on a fixed list of assert-prefix misspellings since 3.5 (documented under the `unsafe` parameter); the claim still holds for other misspellings and other libraries. The cast clause rests on no-unsafe-type-assertion, whose own When-Not-To-Use-It admits heavy reporting in stub-heavy test files; a team that accepts that trade uses the project-tolerance Limit. A direct cast to the real type is not in the rule: tsc 6.0.2 (strict) still compares the literal with the type, and the example's jest.fn() literal cast directly to the type fails with TS2352 after a member rename, though a subset literal whose members are plain functions of the member types still compiles under a direct cast (a jest.fn() subset literal fails with TS2352 even before any rename); the card targets the cast through an unchecked type (`as unknown as`, `as any`), which switches the comparison off entirely. The compile-time forms fail only where the test files are type-checked; the Jest "Via babel" passage is the source for that Limit. flake8-mock-spec TMS020–TMS022 and the S9137 implementation (sonar-python python-checks/src/main/java/org/sonar/python/checks/tests/MocksShouldUseAutospecCheck.java, hasReplacement) treat a patch with an explicit new or new_callable as compliant; with an explicit replacement, patch ignores spec and rejects autospec. Triggers 1, 2 and 5 are the Python and Ruby spellings and cannot match the TypeScript Example; each was checked against a bad line of its own language (S9137's `payments = Mock()` and `with patch("app.notify.send") as send:`, flake8-mock-spec's `mocked_foo = mock.Mock()`, an RSpec `double("book")`) and matches none of the compliant forms (`create_autospec(...)`, `patch(..., autospec=True)`, `Mock(spec=...)`, `MagicMock(spec_set=...)`, `instance_double(...)`).

(fetched) · topic: test-doubles (research/software-craft/test-doubles.md) · formulation: Mock Roles, not Objects — "Only mock your immediate neighbours" and "Too many mocks" (fetched) · reception: not contested · notes: confidence moderate; the partial-double half rests on a mocking framework's official guidance plus a four-system practice observation and one framework developer's view, from a study that counted mocks and not spies, none measuring a defect rate or a cost; the chain half rests on the same guidance, which says a chain "hints at" a Law of Demeter violation or a mocked value object, and on an experience report — the card keeps it a hint and bounds it in Limits (an object the unit obtains by design from a factory, pool or connection is created through its neighbour, not navigated to; a returned double that is only verified is outside the chain); the Limits bound on created objects rests on §4.9 of the same paper; its §1.2 excludes returned references from an object's immediate neighbours, so the card does not call a created object an immediate collaborator; the third-party-interface exception is carried for partial doubles only: the RETURNS_DEEP_STUBS javadoc names legacy code alone, and §4.1 of the OOPSLA paper says not to mock types defined by external libraries. The card does not carry the §4.7 heading as a general limit on which dependencies a test may double: §4.7 limits expectations on the objects a unit navigates to, §5.1 separates mocks from stubs, and a test that runs a real collaborator and doubles a dependency behind it is left unjudged.

The card follows the concepts side, that independent actions on other code or with other checking logic, each with assertions on its own outcome, are split; the other two positions flag only part of that case (tsDetect's Eager Test needs multiple calls to multiple production methods, so the Example's two calls of one function are not an Eager Test, and the Example's three assertions stay under the jest default 5 and the S5961 default 25), and carries the separating condition (one behaviour, that is one action's outcome or the same call checked by the same logic on several inputs, versus independent actions that call other code or need other checking logic) in Limits, with each side's evidence · notes: confidence moderate. The research evidence is observational association (Spadini et al.: smell-level change- and defect-proneness, not causation, with the smells measured by Table II's definitions, Eager Test as exercising more methods of the tested object and Assertion Roulette as several assertions with no explanation; 'several assertions checking different behavior' is the authors' explanation, not the measure; Grano et al.: perceived quality from 199 evaluations of 10 tests). No source measures the separating condition itself; it reconciles the tool rules and the studies, and its same-call case rests on S5961's compliant solution (two calls of f kept in test_f, the call of g split into test_g) and the Go style guide's table-driven guidance. The Validator reads an accessor on a returned value as part of the assertion on that outcome, and treats a named subtest as its own test, following the Go style guide's subtests sentence. The original statement's 'a name that joins two behaviours with and is the usual sign' rests only on SEG ch. 12, a practitioner text, so the card keeps it only as a Validator grep pointer and in the triggers, not as a claim. The original 'the number of production methods called is not the measure' rests only on SEG's many-to-many sentence, and Spadini et al. measured Eager Test as more change- and defect-prone, so the card softens it to 'a sign to inspect' and makes setup calls part of the setup step (Rust book three-step structure). The Go style guide's table-driven guidance is used for the table and parameterized case and its tolerance for simple error-check rows. The Go blog 'Using Subtests and Sub-benchmarks' was fetched (golang/website _content/blog/subtests.md) but is not cited, because the Go style guide states the same table-driven guidance without a blog locator

Two frameworks' documentation state the rule outright: a TypeScript property-testing library (should not change, clone first, bad shrinking and wrong display) and Go's native fuzzing engine (must not modify the underlying argument data; should not retain mutable arguments, because their memory may be mutated in a later invocation). No research paper was found that states it, and WebSearch was exhausted; the relayed candidates (property-based testing in practice, Tyche, the QuickCheck origin paper) cover adoption, usability and bugs found, not this rule. The proptest book chapters (strategy-basics, shrinking-basics, test-runner, tips-and-best-practices, failure-persistence) do not discuss mutating inputs. The Thesis, Limits and Validator question are scoped to generated inputs, so a value the framework generates for the predicate to act through (a per-run logger such as fc.context(); Go's *T, whose methods fail the test) is outside the rule. A shallow copy (spread, slice copy, ArrayList.clone) still shares the nested values the input holds by reference, so the Limits and the Validator treat changing an element or field of such a value as changing the input. An element that a shallow copy holds by value belongs to the copy alone (Go standard library, package slices, doc comment of Clone, golang/go master src/slices/slices.go, https://raw.githubusercontent.com/golang/go/master/src/slices/slices.go, fetched: "The elements are copied using assignment, so this is a shallow clone."), and the fix asks for a clone deep enough that the changed part shares nothing with the input. Rust quickcheck's source shows it passes a clone and shrinks and reports from its kept copy; that supports only the narrower claim that a clone sharing no mutable data with the kept copy is safe to change (a clone holding, for instance, a shared Arc to mutable state carries the change back), so the statement's line 'Where a framework hands the property an owned copy, the rule is met without effort' is not carried. The orchestrator's title clause 'because the framework reuses those values to shrink and to report the failure' was dropped, because no fragment states that the values are reused for shrinking. The Go retention requirement appears in the Rationale as context and is not checked separately by the Validator. The Rust Example's &mut Vec<i32> parameter is a stylized form forced by the assigned example language: Rust frameworks hand the property an owned clone, which the Validator skips when it shares no mutable data with the framework's copy. The orchestrator's four trigger patterns and the added Rust pattern are merged into one alternation, so the single trigger matches the bad half and keeps the Go, Java, Python and Rust spellings. Trigger recall gap: no pattern matches element or field assignment (xs[0] = 5, ys[0].n = 5), Java add/set, or random.shuffle(xs), although the Validator names element and field assignment.

the Java and Rust frameworks were not re-checked for this rule and are not cited.

The comparison is made at the callers a change leaves unedited and at the public or exported routines it edits, not inside every edited routine: the cited definition is at program level ("external behavior of a program"), and the RefactoringMiner catalogue counts Change Return Type, Add/Remove/Reorder Parameter and Add/Remove/Change Thrown Exception Type as refactorings, which change a non-public routine's interface together with its callers; that README item is in the card's Source to anchor the Thesis clause on such routines. The title and H1 say "the order of its side effects", not the order in which expressions are evaluated, because reordering side-effect-free expressions is not observable and the inliner documentation adds a binding declaration only "When it cannot safely eliminate all parameter variables"; the Rationale says the inliner "takes care" to avoid behaviour changes, as its documentation states. The Rationale says "three refactoring engines", not three mainstream ones, because the abstract does not call all three tested engines mainstream. The Java-modifier declaration pattern is merged into the routine-declaration trigger, the raise/throw trigger is left out until an Example shows a raise in its bad half, and the Example's bad half carries an import line that the import trigger matches. SWEBOK V3.0 ch. 5 §4.2 ("Refactoring is a reengineering technique that aims at reorganizing a program without changing its behavior", ligurio/swebok-v3, fetched) stays out of the card: GitHub code search turned up no V4.0 copy to re-anchor it to, and the definition rests on the fetched TSE 2013 abstract instead. Mixing structural and behavioural edits in one commit, the safety net for untested code, and API renames for external callers are left out of the card as other topics' ground; the scope sentence in Limits carries no evidence fragment.

(markup removed) · topic: code-smells-and-antipatterns (research/software-craft/code-smells-and-antipatterns.md) · formulation: Fowler and Beck, Refactoring 2nd ed. ch. 3 'Temporary Field' (**unfetched**); Jerzyk and Madeyski, Code Smells Catalog, Luzkan/smells main content/smells/temporary-field.md (fetched; description "A field that's null eleven months of the year and suddenly matters during one specific calculation") · reception: not contested · notes: confidence moderate; the card rests on one Java static-analysis rule that sits in its tool's quickstart set, together with the rule's implementation, its dataflow pass and its test suite. The step to Python, TypeScript, Go and Rust rests on the rule's own mechanism: no method observes the value from before the call. Scope by use rather than by declared visibility follows from three language sources, fetched: The Rust Reference, rust-lang/reference master src/visibility-and-privacy.md — "If an item is private, it may be accessed by the current module and its descendants."; The Go Programming Language Specification, golang/go master doc/go_spec.html, Exported identifiers — "An identifier may be exported to permit access to it from another package." (HTML markup around "exported" removed); Python tutorial, Classes, python/cpython main Doc/tutorial/classes.rst — "\"Private\" instance variables that cannot be accessed except from inside an object don't exist in Python." So the card searches a field's uses across its module or package and sets aside public or exported fields. The equivalence of field and local is conditioned on no other code assigning the field between a method's assignment and its read: PMD's disabled test #4616 shows the rule reporting such a field, and its dataflow pass joins an unknown call's possible kill with the earlier definition, so a call on the same object, a callback or a concurrent writer each break the rewrite; the card puts all three outside the rule, where the source names threading alone. Pylint W0201 serves only as a detection cue in the Validator, because it flags first definition outside the constructor and not the assign-before-read test. No empirical study of temporary fields' maintenance effect could be reached in this run, so the card carries no effect size. Three parts of the statement are left out. (1) The "pass it as an argument where one operation's helpers share it" alternative is dropped: no fetched source states it, and under the rule's condition a helper that reads the field before assigning it puts the field outside the rule. (2) The "through reflection" exclusion is narrowed to the annotations that hand a field to generated accessors or a framework (PMD's default ignoredAnnotations). (3) The kind-tagged-type case (DSN-49) is not named in the card, which stays self-contained; the Limits keep only "a field that any method reads before assigning it is outside the rule".

Nine checker documents for Java, Go, Python and TypeScript/JavaScript report an unread parameter as one to remove. The private/unexported precondition is stated by PMD (private methods by default), Error Prone (private and effectively private members), gopls (exported functions ignored) and IntelliJ's visibility settings; TypeScript, ESLint, Ruff, pylint and Sonar check routines of any visibility, so the card's narrower precondition follows from them a fortiori. The exemptions are the union of the documents', not each one's: overrides and implementations (Sonar; pylint; Ruff when marked @override; gopls for a same-package interface name; IntelliJ when any implementation or overrider reads the parameter; TypeScript and ESLint name none and rely on the underscore marker), interface defaults (Sonar), function values (gopls), empty or throwing bodies (gopls, pylint and Ruff at any visibility; Sonar only for non-private methods, and PMD's own example flags an empty private method), annotated methods (Sonar; IntelliJ for framework annotations), and underscore/unused/ignored markers. Every anchor is tool documentation, though, and no empirical study measures the cost of an unread parameter. The class-level smell studies of the topic (Sjøberg 2013, Khomh 2012, Palomba 2018) say nothing about parameters and are not carried. A method's receiver is excluded, following pylint's first-argument exemption (Ruff's method check also skips it). The unused-name marker applies only to a kept parameter that callers pass by position: per Ruff, renaming an override's parameter can break the Liskov Substitution Principle, so a parameter that may be passed by name keeps its name, and an override takes the override marker. Removal across a private family of implementations is permitted, not required, because the Validator cannot flag a member that implements or overrides. "trait" and "protocol" extend the sources' "interface", and pylint's protocol-class exemption, to the languages that use those words. Rust's unused_variables lint (rust-lang/rust master compiler/rustc_lint_defs/src/builtin.rs, fetched in the skeptic pass) gives the underscore prefix ("prefix it with an underscore such as `_x`") but says "variables" and never names parameters, so it is not carried as an anchor. "internal" visibility from the original statement is dropped because no fetched fragment names it. The original's "breaking change in a published library" becomes the PMD/gopls ripple and other-package reasons, without the word "breaking". ESLint's after-used positional default is not carried, since it would contradict full removal in a private routine.

It is much easier for reviewers to understand the changes introduced by each CL when they are separate."; "Small cleanups such as fixing a local variable name can be included inside of a feature change or bug fix CL, though."; "make sure the whole system keeps working after each CL is submitted" · topic: small-steps-and-minimal-diffs (research/software-craft/small-steps-and-minimal-diffs.md) · formulation: Linux kernel Documentation/process/submitting-patches.rst §'Style-check your changes' (openable formulation, whose wording the card follows) · reception: not contested · notes: confidence moderate. Two fetched project-guidance documents state the practice and give its reasons: the move is clearly delineated, review sees the actual differences, tools track history better, and reviewers understand separate changes more easily. Neither reports a measured effect, so the card carries no number. The kernel limits the rule to code moved from one file to another. In Google's example, moving and renaming a class form one refactoring kept apart from a bug fix. The kernel leaves the moved code wholly unmodified. The card follows the stricter kernel wording, so its validator counts a rename inside the moved block as an edit. Neither source addresses the lines the new location needs (package or module declaration, imports, caller references). The card assigns them to the move through both sources' requirement that the system builds and works after every change. On the same ground it assigns to the move the edits inside the block that the new location forces and no earlier change can make in place (a modifier the new location forbids, the indentation a new nesting depth requires). The topic's tangled-change studies (Herzig and Zeller, MSR 2013; Barnett et al., ICSE 2015; Di Biase et al., PeerJ CS 2019, DOI 10.7717/peerj-cs.193) are about mixed concerns in general, not moves, and are not cited.

The evidence is official documentation and source code from two toolchains (Go: go generate, go fix and its driver; Rust: cargo fix edition migrations) and the Java platform's Generated annotation. It shows that the go fix driver skips fixes that touch generated files, that cargo fix cannot reach code a build script generates, and that the fix goes to the generator or the build script. Only the go fix driver is documented to skip such fixes; gopls recognises the marker and warns when a generated file is edited (golang/tools gopls/internal/server/text_synchronization.go, "Warning: editing %s, a generated file."; "Warn the user that they are editing a generated file, but don't try to stop them: there are often good reasons to do so, such as adding temporary logging, or evaluating changes to the generated code without the trouble of modifying the generator logic") yet its rename has no generated-file check, so the Rationale says a rewriting tool can skip such fixes, not that every one does, and the Source caveat carries that narrowing. The driver logs skipped fixes only in verbose mode and go fix otherwise "silently updates your source files", so the card does not say the tool reports what it skipped. No empirical study measures the cost of hand-editing generated files, so the card makes no cost claim. It also does not say that hand edits are lost when the generator runs again, because no fetched source states that. The topic statement's "template or input" is narrowed to "the generator's logic" in the Thesis and Limits, because that is the sources' wording; template and input appear only in the Validator, as the finder's working reading of "the generator", and the Validator also accepts a regeneration shard whose generator change landed in an earlier shard of the same migration. check_kind is semantic because the finder traces the generator and its output before it can decide.

Obsolete tests related to the flag should also be deleted."; §2: "the flag needs to be disabled in the feature flag management system and all code artifacts related to the flag need to be removed from the source code … In practice, this simple post cleanup process is not always performed", plus the four costs of unnecessary paths (reliability via payload corruption, test-coverage effort, build and testing time, reasoning about obsolete control paths); §3: "the flag should have been rolled out 100% either as treatment or as control. Even when it is rolled out, the developer may still not be ready to eliminate the flag. For example, certain flags are used as kill switches … Therefore, even when flags are completely rolled out, they may not necessarily be stale" and the test-cleanup ambiguity; §4.2–4.3: "determining reachability in a sound and complete manner is infeasible [42]. This necessitates some form of manual intervention by the developer after the cleanup is performed by the tool" and the AST rewrite rules for checks, conditions, declarations, assignments, wrappers and @ExpTest tests; §5: "Piranha pipelines use a heuristic to consider flags that are unmodified in the flag management system for more than a specific period (e.g., 8 weeks) as stale and generate diffs for those flags. The exact time period for staleness of a flag is configured by the individual teams that process the diffs generated using Piranha."; related work: "standard dead-code elimination used in optimizing compilers [6, 25, 59] cannot remove them"; abstract: "generated code cleanup diffs for 1381 flags (17% of total flags), (b) 65% of the diffs landed without any changes, (c) over 85% of the generated diffs compile and pass tests successfully, (d) around 80% of the diffs affect more than one file" · topic: large-scale-changes-and-migrations (research/software-craft/large-scale-changes-and-migrations.md) · formulation: Paul Hammant, 'Branch by Abstraction', trunkbaseddevelopment.com, §'Ideal steps' 3–5 (fetched, https://raw.githubusercontent.com/paul-hammant/tbd/master/content/branch-by-abstraction/index.md) | Paul Hammant, 'Feature flags', trunkbaseddevelopment.com, §'Tech Debt - pitfall' (fetched, https://raw.githubusercontent.com/paul-hammant/tbd/master/content/feature-flags/index.md) · reception: not contested · notes: confidence moderate. The paper states the rule outright and backs it with deployment numbers, but it is one industrial experience report: one company's mobile apps in Objective-C, Java and Swift, and no controlled comparison. Following §3 and §5, the card separates a rollout (a value or rollout-share change with every lookup left in place) from a retirement, and flags only the latter. The card leaves out the outage's dollar figure because the paper gives two inconsistent versions (465M USD in 30 minutes in §1, more than 460M USD within 45 minutes in §2). It also leaves out the 17%-of-all-flags share, the 8-week staleness heuristic as a threshold, the deep-cleaning depth parameter and the ownership and assignment workflow, which are process and tool details. The flag-management-system step is kept only as a Limit, because it lies outside the source a reviewer reads. The Pete Hodgson martinfowler.com formulation was dropped because it cannot be opened from this environment and the openable Hammant pages and Piranha §1 carry the same formulation.

WebSearch was exhausted, so no further research was searched. Checkstyle's IllegalImport bans packages and classes, and a message element in the check's configuration sets its custom message; forbidigo bans Go identifiers with a per-pattern msg.

"We found that that (i) between 20% and 50% of SATD comments are accidentally removed while entire classes or methods are dropped, (ii) 8% of the SATD removal is acknowledged in commit messages, and (iii) while most of the changes addressing SATD require complex source code changes, very often SATD is addressed by specific changes to method calls or conditionals." · topic: technical-debt (research/software-craft/technical-debt.md) · formulation: Robert C. Martin, 'The Boy Scout Rule', 97 Things Every Programmer Should Know, en/thing_08/README.md (fetched): "Always check a module in cleaner than when you checked it out." · reception: not contested · notes: confidence moderate. Evidence scope: one review guideline (Google), one tool study with developer confirmation of superfluous on-hold markers (SCAM 2020), one mining study plus a 14-response survey (ICSME 2017, five open source projects), one in-depth study of five Java projects (MSR 2018); no study measures the cost of a stale marker, so the card claims no harm figure. The removal-in-the-same-change condition rests on the Google guideline ("comments that were there before this CL ... a TODO that can be removed now") and on the superfluous-marker definition; the "temporary code goes too" half rests on the hack-plus-comment definition and on the finding that addressing SATD is a code change. The card narrows the SCAM 2020 closed-issue test, whose own example (an open issue that must be closed before a function can be implemented) still leaves the function to write once the issue closes: a closed referenced issue removes the marker only when the closing ends the need for the covered temporary code or the change also does the deferred task; the stays-while-the-deferred-task-remains boundary rests on the tracking purpose in the MSR 2018 abstract (The purpose of such comments is to keep track of TD and appropriately address it when possible.), not on SCAM 2020. Not carried: the 20–50% accidental-removal and 8% commit-message figures (they describe how markers disappear, not when a paid one has to go); the ICSME 2017 conclusion's clause on dedicated code improvement activities (the paper's own tally at results.tex line 275 ranks improving the code overall level with adding a feature); the Clean Code ch. 4 'TODO Comments' and Refactoring 2nd ed. ch. 2 'Litter-Pickup Refactoring' formulations (both **unfetched**) are dropped because openable sources carry the same formulation (the Google guideline for the TODO wording, the Boy Scout essay for the cleanup wording).

(95159) · topic: technical-debt (research/software-craft/technical-debt.md) · formulation: the rust-clippy `todo` lint text quoted above (fetched) · reception: not contested; The Pragmatic Programmer, 20th anniversary ed., ch. 1 Topic 3 'Software Entropy' (**unfetched**) recommends 'boarding up' an unfixed problem, e.g. with a 'Not Implemented' message, as an interim measure. That is a stand-in for code left unfixed, which is different from merging functionality not yet written. The rust-clippy maintainers file `todo` as an opt-in restriction that may flag reasonable code. · notes: confidence moderate. The rule rests on official documentation for two languages (Rust, Python) and one linter. The card carries their statement over to an equivalent throw or panic whose message says not (yet) implemented in Java, TypeScript and Go, and says so in a Source caveat. No empirical study of the cost was reachable in this run because the WebSearch budget was used up. None of the relayed studies of self-admitted technical debt or broken windows states a claim about run-time placeholders, so the card carries no number: the evidence gives none. An abstract member and a member left deliberately unimplemented (clippy's 'explicitly unimplemented', Python's 'leave undefined') are in Limits because the documentation treats them as legitimate. A deliberate omission is recognised by a comment or message that states why the member is left out, as in Rust's `unimplemented!` example. A bare 'not implemented' message does not count, because TypeScript's generated stub for a member still to be written carries exactly that message. Test code is out of scope because clippy's statement is limited to production code. Severity is major because the evidence states that the placeholder always halts when reached.

(the same sentence is the epigraph of §4 of the fetched ISSTA 2000 paper) — and section 'Lessons Learned' — "Reducing failure-inducing inputs to a minimum is helpful for testing and debugging"; "Precisely specifying failure conditions helps to avoid false diagnoses." · reception: not contested · notes: confidence high for the mechanism (one peer-reviewed paper fetched in full whose authors recommend that automated test-case simplification be part of automated testing; the Go toolchain writes the minimized failing input as the regression test); moderate for the numbers' generality (a single 2000-era browser case study); the TSE 2002 paper is relayed only and could not be re-searched (WebSearch budget exhausted), and the card does not rest on it because the fetched ISSTA 2000 text states the same claim; the card does not carry history bisection, the regression test's assertions, timing-sensitive or concurrency failures, or cross-service failures.

Fix the problem, not the symptom"); 'Fixing the Bug': 'Checking Diagnoses' (causality and incorrectness) · reception: not contested · notes: confidence moderate. The direct evidence for bypassing a failure is the several occurrences the paper observed, shown in one task (a 2,403-LOC Java Tetris) given to graduate students; the paper's 'preliminary observation' (Observation 1) is the tool conclusion it draws from them, and the paper calls the study as a whole preliminary (abstract, line 8: "we perform a preliminary study"; §1, line 39: "although the results of our study are still preliminary"). The OS study measures how often fixes are incorrect and how little the fixers knew the code, not how many incorrect fixes were symptom patches, and the card does not claim that link. Special-casing the exposing input and suppressing the raised error are carried as instances of the paper's 'stop the failure from occurring without actually fixing the fault'; no reachable source observes them separately. The card leaves out the diagnosis half 'why the code there is wrong' (the incorrectness check), which comes only from the practitioner formulation and had no reachable research fragment. Also left out: Parnin and Orso's tool findings (only traditional-debugging participants bypassed the failure; the ranking tool helped only experienced developers on the simpler task), since the rule is not about tools. The 39% concurrency figure appears only to mark concurrency as out of scope.

Kernighan and Pike (PoP §5.3) and McConnell (CC §8.6) keep self-checking and diagnostic code in the source behind a debugging option, and the Rust std dbg! documentation tolerates the macro in tests and in version control for short periods. The card separates the cases by what the output is: ad hoc observation output is removed, command-line and user-facing console output stays, and lasting diagnostics stay through the logging facility (Ruff T201, ESLint no-console, Rust std dbg!, PMD SystemPrintln) · notes: confidence high for the convention, since seven tool rules across five languages and one official language document agree. The evidence class is tool rules plus official documentation, and no study measures how often a remnant leaks data or what it costs. The command-line exemption rests on Ruff and ESLint only; Error Prone SystemOut carries none, and ESLint's console rule is written for browser code. PoP and CC reach this corpus only through third-party transcriptions and serve as the formulation, not the evidence. Beller et al., ICSE 2018 (relayed: 'printf debugging remains a feasible choice for many programmers') is left out because it does not state the removal claim. Debugger and breakpoint statements (ESLint no-debugger, Ruff T100) fall outside this card's title and are not carried. The deliberate-logging side's levels and contents belong to the logging topic

The two triggers together match the documented focus forms, including fit.each, describe.only.each, test.only.failing, fit.failing, test.concurrent.only.each, FDescribeTableSubtree, and package-qualified Ginkgo nodes and decorators such as g.FIt and g.Focus.

Eight fetched sources back it (a standard, official language FAQ, three organization style guides, a lint's documentation), plus one relayed paper. The evidence sets no numeric share of run time or memory that makes code a hot spot, so the card relies on 'hot spots', 'hot path' and 'realistic benchmark' and adds no percentage. The 97%/3% figures are the paper's own rough estimate ('say about'). The requirement that the change name its measurement rests on Per.6's 'Don't make claims about performance without measurements' and turns the Go guide's 'accompanying commentary that explains the rationale' and clippy's 'having done the measurement' into something a reviewer can check (moderate). The Limits sentences that exclude correctness-serving caches and checks, and that name the low-latency and parallelization specialties, set the rule's scope and are not drawn from a source. The profiler-accuracy and measurement-bias papers (DOI 10.1145/1806596.1806618, DOI 10.1145/3617651.3622985, ASPLOS 2009, OOPSLA 2007) are left to the benchmarking and profiling rules of this topic. The perflint, PMD and SpotBugs rule texts were not needed: the Uber hot-path sentence covers guideline- and lint-suggested rewrites.

Fowler's Refactoring says to refactor for clarity first and tune afterwards. Google Go Style Decisions, on passing a value or a pointer, puts readability and correctness first "in most circumstances", and the Uber Go Style Guide limits performance guidelines to the hot path. The Google Go Style Guide treats complexity added for performance as a clue that the code is performance-critical, which should influence the care taken in later changes, and the Abseil performance hints say a microbenchmark that covers the code can help prevent future performance regressions. What separates the two sides is whether the code being restructured is marked as performance-critical · notes: confidence moderate. The evidence is official project guidance (Google Go, Abseil C++, Uber Go, and the Go project's contribution guide and benchstat documentation). No controlled study of regressions caused by refactoring performance-critical code was found. The card leaves out the measured 3-4x slowdown after a single loop was split into two methods, because its only source is a practitioner dialogue, so it is kept here as formulation. The "records in the change description" step rests on the Go contribution guide, whose condition is "if the change affects performance". The card applies it to every restructuring of marked code, since that is the change whose effect on performance is in question. Cache-line, lock-free and garbage-collector tuning is not carried.

the evidence gives no numeric k at which a full sort overtakes heap-based selection, so the card says "smaller k" / "larger k" as the source does and the validator flags only a literal constant prefix or suffix that the hunk does not show to approach the collection's size; an in-place sort of a parameter, a field, a value returned or passed on, or a local that a later line of the function reads in order is outside the rule, and the card's scope is file so the finder can read those later lines; the card does not recommend linear-time partial selection (nth-element style reordering) on its own and admits it only as the standard library's selection function in the fix, nor language-specific tie-breaking order, nor any claim about when the difference matters at the observed size, which is left to measurement

Entries sourced only from a version-control repository, a URL or a local path, with no registry version, are outside the rule, following the lint's registry-only check, the Cargo path-dependency text, cargo metadata's "*" for an entry without a version requirement, and pip's URL-based form; an entry that pairs such a location with a registry version is checked on that version, which the published package carries (Cargo 'Multiple locations'); an entry whose requirement is declared elsewhere (a workspace root, a platform or bill of materials, a dependency constraint or a constraints file) is read at that declaration, following the Cargo workspace text and the Gradle, Maven and pip texts cited above. The card does not carry the drafted sentence that Go's require directive and Maven's version element always name a version so the defect arises only in npm, Python, Cargo and Gradle manifests: the Go half is kept, generalized, as a Limit; the Maven half is unsourced (Maven accepts open version ranges) and is dropped; the Gradle '+' and 'latest.release' forms rest on the Gradle User Manual's definitions cited above. The SEG ch. 18 formulation leans toward explicitly pinned versions; the card keeps the narrower lower-bound claim the documentation states and leaves exact pinning and reproducible resolution to the lock-file rule. The Example shows one manifest line per trigger form (Cargo.toml, package.json, build.gradle, pyproject.toml) as Rust comments beside a call to an API introduced in a later release; its good half compiled with rustc 1.97.0 --edition 2021 --emit=metadata inside a stub module scope.

The defect is a lock that disagrees with the manifest after the change, not a lock the change left unedited. Cargo keeps a locked version "if it can" and drops the entry only when it no longer matches the requirement, so an unchanged lock that still agrees is not a finding. The evidence covers npm, Yarn (through OWASP), Go, Cargo and uv, and the card carries a one-line caveat saying so. uv's documentation carries the rule for Python, including a re-constraint the locked version still satisfies; Java's lock tools are not cited. The Cargo book source now lives under doc/book/src/; a blobless clone's tree listing found it, and the old src/doc/src paths answer 404. The trigger pre-pass sees only added lines, so an edit that only removes a dependency is caught at implement, not at review. The card does not say whether a project should commit a lock at all, and it leaves out npm-ci's note that install flags shaping the tree must be repeated at a frozen install. The formulation's Bazel hash manifest is used for wording only.

The evidence covers the npm and PyPI registries only; the cheat sheet reports that typosquatting has also been seen on PyPI. The card leaves out the cheat sheet's npm-specific mechanisms (install-time run-scripts, process.env access) because they do not hold in every ecosystem. It also leaves out registry-side defences, dependency confusion and artifact signing or checksum verification, which belong to supply-chain design, and the cheat sheet's CI-check advice, which is process.
